# C01 dossier: "Progressive for Turbines" (P036, idea 5), a condition-priced, insurer-backed independent LTSA

Date: 2026-10-18. About 55 searches and fetches. Tags: [S] sourced, [D] my arithmetic on sourced inputs, [A] assumption. Where a page would not load and I relied on a search-result summary, I say so.

## 1. Bottom line

**Verdict: wounded to dead as specified. Overall 3/10, upside 3/10.** The budget line is real and buyers do run competitive RFPs for exactly this contract. But the product (a fixed-fee, multi-year parts-plus-outage agreement from a non-OEM) is already sold, and won, by funded independents. The two things the idea adds, condition pricing and an insurer wrap, have no demand evidence and no insurer evidence. The gate's arithmetic (25-35 units = 3-5% of 600-800 units) uses the wrong denominator. Corrected, $100M needs roughly 8-22% of the units a new entrant can plausibly reach. That is at or past the "heroic share" line in lessons.md.

Five findings drive this:
1. The independent LTSA already exists and just won a municipal RFP against GE (section 4).
2. Only about a quarter of GE's installed base is under LTSA, so the "takeout of expiring OEM LTSAs" pool is small (section 3).
3. The 10-20% discount the idea promises is mostly available from non-OEM parts, not from condition pricing (section 6).
4. Buyers demand bonds and references a start-up cannot show (section 5).
5. No insurer product for gas-turbine parts-cost cover turned up, and standard property cover excludes wear and tear (section 7).

## 2. Assumption ledger (the upside case, tested)

| Claim in idea / gate | What I found | Status |
|---|---|---|
| "No condition-priced, reinsurer-backed F-class offer exists" | True as far as I can find, but nobody asks for it either. Austin's 2026 RFP bundled rotor end-of-life assessment and optional remote monitoring into a fixed quarterly fee, so buyers already get a condition element from independents (section 4). | Gap exists, demand unproven |
| "Only OEMs offer F-class LTSAs" (idea) | False. Third-party F-class term deals date from 2007 (NYPA), 2011 (AECI), 2015 (MEAG); Hanwha Power won Austin's 7FA deal in 2026. | Refuted |
| "~1,100 US baseload F-class units" (idea) or "600-800 addressable" (gate) | GE says 960+ 7F-family units worldwide. A 2008 CCJ report put ~700 operating in North America. Addressable for this product is far smaller (section 3). | Refuted |
| "OEM cannot price on condition (adverse selection)" | Plausible but untested. GE can discount selectively, and its LTSA book is only ~26% of its fleet, so it prices most of the fleet transactionally anyway. | Unproven |
| "10-20% under OEM for top-quartile units" | Chromalloy says non-OEM parts save "thirty or more percent" vs OEM list. Any independent can deliver this without a condition model. | Real saving, wrong source |
| "Reinsurer parts-cost excess-of-loss" | Nothing found for gas turbines. The one precedent is Munich Re's 2012 wind serial-loss cover. | Unproven |
| "Real buyer is the lender's independent engineer" | No source found. The documented buyer is the owner's procurement office via RFP (Austin). | Unsupported |
| "Share isn't the problem" | It is, once the denominator is corrected. | Refuted |

## 3. Market and bottom-up

Metrics this industry runs on: LTSA fee per unit-year, share of fleet under LTSA, equivalent operating hours (EOH) and starts to the next inspection, service gross margin, and forced-outage cost.

**Top down.** GMI sizes services at $27.1B (2025) and $4.5B in the US (pool file: https://www.gminsights.com/industry-analysis/gas-turbine-service-market). Parts are 68% of F-class aftermarket spend, repair 18%, field service 14% (https://www.turbomachinerymag.com/view/aftermarket-parts-is-there-life-after-the-oem). GE Vernova's Power EBITDA margin was 18.8% in Q2 2026 (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001996810/000199681026000147/gevpressrelease2q26.htm).

**The LTSA book is a minority of the fleet.** GE Vernova's FY2025 10-K: "a gas turbine installed base of approximately 7,000 units with approximately 1,800 units under long-term service agreements and an average remaining contract life of approximately 10 years" (https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1996810/000199681026000015/gev-20251231.htm) [S]. So about 26% of units are on LTSAs, and the book is long-dated. This undercuts the "free forensic audit of expiring LTSAs" door. The older roll-off wave was a 2009-2012 story: a 2009 article said ~70% of turbines had been under OEM agreements and predicted more than half would not renew by 2011 (https://www.power-eng.com/environmental-emissions/turbine-maintenance-market-heats-up/). Most units today buy transactionally (parts and outage events), a different and smaller-ticket product.

**US F-class base.** GE reports 960+ 7F units worldwide (https://gevernova.com/gas-power/resources/articles/2020/7f-30-years-of-performance-reliability). CCJ reported ~700 operating in North America in 2008 (https://www.ccj-online.com/7f-users-group-a-really-big-show/). I found no US count for Siemens or Mitsubishi F-class. My estimate of the whole US F-class base across OEMs: 900-1,100 [A].

**Addressable units [D/A].**
- Big fleets with scale or in-house programs: per a search-result summary of the 7F Users Group steering committee page (https://na.eventscloud.com/website/89691/steering-committee/; the page itself would not show the list), FPL runs 52 units, Southern 39, Calpine 34, Dominion 19, Xcel 16. That is 160 units from five owners. Adding Vistra, NRG, Constellation, Duke, LS Power and Talen, I assume 40-50% of units sit in about 15 fleets.
- Subtract units already on long OEM LTSAs (~26% [S, GE] applied to the rest) and units under about 10 years old, where independents advise using OEM parts.
- Result: about 150-300 US units a new entrant could realistically contract in 5-7 years. This is a wide estimate, and the first thing a 20-call primary study should fix.

**Fee per unit-year.**
- NYPA's 2007 independent term agreement was $88M over 16 years for two 7FA+e units (https://www.investegate.co.uk/announcement/prn/wood-group-john---wg./re-contract/1189062) = ~$2.75M per unit-year nominal [D]. At 3% a year that is ~$4.8M in 2026 dollars [A].
- Cross-check: EIA's contractor study gives $3.41/MWh variable O&M (2023$) for a 1,227 MW H-class combined cycle (https://www.eia.gov/analysis/studies/powerplants/capitalcost/pdf/capital_cost_AEO2025.pdf). For a ~230 MW F-class unit at 55% capacity factor that is ~$3.8M a year [D/A], and it includes some non-turbine items.
- So $3-5M is sound.

**Path to $100M.** 25-35 units x $3-4M = $100M of gross fees [D]. That is 8-22% of 150-300 addressable units. Most of that revenue is pass-through parts. At 12-18% gross margin (gate assumption), $100M of fees yields $12-18M of gross profit before insurance premium, capital and overhead. A realistic ramp is 1-3 contracts a year after a 2-year build: roughly 8-15 units and $25-60M of fees by year 7 [A]. The visible independent record supports a slow ramp: the press-announced US F-class independent term deals I found are NYPA (2007), AECI (2011), MEAG (2015) and Austin (2026), though many contracts go unannounced.

## 4. Competitors (confirmed, refuted, added)

| Player | Evidence | Read |
|---|---|---|
| GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi | GE: 7,000 units, 1,800 on LTSA; company RPO ~$94.4B; "higher volume and favorable price" at Gas Power (links above). | Incumbent with pricing power now |
| Hanwha Power (PSM + Hanwha Power Systems, merged March 2026) | LTA, LTMA and Frame Agreement tiers, "full-scope or modular pricing," does not require buying all parts from it (https://www.psm.com/services/service-agreements). LTA business since 2007; 9-year "subscription" LTSA at Trumbull, 950 MW, June 2026 (https://www.turbomachinerymag.com/view/hanwha-power-commissions-fuel-gas-compressors-at-ohio-ccgt-plant). Hanwha Group parent. | Direct competitor with balance sheet |
| Wood Group GTS / PW Power Systems | NYPA, AECI, MEAG deals above. | Direct, older wins |
| EthosEnergy | ~3,600 staff; Wood sold its stake for $138M; $34M adjusted EBITDA for 2023 (https://www.woodplc.com/news/latest-press-releases/2025/wood-completes-sale-of-ethosenergy-for-$138-million). One Equity Partners owns it. | PE-backed |
| Allied Power Group | Owned by Warren Equity Partners (not AEA, as the idea said): https://www.rwbaird.com/transactions/investment-banking/dealcard/6793/. Bought EthosEnergy's generator assets, April 2026. | PE-backed |
| MD&A, Sulzer, Chromalloy | MD&A bid at Austin. Sulzer Services: CHF 1.31B sales, 18.3% EBITDA margin, 39.6% gross margin on orders, 2025 (https://report.sulzer.com/ar25/en/business-review-services). | Repair and parts side |
| Advisers (free or cheap substitute) | IEM Energy Consultants and Mercer Thompson ran a 7F Users Group session on re-thinking LTSAs (https://www.ccj-online.com/7fug-2020-mercer-thompson-llc-iem-energy-consultants/); Troutman says it has structured LTSAs for 200+ gas turbines (https://www.troutman.com/images/content/4/7/v1/4795/LTSAPDF.pdf). | The "free audit" is a commodity |
| In-house teams | Big fleets self-manage; one owner with 24+ 7FAs standardized its own practices (CCJ 2008 above). | Removes the best customers |
| Funded start-ups | None found for turbine LTSA or parts. Nearest are monitoring firms such as Novity (compressors, Tokyo Gas investment). | Open, but for a reason |

**The best single piece of evidence: Austin Energy RFP 1100 MMH3038** (Sand Hill Unit 5, 7FA+e and D-11 steam turbine; published 2026-02-16, award recommended 2026-07-29).
- Scope: quarterly fixed payments for 9 years plus two optional 3-year extensions, contract parts pricing, rotor end-of-life assessment or exchange, optional remote monitoring (https://assets.austintexas.gov/financeonline/downloads/vc_files/RFP_1100_MMH3038/RFP_1100_MMH3038_0600_v1.pdf).
- Bidders: Allied, GE Vernova, Hanwha, MD&A (https://financeonline.austintexas.gov/afo/account_services/solicitation/solicitation_details.cfm?sid=142784).
- Scores out of 100: Hanwha 61, MD&A 30, Allied 29, GE 20 (https://assets.austintexas.gov/financeonline/downloads/vc_files/RFP_1100_MMH3038/RFP_1100_MMH3038_RESPONSE_v2.pdf). Price points out of 25: Allied 25, MD&A 16, Hanwha 11, GE 7. Experience points out of 25: Hanwha 25, others 4.
- Reading: three independents bid and one won. If price points scale with the low bid (formula not disclosed), GE priced about 3.6x the lowest and Hanwha about 2.3x, yet Hanwha won on experience. Buyers pay for proven 7FA+e work, not for novelty.

## 5. Demand and willingness to pay

- **Budget line and signer exist.** Austin's RFP shows a municipal utility procuring this as an O&M contract.
- **Availability has a price.** In Winter Storm Elliott, ~$1.8B of PJM non-performance charges were assessed (settled near $1.2B), gas plants were ~70% of unplanned outages, and charges were 83% of the capacity payments of the penalized resources (https://www.utilitydive.com/news/pjm-winter-storm-elliott-report-gas-generation/688217/; settlement: https://www.publicpower.org/periodical/article/ferc-approves-winter-storm-elliott-settlement-agreement). That supports an availability guarantee, but the owner would need the guarantee to cover market penalties, not just repair costs.
- **Contract literature flags the OEM structure as owner-unfriendly.** LTSAs are treated as non-terminable except for breach (https://www.power-eng.com/gas/turbines/gas-turbineslong-term-service-agreementstop-10-contractual-pitfalls-and-how-to-avoid-them-ndash-part-ii/), and title to the remaining life of parts bought under the contract can revert to the OEM (https://www.turbomachinerymag.com/view/servicing-the-aftermarket). I found no owner-versus-OEM dispute over EOH formulas. A JEA procurement spec (surfaced in search; the page would not load) reportedly requires EOH formula disclosure and lets the owner shift intervals by 10%, which suggests informed owners can already extract transparency.
- **Barriers a start-up cannot clear.** Austin requires a payment bond and a performance bond, each 100% of the annual contract with a $10M minimum, and five references each for similar maintenance, parts supplied and monitoring in the last five years (RFP link above). A new entrant would likely score near 4/25 on experience, as three of the four bidders did.
- **Not found:** any RFP or contract that prices on measured condition, or any owner statement that it would pay for it.

## 6. Unit economics and capital

- Selling at 85-90% of the OEM price [A, gate range 10-20% under]. Sourcing cost under independent parts: parts 68% of spend at ~70% of OEM price (Chromalloy's "thirty or more percent" saving), repair 18% at ~85%, field service 14% at ~100% [A]. That is a cost of ~77% of OEM price, leaving ~12% gross margin before reinsurance, condition-model cost and bonding [D]. Margin comes from parts substitution, which every independent has.
- Price versus value (lesson 5): the customer's saving is $0.3-1M per unit-year on a $3-5M fee [D]. A reinsurance premium has to come out of that same slice.
- Capital: a 10-year fixed-price obligation across 30 units is $300M+ of contingent liability [D]. Bonding, parent guarantees or letters of credit, plus a risk-capital facility, come first (Austin's bond terms above; JEA's credit appendix allows a guarantor: https://www.jea.com/About/Procurement/Formal_Procurement_Opportunities/1411846048_Appendix_G_-_Credit_Requirements).
- Even the OEM warns that LTSA profitability "depends on our ability to execute and estimates of product durability" (GE 10-K above). Sulzer's H1 2026 report, per a search summary, noted customers deferring service cycles on high energy prices.
- Supply: independents' backlogs run into fall 2026, OEM component quotes went from ~4 to 12-16 weeks (vendor claims: https://blog.psm.com/blog/spring-2026-outage-season-why-this-year-is-different), rotor queues fill into 2028-29 (https://www.ccj-online.com/hanwha-power-and-the-new-value-of-the-installed-fleet/). A wrapper without shop capacity depends on the same constrained suppliers.

## 7. Regulatory and liability

- **Insurance classification.** Courts and attorneys general ask whether risk transfer is the "principal object and purpose" or incidental to a service; the label does not control (Kansas AG opinion: https://ksag.washburnlaw.edu/opinions/1980/1980-008.pdf; New Mexico AG: https://nmonesource.com/nmos/ag/en/14625/1/document.do; both via search summaries). A fixed-price O&M contract with a service principal-object is the safer side, but a standalone "cap on parts cost" sold to owners is the home-value-guarantee pattern that killed a round-1 finalist. It needs a licensed fronting carrier, state by state.
- **Insurer appetite.** Wear and tear is generally excluded from property policies, and insurers pay only resulting damage (https://www.powermag.com/forced-outage-parametric-insurance-solutions-for-ccgts, by three Aon consultants). The same piece says an OEM LTSA is "viewed favorably" by insurers, a point against an independent. FM reports 427 power-generation losses and ~$3.7B gross over 2021-2025, with gas turbines the largest single source of property damage (https://insurance-canada.ca/2026/07/31/fm-power-risks-electricity-demand-soars/). I could not confirm a separate figure of 52 gas-turbine events and $540M that appeared in one summary, so I do not use it.
- **Precedent.** Munich Re's 2012 serial-loss cover for REpower took a broker two years and a survey of the manufacturer's production (https://www.munichre.com/en/company/media-relations/media-information-and-corporate-news/media-information/2012/2012-12-04-munich-re-insures-serial-loss-risk-on-offshore-wind-turbines.html). It shows component-level cover is possible, but it was sold to the manufacturer of a new, uniform product, not to an integrator of mixed 20-year-old frames.
- **IP and warranty.** Independents face OEM IP and warranty limits on newer designs (Chromalloy advice above). I found no 2025-26 GE suit against independent F-class parts.

## 8. Why now: real, partly used up

Real: GE's equipment backlog plus reservations rose to 116 GW (release above). Casting is the stubborn constraint, and GE Aerospace's $11.75B CPP deal is expected to close in 2H 2027 (https://www.turbomachinerymag.com/view/ge-aerospace-cpp-acquisition-spacex-turbine-blade-foundry). PJM capacity cleared at the cap for 2028/29, and FERC extended the collar through 2029/30 only (https://insidelines.pjm.com/ferc-approves-capacity-auction-price-collar-to-next-two-capacity-auctions/).

Not as strong as pitched: scarcity squeezes independents' casting supply and shop slots as much as the OEM's. The LTSA roll-off wave is old news, and the capacity-price cliff after 2029/30 falls inside the 10-year contract term.

## 9. Verdict and cheapest decisive test

Defensible and big cannot both hold here, so I call the specified business dead rather than narrow it. Gate ceiling of ~$70M (range $40-110M) is too high; I put the 5-7 year fee ceiling at $25-60M with $3-10M gross profit [D/A].

Only unvalidated variant with scale economics: a capital-light underwriting layer (parts-cost cover sold through ISPs), where revenue is premium, not pass-through parts. No evidence yet that a carrier will write it.

Kill tests, in order: (1) two reinsurers decline or price parts-cost cover above the saving; (2) a surety will not bond a start-up for $10M+ annual contracts; (3) three or more of five audited owners already hold an independent bid within ~10% of the OEM price; (4) measured saving under ~8% (gate threshold).

Open gaps: US F-class unit count by OEM and owner (needs the EIA-860 generator file and model data); actual LTSA fee distribution; whether any carrier has quoted this; independents' US win count. Allied/Hanwha revenues were not found.

# C05 Dossier: The Non-GE Foundry (P079, Dilemma 1)

Prepared 2026-10-18. Convention: "[unopened]" marks a figure taken from a search-result summary whose page I did not open. "(my arithmetic)" marks a derived number. Everything else I read in the cited source.

## 1. Verdict

**Dead as a founder-led startup. At best it is a capital-allocation bet for infrastructure or PE money.** Four findings decide it:

1. **The "gap" is a listed company's sales pitch.** Doncasters' June 2026 IPO prospectus says it is "currently the only competitor able to provide Aerospace and IGT OEMs with dedicated capacity" and describes four signed partnerships with customer-funded capex, capacity reservation payments and guaranteed volumes ([424B4](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2107018/000110465926077968/tm269965-19_424b4.htm)). Customer funding covers "up to 80%" of capital investment. That is this idea's business model, already operating at a qualified incumbent.
2. **The "lost neutral supplier" premise is mostly false.** See section 2.
3. **The economics need the customer to fund most of the plant, and customers already do that for incumbents.** An independent caster earns roughly 18-22% EBITDA margins (Doncasters), not Howmet's 37.7%.
4. **Timing and cycle.** A plant started in 2027 produces after Howmet's August 2028 capacity wave and Doncasters' 2028-29 ramp, and Wood Mackenzie expects turbine orders to peak in 2026.

## 2. Premise test: did non-captive buyers lose a neutral supplier?

- **The deal is real.** GE Aerospace agreed on 2026-09-08 to buy CPP for $11.75B, about 18x 2027 EBITDA with synergies and about 26x without, closing 2H 2027. CPP has about $2.0B of 2027E revenue, about 6,600 staff and more than 20 facilities ([GE deck](https://www.geaerospace.com/sites/default/files/GEAerospace_to_acquire_Consolidated_Precision_Products_Presentation.pdf)).
- **Only about 20% of CPP is "power and other."** CPP's mix is about 60% commercial aerospace, 20% defense and 20% power and other, so power is roughly $400M (same deck, my arithmetic). The deck cites Avio Aero, Unison and Dowty as a "proven model" that "serves external customers." Press reports say GE will run CPP as a separate unit and keep working with Howmet and ATI ([Leeham](https://leehamnews.com/2026/09/09/ge-aerospace-moves-to-secure-critical-engine-casting-capacity/)). Culp calls the shortage "much more a supply-side challenge" than a demand one (same source).
- **GE Vernova is not GE Aerospace.** The largest gas-turbine maker files separately ([GE Vernova Q2 release](https://www.gevernova.com/news/press-releases/ge-vernova-reports-second-quarter-2026-financial-results-raises-2026-financial)). GE Aerospace does not build heavy-duty gas turbines, so IGT makers do not face a rival-owned supplier. Only the aeroengine OEMs (Pratt, Rolls-Royce, Honeywell) are exposed, and they have other routes.
- **Neutral capacity exists and is spoken for.** Howmet holds over 50% of global IGT blade share and says it has "completed negotiations with the last of our 7 major customers" ([Q2 call](https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/08/13/howmet-aerospace-hwm-q2-2026-earnings-call-transcript/)). Siemens Energy signed a $1B+ multi-year deal with Doncasters in Aug 2023 ([Doncasters](https://www.doncasters.com/news/contract-worth-over-1-billion-usd-signed-with-siemens-energy)). Doncasters lists Ansaldo, Doosan, GE Vernova, Siemens Energy, Honeywell, Pratt, Rolls-Royce, Safran and GE as customers (424B4).
- **The real squeeze is slower.** GE expects its airfoil demand to grow over 30% from 2026E to 2030F (GE deck), and CPP supplies about a quarter of GE's needs ([Reuters analysis](https://www.globalbankingandfinance.com/analysis-ge-aerospace-bets-black-art-casting-secure-jet/)). Allocation inside CPP will drift toward GE after a 2H 2027 close, and AlixPartners expects GE to be required to divest some facilities (same Reuters piece). One analyst said it "remained to be seen" whether non-GE customers are affected.

## 3. Competitor map (confirmed, refuted, new)

**Scaled independents.** Doncasters' prospectus counts four globally scaled manufacturers: Howmet, PCC, CPP and itself (424B4). Trade press says only "three or four foundries worldwide" can cast hot-section blades and vanes ([Turbomachinery](https://www.turbomachinerymag.com/view/ge-aerospace-cpp-acquisition-spacex-turbine-blade-foundry)).
- **Howmet**: Q2 2026 revenue $2.55B, Engine Products $1.37B at 37.7% segment EBITDA margin, gas turbines $321M (+38%), 2026 capex above $500M and rising in 2027 ([Q2 release](https://www.howmet.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2026/08/Howmet-Aerospace-Reports-Second-Quarter-2026-Results.pdf); [10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000004281/000000428126000025/hwm-20260630.htm)). Its CFO says "Investments are backed by customer contracts." A commitment made in August 2026 yields capacity around August 2028 (Q2 call).
- **Doncasters (DPC)**: FY25 revenue $837M, adjusted EBITDA $138M (16.5%), capex $31M, top-2 customers 38% of sales, 70% of revenue under LTAs (424B4). Four partnerships (two aero, two IGT) are expected to add more than $200M of annual revenue at full run rate. Three reach run rate in 2028; the greenfield superalloy plant starts production in 2029.
- **PCC (Berkshire)**: no public detail on airfoil capacity or customer terms found.
- **Chromalloy (Veritas)**: runs the Siemens-exclusive Tampa JV ($139M, 350 jobs, deliveries from 2018, [Foundry](https://foundrymag.com/molds-cores/article/21931673/chromalloysiemens-investment-casting-venture-slated-for-florida)). This is a 2017-era precedent for exactly this structure. It also announced a $16.5M Tampa expansion in May 2026 [unopened, [AIN](https://backend.ainonline.com/sites/default/files/article_export/rtf/Chromalloy_Plans_$16.5_Million_Tampa_Expansion-21-05-2026.rtf)].

**Captives (in-house teams).** Pratt's Asheville plant (at least $650M through 2027, [Foundry](https://www.foundrymag.com/molds-cores/article/21145965/engine-builder-plans-new-turbine-airfoil-plant-pratt-whitney)), Safran Rennes (about 200 staff, opens 2027, [Foundry](https://www.foundrymag.com/melt-pour/article/21283776/engine-builder-plans-investment-casting-foundry-safran-aircraft-engines)), Rolls-Royce Rotherham (about £19-21M to double blade output by 2030 [unopened, [The Manufacturer](https://www.themanufacturer.com/articles/rolls-royce-invests-21-3m-to-double-turbine-blade-output-at-rotherham-facility/)]), SpaceX Bastrop (blades and vanes foundry; jobs posted April 2026, [Foundry Magazine](https://www.foundrymag.com/issues-and-ideas/article/55401710/ive-got-a-job-for-you-editors-note-september-2026)). GE Vernova advertised a "Supplier Capacity Leader, Investment Castings" role in Jan 2026 (search snippet; the posting page now returns 404). Hadrian is hiring casting engineers ([posting](https://jobs.buildsubmarines.com/jobs/538260256-lead-manufacturing-engineer-casting-special-projects-at-hadrian)). I found no Anduril casting source.

**PE roll-ups.** Pursuit Aerospace (owned by CD&R and Greenbriar, [CD&R](https://www.cdr.com/news/cdr-and-greenbriar-equity-complete-acquisitions-to-create-a-new-leading-supplier-to-the-aerospace-industry-called-pursuit-aerospace); $635M unitranche per [Golub](https://golubcapital.com/?p=1561) [unopened]) bought Creasey Castings on 2026-08-11, its sixth deal since 2023, and is expanding its Tunis nickel and cobalt investment-casting site to over 1,000 staff ([Pulse 2.0](https://pulse2.com/pursuit-aerospace-acquires-creasey-castings-and-expands-aerospace-casting-capacity/)). CPP is itself buying GF's Precicast (about 600 staff, CHF 220M cash proceeds, [GF](https://www.georgfischer.com/en/newsroom/media-releases/newsdetail.html/news/gf/2026/gf-signs-agreement-to-divest-aerospace-and-industrial-gas-turbine-operations-of-the-former-casting-solutions-division)).

**Startups.** Fabri has raised about $13.5M with RTX and Lockheed venture arms as investors and plans a second foundry for 2027 [unopened, [Tectonic](https://www.tectonicdefense.com/fabri-announces-its-raised-13-5m-for-new-age-casting/)]. Rangeview won a Kratos development contract on 2026-07-30 and holds a $1.43M Air Force SBIR Phase II ([Runtime Wire](https://runtimewire.com/article/rangeview-kratos-turbine-engine-superalloy-castings)). I found no seed or Series A for a turbine-casting startup.

**Free or public substitutes.** DoD casting and forging modernization money exists (a 2024 trade-group article described a $2B five-year initiative [unopened]), and OSC lends $10-150M for facilities with $97.8M of FY26 credit subsidy ([CRS](https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/IF13215.html) via search summary). I found no 2026 award or OSC loan for airfoil casting capacity.

## 4. Bottom-up market

- **IGT airfoil pool.** Howmet's gas-turbine sales annualize to about $1.28B (Q2 $321M x4, my arithmetic). At over 50% share, the pool is roughly $2.6B or less (rough, because Howmet's "gas turbines" line may include non-airfoil work). Doncasters' IGT sales are $351M (424B4). CPP's power and other is about $400M.
- **Aero pool.** Howmet Engine Products alone runs about $5.5B annualized (includes rolled rings). CPP adds about $1.6B of commercial and defense, Doncasters about $0.3B of aerospace. PCC is undisclosed. The relevant pool is therefore roughly $8-10B or more, not the $53.7B US metalcasting figure.
- **Payers.** About 7 major IGT OEMs (Howmet's own count) plus roughly 5-6 non-GE aeroengine makers. All hold LTAs with an incumbent.
- **Share.** One $100M plant is about 4% of the IGT pool or about 1% of the combined pool (my arithmetic). It would need 4-5 buyers at $20-25M a year each. Pool share is not the obstacle. Capital, qualification and incumbent contracts are.

## 5. Evidence of demand and willingness to pay

**Strong, but it flows to incumbents.**
- Doncasters: a 15-year aeroengine blade and vane deal with customer-funded capacity; a 7-year IGT extension with guaranteed volumes; a 9-year IGT extension for directionally solidified airfoils; three agreements underwriting a greenfield superalloy plant that starts production in 2029 (424B4).
- Siemens-Chromalloy dedicated JV (2017) and the Siemens-Doncasters $1B+ LTA, which Doncasters' CEO called "the backbone" of its capacity investment.
- GE Vernova's gas equipment backlog plus slot reservations hit 116 GW, 63 GW of it slot reservations, and it targets 20 GW of annual output in Q3 2026, 24 GW in 2028 and 30 GW in 2030 (Q2 release). Wood Mackenzie sees turbine prices near $600/kW by end-2027, with turbines 20-30% of combined-cycle cost, six-year lead times and 60-70 GW of global capacity against 110 GW of orders ([Power Engineering](https://www.power-eng.com/gas/turbines/gas-turbine-prices-climb-195-as-supply-crunch-reshapes-power-development/)). Castings are a small slice of a very expensive, delayed asset, so buyers can rationally pay to secure supply (my inference).

**Not found.** Any OEM prepayment, take-or-pay or capacity deposit to a new, unqualified entrant. Fabri's backers are equity investors. Rangeview's Kratos award is a development contract of undisclosed value. No source shows an OEM signing a 10-year take-or-pay with a plant that does not yet exist.

## 6. Unit economics and capital

- **Margins.** Doncasters' segment EBITDA margins are 18.2% (North America) and 21.9% (Europe). CPP's implied pre-synergy margin is about 22.6% ($11.75B / 26 = $452M on $2.0B, my arithmetic). Howmet's 37.7% reflects scale, alloy and process ownership.
- **Capex per plant.** Greenfield anchors: $139M for 350 jobs (2017 JV), $650M+ for Pratt's integrated Asheville, SpaceX Bastrop reported at about $280M in Texas records, per a search summary [unopened; the [aiweekly](https://aiweekly.co/alerts/spacex-lays-groundwork-for-bastrop-gas-turbine-blade-foundry) page I opened did not show it]. The idea's $150-300M per $100M of revenue is credible for greenfield. Brownfield expansion is far cheaper: Howmet Wichita Falls about $70M for 230 jobs and 100,000 sq ft ([Area Development](https://www.areadevelopment.com/newsItems/9-29-2026/howmet-aerospace-wichita-falls-texas.shtml)), Doncasters Bochum $52M, Auburn $50M (superalloy melt, 70 jobs). Incumbents hold the cheap option.
- **Illustrative plant (my arithmetic).** $100M revenue at 18-22% EBITDA is $18-22M. On $150-300M of capex that is a 6-15% yield and 7-17 years simple payback, with no ramp losses. If customers fund 80% (the Doncasters ceiling), founders' equity is $30-60M. Without customer money it does not clear a hurdle rate.
- **Valuation.** CPP is priced at 5.9x revenue. Doncasters' first-day close implied about $6.8B of market value ([Bloomberg Law](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/private-equity/doncasters-gains-33-after-1-06-billion-ipo-private-placements)), or about 8x sales and 49x FY25 adjusted EBITDA (my arithmetic), at the top of a cycle. A de novo plant lacks the qualified positions that earn those multiples. Precicast's sale (about CHF 0.37M of cash proceeds per employee, my arithmetic) is the more honest mid-size comparable, though its revenue is undisclosed.
- **Inputs and people.** Doncasters says vertical integration into superalloys and ceramic cores matters because external supply chains are "currently experiencing significant capacity constraints," and critical quality roles take 6-12 months to train (424B4). A.Y. McDonald's "nine-figure" foundry cited elsewhere in this pool is a brass foundry ([Foundry Planet](https://www.foundry-planet.com/d/usa-new-foundry-estimated-to-cost-more-than-100-million/)), so it is a weak anchor.

## 7. Regulatory, qualification and liability landscape

- **OEM approval is the gate.** Doncasters says OEM approvals are "often taking years to obtain." Typical credentials are AS9100, Nadcap for special processes and GE's S-1000 review [unopened summary, [Certivo](https://www.certivo.com/frameworks/ge-supplier-requirements-compliance)]. A 1995 GAO decision shows the OEM's testing defines an approved source for engine blades ([GAO](https://www.gao.gov/products/470676)).
- **Liability.** Recalls, customer penalties and product liability attach to flight-critical parts (424B4 risk factors). Scrap risk is high on new designs: "half or more" may be discarded (AeroDynamic Advisory, in the Reuters piece).
- **Antitrust.** GE-CPP faces review, with Avio Aero as the stated overlap (Reuters piece). No remedy has been reported. A forced divestiture would be sold to an approved buyer, which could create an acquisition nucleus, but regulators favor experienced operators.
- **Export controls.** Fabri advertises ITAR registration and CMMC Level 2 [unopened]. Defense parts need the same.
- **Tax and capital.** OBBBA allows 100% expensing of qualified production property if construction begins after 2025-01-19 and before 2029-01-01 and the property is in service before 2031-01-01 ([BDO](https://www.bdo.com/insights/tax/one-big-beautiful-bill-act-expands-100-depreciation-expensing-opportunities)). A build starting in 2027 and taking four years would likely miss the 2031 cutoff.
- **No rule forces this spend.** The shock is commercial. The DoW plan names castings as single points of failure but adds no dollars (per the P079 idea file; I did not open the plan).

## 8. Why-now check

The shortage is real: Rystad reports 100 GW of gas turbine and engine orders in 2025, 30% above what OEMs could deliver ([Rystad](https://www.rystadenergy.com/insights/gas-turbine-report-H2-2026)). But the window is closing. Howmet's August 2028 wave, Doncasters' 2028-29 ramp and Safran's 2027 plant all land first. Jefferies puts SpaceX's products about four years out [unopened]. Cycle risk is on the record: Wood Mackenzie expects turbine orders to peak in 2026, and 2025-26 trade coverage quotes Siemens Energy's CEO saying the industry "will remain cyclical" and Mitsubishi Power Americas' CEO expecting some orders will not materialize [unopened]. A Bloomberg report, via ECMag, says a third to a half of US data centers planned for 2026 may slip or be cancelled [unopened]. A 10-year take-or-pay signed in 2027 runs to 2037 or later, past the likely peak.

## 9. Do the upside-case assumptions hold?

| Assumption | Test | Result |
|---|---|---|
| One plant is about $100M of revenue | CPP and Doncasters revenue per employee is about $280-300k; JV and Rennes job counts imply $55-105M | Holds |
| Capex $150-300M per plant | $139M (2017), $280M (reported), $650M integrated | Holds for greenfield |
| Non-captive buyers lost a neutral supplier | Howmet, PCC and Doncasters remain; GE Vernova is separate; CPP is 20% power | Mostly fails |
| Buyers will prefund 10-year take-or-pay | Yes, at Doncasters (7-15 years, up to 80%); nothing for new entrants | Holds only for qualified incumbents |
| CPP's 5.9x revenue transfers to a new plant | Applies to qualified, installed positions | Fails |
| Margins comparable to CPP | Independents earn 18-22%, not 38% | Weak |
| Plant lands inside the shortage | Capacity arrives 2030-31 vs. Aug 2028 and 2028-29 | Fails |

## 10. What would change the call

- A signed take-or-pay or prepay from a turbine OEM to a non-incumbent (none found).
- A divested CPP plant package offered to an OEM-backed buyer after the antitrust review.
- Doncasters or Howmet publicly declining new partnerships (Doncasters says more are "under negotiation").
- A distressed qualified foundry available at roughly 1x revenue with an OEM willing to co-fund expansion. That is an acquisition, not a startup, and it competes with Pursuit, CPP and Doncasters.

## 11. Gaps

- Customer-by-customer mix of CPP (no named non-GE customers found beyond a Pratt & Whitney Canada plant purchase in older coverage).
- PCC economics, Chromalloy's JV results, and total hot-section market size (no analyst report opened).
- Exact OEM qualification duration for airfoils. Sources say "years," none gives a number.
- Bastrop cost and permits, GE Vernova supplier-capacity spending, and the DoW plan itself.
- Howmet's alleged remarks about avoiding a single-year peak. I could not confirm them in the Q2 call.

objections: CAPITAL AND UNIT ECONOMICS. The only version that reaches $100M of revenue needs about $0.7B of balance sheet and earns roughly its cost of capital. The dossier's own table shows break-even at about 78% utilization and about a 9% equity return even at 100%. That table leaves out staff, test crews, transport and install, bad debt, and warranty costs on stored units. The equity layer is about $210M, versus the $25-26M that Ayr and FluxCo have raised. Equity is also first-loss on price: a 10% mark-down on a $700M fleet is $70M, one-third of the equity. Wood Mackenzie data say power-transformer prices are up about 77% since 2019, so partial mean reversion is plausible. Rystad does not forecast a glut and says price direction is 'hard to predict', but it does say prices and lead times have stagnated. A fleet bought now is bought at or near the peak. The sale route is a 12-15% dealer spread, about $11-14M gross profit on $100M of sales. JCL, Maddox, Giga and Sunbelt Solomon already work that spread. Sunbelt Solomon has 42 locations and a private-credit-financed PE sale in progress. Of the 7 Powers, the only reachable one is cost of capital, and that belongs to infrastructure funds and PE roll-ups, not a startup. The per-utility spec approvals are separate per SKU and give little switching cost. Pre-mortem for 2028: slots bought in 2027 at peak pricing, delivery in 2028-29 into new OEM capacity, and a neocloud lessee in distress.

COUNTERPARTY AND DEMAND QUALITY. The fleet's marginal customer is the buyer who cannot get a direct OEM slot. That buyer is the speculative or neocloud tier, the same credit tier the market is now rationing. Data Center Knowledge reports operators turning away AI-cloud tenants even at 15-year leases with upfront cash. Bisnow puts neocloud debt at about 275-325 bp over investment grade. AlixPartners says two-thirds of the market expects distress within 18 months. Wood Mackenzie says only about 12% of the 1,066 GW requested is firm and about 17% likely, and it does not expect the visibility problem to resolve before 2028. The credit-worthy buyers already buy slots directly. Burns & McDonnell says developers buy slots 'sometimes without a specific project'. LS Electric has a $312M 525 kV contract for 2027-29. Roseville buys years ahead. The fleet's 'portfolio effect' assumes dropped projects are independent. They are correlated, because AI funding conditions hit every lessee together. Tariff rules also remove speculative demand: AEP Ohio's 85%/12-year requirement, Virginia's 14-year contracts and collateral from January 2027, and Texas SB 6. The fleet is left holding the downside of the same demand pool. PwC's Walcroft warns about stranded assets even on the buyer side.

SLOT ACCESS AND TIMING. The fleet needs the scarcest input from OEMs who allocate on forecast certainty and prefer 'framework agreements and high-volume commitments' (Rystad). Allied-origin capacity is being absorbed by multi-year contracts. Astor Enerji has $769M of US transformer contracts for 2026-28. LS Electric's contract delivers 2027-29. HD Hyundai is building a second Alabama plant due April 2027 that adds about 50% capacity. Hyosung is going past 250 units a year in Memphis by 2027. A newcomer with no frame agreement queues behind hyperscalers and incumbents. Units ordered now land in 2028-29, just as Hitachi Virginia (2H 2028), Siemens Charlotte (early 2027) and Eaton (2027) come online. Rystad says peak lead times 'could ease within the next 12 months' and expects almost 200 GVA of additions in 2026, most of it in the US. The '8-16 week' promise is beyond any sourced made-to-order claim (Giga 26 weeks, Ayr 40-72), so it is a stock sale. Time-to-power is mostly bounded by interconnection, not the transformer. PJM projects average over 3 years to an interconnection agreement plus about 4 more years to energize (secondary source), and Wesco's CEO calls power availability the main constraint. A stocked transformer shortens one leg of a longer chain.

REGULATORY TAIL RISKS SPECIFIC TO AN INVENTORY-HOLDING BUSINESS. (a) Anti-hoarding. The April 2026 DPA Section 303 determination calls US grid-equipment capacity 'dangerously limited'. The DPA's Section 102 hoarding ban covers accumulating designated scarce materials beyond reasonable business demand or for resale above prevailing prices. The government used it in the 2020 PPE shortage. I found no scarcity designation for transformers, so the trigger is not tripped. But a fleet that speculatively buys scarce slots to rent at a premium matches the statute's fact pattern, and the exposure is asymmetric. (b) EO 14420/14421. The DOE RFI closed Oct 9 and rules are due Dec 24, 2026. A DWT summary says DOE may not issue one comprehensive rule by then. The RFI asks how deep sub-tier tracing should go. Speculative stock, such as a Korean unit with a Chinese bushing or controller, cannot be certified before the definitions exist, and the order can reach installed equipment. (c) Tariffs. The Section 232 regime was restructured in April 2026, with a 15% rate 'through 2027' for certain grid equipment (whether transformers are in the annex is unconfirmed). Units landing in 2028-29 face an unknown duty, so the cost basis depends on a rule that has changed twice in eight months. (d) Utility customers. Public utilities must bid competitively. IOUs earn a return only on owned rate base, and I infer from that that a lease is a pass-through expense with no return. I could not confirm the lease treatment in sources. The lease market is therefore mostly developers, which loops back to objection 2.

THE SPEC-STANDARDIZATION PREMISE AND IDLE-TIME LIABILITY. The claim that 'about 80% of substation units are the same few designs' has no source. DOE calls large units very site-specific and impedance a particularly difficult parameter to standardize. PJM's spare-equipment philosophy says winding configuration and BIL must match, and DHS/EPRI flexible spares need close impedance and some transmission owners vetoed a common design. Flexible designs run heavier and cost more (one is about 12% heavier). Each combination of high side, low side, MVA, impedance and vector group is a separate SKU, so redeployment pools shrink to within-SKU, and the portfolio effect shrinks with them. A fleet is also idle inventory by design. Maddox's guide says a unit unenergized for 6 months or more needs a formal storage plan (written for distribution units under 69 kV). IEEE working-group minutes say some manufacturers permit dry-gas storage only up to about 6 months (the sentence is truncated). I found no evidence that OEM warranties toll during a fleet's storage. The seller carries early-failure and energization risk (HSB). Nobody has built a leased 30-100 MVA fixed fleet. The existing rental fleets I found are container-scale (Kontena 2.5-10 MVA) or temporary mobile substations. That absence more likely reflects the economics above than an unseen opening.

All of the following would have to hold. Items 1 to 3 are the dossier's own tests, and the others are additions.
1. Three or more utilities sign off in writing on one multi-ratio design, including impedance, BIL and bushing layout, with a purchase intent or reservation fee behind it.
2. An OEM commits slots at fixed prices with a buy-back or resale floor and tolls the warranty during storage. That addresses the first-loss price risk and the storage liability together.
3. An infrastructure lender prices the fleet non-recourse at more than 70% loan-to-value, and a real transformer lease comp shows a yield well above cost of capital. Today the only comp is aircraft engines at about 12.5%.
4. Creditworthy lessees (investment-grade parents or letters of credit) sign refundable-deposit reservations for fleet units. A documented RFP for stocked or leased 30-100 MVA units would also count. That would show demand beyond the neocloud tier.
5. Sunbelt Solomon, JCL or Giga turn out to be sold out of 30-100 MVA stock, with quoted waits. That would show unmet demand in the exact class.
6. DOE's December rules, or a federal purchase commitment, create a preferred category for stocked allied-origin units. Counsel confirms no Section 102 hoarding exposure, and the Section 232 duty on 2028-29 deliveries is known.
Without 1 to 3, this is a PE-style dealer and lessor roll-up with a thin spread, not a startup. I would reconsider as a financing play inside an incumbent such as Sunbelt Solomon, not as a new company."

objections: The 'nobody holds stock' gap is false, and the dossier understated it in the exact 30-100 MVA window. Maddox's own product page lists Powerclass substations up to 160 MVA at 69-230 kV and says common sizes are 'in stock and ready to ship'. The dossier called Maddox the same product at distribution scale, based on its cited installs of 1-2 MVA. Maddox is also adding storage yards (400 padmounts in Washington, 1,200 in Ohio). JCL Energy markets 'engineered substations' to 345 kV, same-week shipment, blanket POs, and lists a data-center campus order of eight units delivered in stages (from a search summary of its projects page). Giga Energy keeps stock in Long Beach and Houston, and is also a data-center developer, so it is customer and competitor at once. Sunbelt Solomon has a Quick Ship inventory including three-phase substation units (reconditioned), 42 locations, mobile-substation rental to 230 kV, and a page titled 'Don't Wait on the Utility - Power Your Data Center Now'. Delta Wye advertises ready-to-ship units up to 138 kV. Surplus Record already carries live 30/40/50 MVA listings from JCL and Belyea, plus a Prolec 30/40/50 MVA 34.5 kV listing: 'Three new units available in 2027'. That is slot flipping done by someone else. The fleet is a late entrant into a working secondary market, not a new category. It also holds fewer SKUs (about 280 units across a few specs) than these dealers' pooled stock across all specs.

Every incumbent can copy the only differentiated part (carrying stranded-project risk) at lower cost of capital, and the startup has no power under the 7 Powers test. Sunbelt Solomon is being bought by TJC with private-credit financing and already rents up to 230 kV and 50 MVA-plus. Adding a 30-100 MVA lease-to-own line needs no new customers, crews or sites. United Rentals (public, cheap capital) sells mobile units up to 138,000 kVA with data-center bridge-power guidance (403 on direct fetch; figure is from a search summary). Quanta is committing $500-700M to double transformer manufacturing capacity and can bundle pre-bought equipment into EPC contracts. FluxCo already has 'Transformer as a Service' lease and finance at 10 to 500+ MVA, and Ayr's modular, late-change designs attack the same 'cannot commit' pain without a fleet. Neither funded startup appears to hold inventory, but a warehouse line from an infrastructure lender is a small step for them. Scale economies go to Sunbelt, Quanta and United Rentals. Switching costs from utility spec approval cut against the fleet, since each utility approves its own designs. The OEM slots, the cornered resource, go first to buyers who commit volume. The dossier's own table shows lease break-even near 78% utilization and about a 10% equity return only at 100%. Bolt Electrical (a middleman) says it ships a standard substation unit in 12-14 months for a 12-15% markup over factory cost and 'is not the only firm' that can. So the speed premium is already competed down to a dealer spread.

The fleet depends on OEM slots, and OEM incumbents control them and are about to flood the window. Hitachi's CEO says it invests in capacity only when backed by backlog, capacity-reservation or framework agreements, and its 2024 investor deck lists those agreements as backlog visibility. So the scarce input goes to buyers who commit volume (hyperscalers, E.ON-type utilities), not to a new, unfunded lessor. A new buyer also has no frame agreement and no price power. Meanwhile supply is arriving. Astor Enerji (Turkey) booked about $769M of 60-300 MVA US orders for 2027-28 with 2026 capacity sold out. Hyosung HICO is adding 50% in Memphis, HD Hyundai Electric is building a second Alabama plant (about April 2027), Siemens Charlotte opens in early 2027, Eaton in 2027, Virginia Transformer is adding 70%, and Hitachi Virginia opens in 2028. Rystad says price and lead-time growth has stalled. A fleet bought now is delivered in 2028-29 and financed at about 70% loan-to-value into falling prices. OEMs also have channel-conflict reasons to refuse the fleet: it competes with their direct sales to utilities, and Hitachi already sells capacity reservations itself.

Demand substitutes and the shortage's shape both shrink the fleet's addressable pull. Wood Mackenzie's 2026 shortage estimate is 15% for power transformers and 8% for substations, down from 30% in 2025. It says the shortage is most acute at 100 MVA and above, where data centers turned to Chinese units. The fleet's 30-100 MVA band sits below that peak. Behind-the-meter power is forecast at about 40% of new data-center capacity through 2030 (Enverus) and 34% of large-load demand (utility survey), which skips grid-side substation units. Solid-state transformer startups raised about $280M in a few months. The 'phantom load' the idea calls its hidden asset is also the correlated risk. Bernstein expects cancellations to accelerate into 2027, with 35-40% of announced capacity at risk. PJM now requires financial commitment before counting large loads, and tariffs with collateral and exit fees push out the speculative buyers who would rent from a fleet. The creditworthy buyers (about 12% firm load) already hold OEM frames or buy direct. Cancelled projects also dump units into Surplus Record. That creates competing used supply from the same cohort, so redeployment does not diversify away risk.

Spec acceptance and standardization are unsolved, and the incumbents' bigger pools beat a 'multi-ratio' fleet on fit. The dossier already notes DOE calls impedance 'a particularly difficult parameter to standardize', and the surplus listings show how varied specs are (230/115, 120/12.47, 69/13.8, 34.5/13.8 kV, all as 30/40/50 MVA). A 2026 CIGRE paper says power transformers are far more customized than distribution units. NextMSC's summary of the DOE work says standardization shortens production only if utilities adopt common configurations, and no mechanism for that exists in this class. The 'about 80% are the same few designs' claim is unsourced. Dealers with thousands of units plus remanufacturing cover heterogeneity better than 280 units in a few designs. Add public-utility competitive-bid rules, warranty and early-failure risk on stored oil-filled units, and an unconfirmed allied-origin premium under EO 14420/14421. DOE's rules are due Dec 24, 2026, and any pre-qualified-vendor list is more likely to favor OEMs with US plants than a reseller of imported or reconditioned stock. Pre-mortem for 2028: the fleet holds 100+ units of the wrong specs, financed at 70% LTV, while lessees' projects are cancelled or reorder from a new US plant.

result.what_would_change_my_mind: Evidence from the demand side, not the supply side. (1) A mystery-shopper test: request written quotes for 30-100 MVA units at 69 or 138 kV from Maddox, JCL, Giga, Sunbelt Solomon and Delta Wye. If most cannot deliver in under 16 weeks and quote 12-15% or more above factory cost, the 'dealers already cover it' objection weakens. (2) Three utilities approving one multi-ratio spec in writing. (3) An OEM committing slots at a fixed price with a buy-back or resale floor, so the fleet has an input the dealers lack. (4) A lender pricing the fleet above 70% loan-to-value with a residual-value guarantee, or signed 3-5 year take-or-pay leases from creditworthy lessees (not speculative developers) at 14% or more. (5) DOE's Dec 24 rules creating a mandated allied-origin pre-qualified category that excludes the existing dealers' stock. Even if all five land, this is a financing and roll-up business where Sunbelt/TJC, United Rentals and Quanta have the edge, not a new venture. The most that would move me off 'fatal' is 'weak but fundable as an infrastructure-debt vehicle'."

objections: UNIT ECONOMICS: every route to $100M of revenue is a pass-through dealer spread or a thin-margin balance-sheet bet, and no customer is shown paying enough to fix that. The sale route is about 50 units at $2M, with gross profit of roughly $11-14M on the dossier's own 12-15% markup. The lease route is a $0.6-0.85B book earning roughly its cost of capital, with break-even near 78% utilization by the dossier's own illustration. The only lease yield cited is Willis Lease's aircraft-engine factor of about 12.5% a year (https://allmind.ai/earnings/event/bt_WLFC_2025_Q3). Engines have a deep global lessee pool, and I found no transformer lease or rental-rate comp. Searches for a 30 MVA rental rate or utilization figure returned nothing; Sunbelt Solomon quotes per project. The dossier's own numbers also show the leverage problem. On a $700M fleet with 70% debt ($210M equity), a 20% mark-down is $140M, or about 67% of the equity. The fleet would be bought at peak scarcity pricing. Wood Mackenzie (2024) said supplier margins on power units had risen about 4x and made up about 20% of unit cost (https://www.woodmac.com/es/news/opinion/4-years-into-a-difficult-transformers-market-in-the-us-is-there-a-potential-end-in-sight/). Citi, via secondary summaries, projects global HV transformer capacity up 53% from 2025 to 2028. That makes the fleet a leveraged long position on the scarcity rent, held by the party with no slot priority.

ADVERSE SELECTION AND 'WHO SIGNS': the buyers who need a fleet are the ones who cannot get direct OEM slots and cannot clear utility collateral, which means the weakest credits. The creditworthy buyers already hold direct deals. Reuters (Jul 9, 2026) shows buyers solving the problem by paying OEMs directly: Wartsila's Pukkila says buyers 'pay upfront' for earlier slots, and Roseville now buys for projects five years out (https://www.kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-07-09/us-power-companies-scramble-secure-equipment-surging-data-center). Reservation fees and non-refundable deposits accrue to the OEM that owns the slot, not to an intermediary. The Hallador turbine deal notes reservation deposits are typically non-refundable (https://www.turbomachinerymag.com/view/hallador-energy-bypasses-oem-backlog-secures-unfired-siemens-turbine-in-350-million-deal). The idea treats 'reservation LOIs' as free options. Smaller GPU-backed developers face a 2026-28 refinancing wall, and Nvidia has been asking insurers to backstop lenders on riskier tenants (https://www.bisnow.com/news/national/data-center-capital-markets/nvidia-asks-insurers-to-shoulder-financing-risk-for-some-of-its-largest-customers). The channel splits cleanly. Where the substation is utility-owned, the utility orders it and the developer pays through the interconnection agreement. Where the developer owns it, an EPC or direct OEM order is normal. The leasing customer is therefore the marginal speculative developer, whose credit is the problem. A utility chief engineer also has little reason to lease: leased equipment is an expense, while owned plant earns a return in the rate base (general ratemaking logic; I found no transformer-specific lease ruling).

THE PRICE OF SPEED IS NOT EVIDENCED, AND THE BINDING CONSTRAINT IS OFTEN NOT THE TRANSFORMER. The only sourced speed premium is a broker's claim of 12-15% over factory cost for 12-14 months (Bolt Electrical, which the article says is hard to verify: https://powermag.com/transformers-in-2026-shortage-scramble-or-self-inflicted-crisis/). The one revealed-preference datapoint cuts the other way. A Michigan city paid 3.4% more ($1,323,270 vs $1,279,391) to save 2-3.5 years between two OEM bids (https://transformer-technology.com/harbor-springs-advances-6-million-electrical-substation-project-with-transformer-purchase-transformer-technology-news/). Nothing sourced supports a premium for 8-16 weeks. I found no RFP, tender or contract for a stocked 30-100 MVA fleet, and no named data-center project where utility power was ready and the transformer alone gated energization. The customer-side evidence points elsewhere. Google's head of climate policy said in Jan 2026 that 'transmission barriers are the number one challenge', with utilities quoting 4-5, sometimes 10, years to interconnect (https://www.networkworld.com/article/4117329/google-warns-transmission-delays-are-now-the-biggest-threat-to-data-center-expansion.html). PJM milestone-change data, as summarized by a secondary outlet, attributes 23% of post-approval changes to supply chain versus 29% to permitting (https://datacenterknowledge.com/energy-power-supply/why-ai-data-center-projects-face-years-of-delays-after-approval). A transformer in 8-16 weeks does not help if the rest of the substation is gated. A vendor claims 33-35 weeks for 72.5-170 kV breakers and calls that 'significantly shorter' than industry timelines (https://switchgear-magazine.com/news/business/pennsylvania-switchgear-expands-us-production/). Commissioning-crew shortages are a further, weakly sourced gate. The '8-16 week delivery' headline is not end-to-end.

UPSIDE-CASE VOLUMES SHRINK UNDER A SECOND FORECAST, AND SPEC ACCEPTANCE FRAGMENTS THE FLEET. The idea's 280 units a year rests on Wood Mackenzie's 24 to 110 GW (about 14 GW a year) at 2 units per 100 MW. Enverus puts new US data-center additions through 2030 at about 62 GW, with behind-the-meter generation serving about 22.5 GW, or about 36% (Aug 2026; I saw this through search summaries of its press releases because the page returned 403: https://www.enverus.com/newsroom/behind-the-meter-generation-forecast-skipping-the-queue/). My arithmetic: about 40 GW grid-served over five years is roughly 8 GW a year, or about 160 units a year on the idea's own ratio. That is before removing hyperscalers, who buy direct and at least once use 120-150 MVA units, and before removing utility-owned substations. At about $2M a unit, $100M of sales is about 50 units. The dossier's own revised unit count already makes this a large share of any plausible fleet-addressable flow (this share is my inference). On spec acceptance, the '80% of designs are the same' premise is unsourced. GAO says grid infrastructure is not standardized, spares cannot replace more than one specific unit, and utility officials say standardizing 'would be very expensive and could require rebuilding parts of the grid' (https://www.gao.gov/assets/d23106180.pdf, p.13). That text is about large power transformers, and the 30-100 MVA class straddles that boundary, so it is analogy. Utilities also gate by approved plant. Dominion's list (rev. 9/30/2026) names specific plants per voltage class, and its change log shows suppliers added one at a time (https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/planning/plan-standards/private-dominion/approved-material-and-equipment-suppliers.pdf). A multi-utility 'multi-ratio' unit must come from the intersection of several such lists, which are the same OEMs whose lines are sold out.

THE SUPPLY SIDE DEPENDS ON REJECTED IDEAS, CAPITAL IS NOT A MOAT, AND THE DOWNSIDE IS CORRELATED. The idea says the fleet is supplied by 'OEMs, the idea 4 foundry and the idea 3 consortium'. The gate killed idea 3 and rated idea 4 weak, so the only real source is OEM slots, which are exactly what a newcomer lacks. Capital-light dealers already reach the target revenue. Giga Energy claims more than $150M of 2025 sales and stocked inventory (https://pulse2.com/giga-energy-profile-matt-lohstroh-interview/). It had reportedly raised only a few million dollars of equity, from low-authority snippets. That shows the dealer layer needs no fleet balance sheet and no moat, which leaves the fleet competing on cost of capital against sellers with working capital and OEM relationships (Giga, Maddox, JCL, Sunbelt Solomon now PE-owned). The correlated-bust precedent is the 2001-02 merchant turbine bust. Roughly a quarter of planned turbine capacity was abandoned within six months of the Enron shock, and Calpine alone cancelled 34 GE gas turbines for a $161M charge (https://fortnightly.com/node/11446 and https://eepower.com/news/calpine-restructures-turbine-agreements/; seen via search snippets, not fetched). Long-lead-equipment scarcity trades reversed fast when credit withdrew. The 'portfolio effect' in the idea assumes independent project failures. Utility-queue rules, Texas SB 6 and Virginia contract changes make speculative demand fall together, and UBS (via FutureSearch, secondary) projects hyperscaler capex growth slowing from +76% in 2026 to +25% in 2027. A stranded unit also sells at a discount, as the unfired-turbine resale suggests.

result.what_would_change_my_mind:
Five specific, checkable items, any one of which would move me from fatal to serious, and several together to manageable:
(1) Signed, binding commercial proof of willingness to pay. At least three non-hyperscale buyers with investment-grade or letter-of-credit-backed credit commit non-refundable money (reservation fees or deposits) for pre-built 30-100 MVA units at 8-16 week delivery, at 20-25% or more above the current OEM price for the same unit (the best sourced data are a 12-15% broker claim and a 3.4% revealed premium).
(2) A real lease comp. Documented rates and utilization for fixed (not mobile) 30-100 MVA units, for example from Sunbelt Solomon, JCL or a lender's diligence, showing at least 12% of unit cost a year at 85% or higher utilization through a downcycle. Break-even is about 78% on the dossier's math.
(3) A funded structure that removes the balance-sheet problem. An OEM commits slots at fixed price with a buy-back or resale floor, and a lender prices the fleet above 70% loan-to-value, non-recourse, ideally with residual-value insurance. This must exist before capital is raised.
(4) Proof the transformer is the binding constraint. Ten or more documented projects where the utility connection was ready and the transformer alone delayed energization by 12 months or more, or a utility or developer that states in writing it would pay a premium to close exactly that gap.
(5) Written spec acceptance. At least three utilities, including one on an approved-plant list such as Dominion's, sign off one multi-ratio design in writing, and DOE's December EO 14420 rules or a federal purchase commitment make stocked allied-origin units a recognized category. Separately, if Enverus-style behind-the-meter bypass proves much smaller than 36%, and Wood Mackenzie's 110 GW holds with a low hyperscaler direct-buy share, the volume objection weakens."]

objections: The 'neutral vacuum' is contradicted by what rival plans actually do, and Elevance's incentives point toward closing it. Iowa's state EVV FAQ says the MCOs 'have selected CareBridge as the EVV solution' and that all MCOs use the same one. The dossier ties those MCOs to Elevance, Centene (Iowa Total Care) and Molina, so rivals have already standardized on CareBridge's data layer. Wyoming has run CareBridge as its free state-sponsored EVV since Feb 15 2022. Arkansas plans CareSource and Summit were set to start CareBridge EVV on 3/31/2025 (search summary only, not verified). Elevance is also shrinking its own Medicaid book: it exited DC, Louisiana ends in 2026, it expects 'additional' exits within 12-18 months, and its 2026 Medicaid margin guide is about -1.75%. That cuts CareBridge's captive volume and pushes Carelon to court rivals harder. Neutrality is also a contract clause (a firewall, audit rights, a governance seat), so Elevance can copy it in one quarter. I found no RFP or press report from any rival plan asking for a vendor free of Elevance. Boudreaux's public line was to 'continue to serve all its customers'. The pitch's claim that a neutrality guarantee is hard for an owned competitor to copy is therefore wrong: the guarantee is easy to copy and only hard to be believed. That makes it a sales-trust problem, not a 7 Powers moat.

Plan payment rules cap what an outside vendor can earn and favor in-house or affiliated teams. CMS bulletin CIB 5/15/2019 says a Medicaid plan 'may only include in incurred claims' what the subcontractor actually pays providers. Utilization review, network development, other administrative functions and the vendor's profit on them are 'non-claims administrative expense'. The exception covers only vendors that deliver covered services through their own employees, and the neutral manager employs no aides. So its margin comes out of the plan's administrative and profit slice, not its medical budget. Arithmetic (my assumption): if admin load is about 7% of capitation, then $30k of managed spend carries about $2,100 per member-year of admin and margin. The pitch's 5% net ($1,500 per member-year) would take roughly 70% of that. The dossier's own realistic fee is $300-600 per member-year, which puts $100M at 167-333k members, so the 67-90k path fails. An affiliated vendor like Carelon captures the margin at the parent level, and a plan's in-house team is free. Caveat: some care-coordination cost may qualify as quality-improvement spend in the MLR numerator, and I did not resolve that. The vendor's margin is overhead either way.

The nearest neutral, risk-bearing, plan-facing platforms are shrinking or scaling slowly, and the usual exit is a sale to a plan. Evolent's 8-K shows 2025 revenue of $1.876B versus $2.555B in 2024, adjusted EBITDA of 8.1%, and a $398M goodwill impairment. Its 2026 EBITDA guide is $110-140M on $2.4-2.6B of revenue, about 5%, which is the ceiling margin analog. CareCentrix, the closest independent LTSS vendor, changed hands in 2020 (Anthem talks failed), 2022 (Walgreens) and 2025 (Sycamore). A third-party tracker shows its headcount down 6.2% in 2025, and its president cites plan-client membership headwinds in government programs. Waymark, a neutral Medicaid risk-based vendor, had raised $87M and served about 50k Medicaid lives in two states by late 2023 (company-reported). Cityblock needed a $116M Series E to reach about 200k members. The dossier estimates $100-200M of capital to reach 30-50k lives, so 67-90k at-risk lives is more than any neutral comparable has reached. The recurring exits (naviHealth to Optum, Signify to CVS, CareBridge to Elevance) mean the likely end state for a successful neutral vendor is ownership by a plan, which is the problem the pitch claims to solve.

The sharpened wedge is already occupied, and both suppliers of the key input are competitors. Elevance extended CareBridge into D-SNPs in 2025 (dossier, citing Elevance's page), which is exactly the FIDE/HIDE wedge. HHAeXchange already sells payer tools to 180+ MCOs on the same visit data: provider-network management, program-integrity analytics and change-in-condition insights. In April 2026 it also launched a managed RCM service for agencies, showing it is moving from software into services. CareCentrix sells guaranteed-savings LTSS programs to plans, and Cityblock/Homeward holds four Centene regional deals. Centene runs 338k LTSS members with its own care teams and was hiring an LTSS clinical-management director in 2026 (weak signal). UnitedHealth owns delivery through Optum (LHC $5.4B, Amedisys $3.3B), and CVS owns Signify. The aligned buyer pool is also thin. CMS's 2027 rule lets a D-SNP with an affiliated Medicaid MCO newly enroll only members of that MCO, and existing unaligned members stay until 2030. HCBS use among FIDE/HIDE members is unquantified, and the dossier's guess of an aligned HCBS pool of 0.4-0.7M is unverified. A neutral operating system that must ingest EVV feeds from CareBridge and HHAX/Sandata depends on two competitors, who can slow or degrade access.

Buyer budgets are contracting, each deal needs state sign-off, and a plan losing a state strands the vendor's lives. Georgetown CCF says Big Five Medicaid enrollment fell from 36.2M to 34.0M (-6.5%) over the year to June 2026. Centene now expects full-year Medicaid membership down 8-9% (previously 6%) and a slower margin recovery through 2026-27 (secondary summary). Centene is exiting Arkansas's expansion program in 2027, and Elevance is exiting DC and Louisiana. A margin-squeezed plan insources or uses HHAX tools it already has. Delegating care coordination also needs the state's approval: New Mexico requires explicit written approval, and Ohio requires prior approval of delegation subcontracts. That adds months per state before revenue, and shared-savings-only pilots then pay nothing for the first year or more. CareBridge's first deals worked because four plans were also its investors; a cold entrant has no such anchor. A plan's LTSS cohort has few members and a high cost per member, so one lost state contract can wipe out a large share of the book.

result.what_would_change_my_mind:
Any one of these would move me toward 'manageable':
(1) Written or recorded commitments from at least two non-Elevance plan LTSS leaders (Centene, UHC, Molina, Humana, Aetna, AmeriHealth) to move at least 10k at-risk lives from CareBridge or in-house teams to a neutral vendor. The commitments would need to name a fee that survives the MLR treatment, meaning a fee well above $600 per member-year paid out of admin, and have a state-approved delegation path in at least one state.
(2) State subcontractor lists or provider bulletins showing a rival plan dropped CareBridge, or CareBridge EVV, since the Dec 2024 close. Right now the evidence runs the other way (Iowa, Wyoming, Arkansas).
(3) A state MLR audit or contract showing that a non-employing HCBS manager's fee is booked as quality-improvement spend or incurred claims. That would remove the admin-slice cap.
(4) Disclosure that an independent comparable (CareCentrix Medicaid, Waymark, Cityblock's HCBS arm) is profitable at 50k or more at-risk lives on a fee of $1,000+ per member-year.
(5) Elevance announcing it will wall off or sell CareBridge's non-affiliated book, or a rival plan publicly issuing an RFP for a non-competitor HCBS manager.
Absent that, the defensible version is a regional, contract-anchored risk manager built to be acquired, not a standalone $100M-profit company. For that target I would call the competition lens close to fatal. 'Serious' reflects only that a roughly $20M-revenue outcome is not ruled out."

objections: NO EVIDENCE ANYONE WILL PAY FOR 'NEUTRAL', AND THE MARKET'S REVEALED BEHAVIOR POINTS THE OTHER WAY. The whole thesis is that rivals will not hand their sickest members to Elevance's subsidiary. But (a) rivals already bought from a competitor-backed vendor: HCI reports CareBridge served members 'in partnership with the nation's five largest managed Medicaid care plans' by 2023, and the dossier's Iowa deck shows Centene's and Molina's Iowa plans as CareBridge subcontractors, even though Anthem was an investor in the 2022 round. Neutrality was never the purchase criterion. (b) Two years after the close there is no defection, RFP or plan complaint (the dossier's negative finding; my searches also found none). (c) On the Jul 15 2026 Elevance call, management said 'CareBridge has been very successful for us. We're looking to continue to accelerate the deployment of CareBridge', claimed mid-teens medical savings, and said it is expanding to new markets. (d) Analog: Signify Health stayed 'payor-agnostic' under CVS and kept winning multi-payer MA business (+20% evaluations in Q4 2023; a new plan, Select Health SC, in 2025). Rivals tolerated a competitor-owned vendor when the product worked. (e) The big plans' answer to Elevance is to insource, not to buy neutral: Centene has 338K LTSS lives in-house, Optum owns Amedisys and LHC, Humana bought Onehome, and Bernstein read the CareBridge deal as expanding services that 'can replace existing outside vendors'. That leaves the buyers who can't build, meaning smaller regional plans and Blues, with the thinnest budgets. The '4 of 5 largest MCOs co-invested' fact the gate leaned on shows investors, not purchasers. The 2022 round was also an option on ownership: one co-investor, Anthem, became the acquirer. Any new co-investor plan will want the same option, which ends neutrality.

THE UNIT ECONOMICS BEHIND THE 67-90K-MEMBER, $100M PATH USE THE WRONG BASE. The dossier takes $30k of managed HCBS spend per member and a 5% net fee. CMS's own 2022 figure is $16,491 per HCBS user ($129.4B over 7.85M users); $48,143 is the institutional average, and the MACPAC $49.8k includes nursing facilities. Carelon Services earns 3.4%, and Evolent is going from 8% to about 5%. Elevance guides 2026 as the Medicaid margin trough, at about -1.75%, and Molina's Q2 2026 Medicaid MCR is 92.7%. At 3.4% of $16.5k that is about $561 per member-year, so $100M needs about 178,000 members. That is 9.6% of all 1.86M managed-LTSS users, or roughly 25-45% of the dossier's unverified 0.4-0.7M aligned-HCBS pool. At the dossier's own 5% it is still about 121,000 members. The 67k figure needs both $30k and 5%, plus a sickest-cohort selection nobody has shown a plan will delegate. The savings-only version is worse: 20% of 5-10% savings on $16.5k is $165-330 per member, or 300-600k members, which exceeds the whole reachable pool. Plans in a margin trough will not pay a fixed PMPM before savings appear, so the only contract they will sign is the one that makes the vendor carry the risk and the capital ($100-200M, per the dossier) before revenue.

THE SAVINGS THE BUYER WOULD PAY FOR ARE UNPROVEN, AND THE D-SNP ALIGNMENT FIX IS THE WEAKEST LINK. The sharpened pick says alignment under one parent makes acute savings capturable. The one controlled test I found says integration alone did not move acute use: a JAMA Health Forum difference-in-differences study of UPMC's FIDE-SNP in Pennsylvania (7,967 integrated vs 3,832 comparison) found HCBS use up 0.61 days/person-month but no differential change in inpatient admissions, hospital days or ED use, and no change in care-coordination measures. That plan already had full alignment. Mathematica's national MLTSS evaluation is inconsistent, with Tennessee duals showing more hospitalizations. I found no study linking missed aide shifts to ED visits; only clinic no-show literature exists, so the pitch's causal chain is untested. The only outcome numbers for this model are vendor-reported with no methods (Elevance's 12%/13%/10-15% and 'mid-teens'). The National Association of Medicaid Directors says Medicare-side savings are generally not shared with Medicaid, and savings are pushed back through prospective capitation rebasing (the dossier's California note, unverified). A buyer that measures will find the benchmark ('historic spending') contestable and will renegotiate.

THE BUYER SET IS TINY, EACH BUYER HAS A VETO, AND THE BEST NEUTRAL COMPARABLE SHOWS WHAT THAT DOES TO A VENDOR. Evolent is the closest neutral, risk-bearing platform. Its FY2025 10-K shows revenue down 26.6% to $1,876.2M, driven by $447.3M from moving one customer to a different suite and $267.4M from 'the narrowing of scope of certain Performance Suite customers'. Four customers are 68.5% of revenue (Molina 25.7%, up from 13.7%; Cook County 16.4%; Florida Blue 14.2%; Centene 12.2%). The filing warns that customers 'have in-sourced or may choose to in-source' and 'will, from time to time, seek to restructure their agreements with us'. A $398M goodwill impairment followed. A neutral entrant would have 3-6 real prospects, and the largest are vertically integrated. Every sale is also a two-step gate. A plan keeps ultimate responsibility under 42 CFR 438.230, and states gate delegation of care coordination (New Mexico requires the state's 'explicit written approval'), so each plan-state pair needs plan sign-off and a state sign-off. The VP of LTSS cannot sign a risk transfer alone; the CFO, actuary and compliance will be involved (my judgment). Cycle evidence is weak (no Medicaid-specific data; PHTI says payer digital-health contracts run 1-2 years with annual portfolio reviews; the 12-24 month figure is a consultancy blog). The first revenue is realistically 18-30 months out, and the dossier's own comparable (Cityblock) starts at 10,000 lives per deal, so $100M needs 7-11 such deals.

THE BUYERS ARE SHRINKING AND CUTTING COSTS RIGHT NOW. On the Jul 15 2026 call Elevance said it expects 'to exit additional Medicaid markets over the next 12 to 18 months' and will stay only where it has 'alignment with duals, our Carelon strategy, and a sustainable operating framework'. That is the exact wedge this pick targets, and Elevance is concentrating its own capital there. Georgetown CCF's Q2 2026 review shows Medicaid enrollment down 2.6-9.5% year over year at all five big plans and Centene leaving Arkansas expansion in 2027. Centene's June 2026 10-Q books 'severance costs due to enterprise optimization and contract exits' and it opened a voluntary separation program on Jul 27 2026 (a Becker's report puts 2026 severance at $315-365M); a plan in that mode defers new vendor spend and favors vendors it can fire or absorb.
