objections: The entry ticket is held by funded incumbents, and capital is flooding in. New York's RFP required a statewide FI contract elsewhere and a $100M line of credit (dossier, Holland & Knight). Every award the dossier found went to a multi-state incumbent. The 'buy a small FI for past performance' route then competes with H.I.G. (GT Independence, 50k+ participants, Nov 2025) and General Atlantic, which closed a roughly $3B purchase of TEAM Services from Alpine in April 2026 at about 10x EBITDA. TEAM sells financial management services for consumer-directed care. I could not confirm that Acumen sits inside TEAM; the dossier's link rests on an unopened CB Insights page. Acumen itself reports 22-23 states and 100+ programs. A first-time consolidator buys against 10x-multiple sponsors. The only cheap targets are the money-losing ones, since the four Wisconsin FEAs lost 12.5% in aggregate. A new entrant would end up buying either an overpriced or a sick asset.

The 'exception-free' technology edge is a feature the platform vendor already sells to every competitor. HHAX bought Annkissam in Oct 2020, software for state FMS organizations serving self-direction programs, which HHAX described as supporting HCBS agencies in 38 states. It also bought Sandata. PPL already markets a payroll engine handling more than a million timesheets in near real time, with automated edits for overlapping shifts and hours over authorization, prepayment holds, and participant approval of EVV time. Correction to the dossier: HHAX's CarePay press release is aimed at agencies and does not mention self-direction or FMS. But the FMS software layer under the FIs is already HHAX's, and the dossier never mentions Annkissam. Any incumbent can adopt the workflow at roughly zero cost. Process power built on a rented platform is not a moat. The dossier's own Wisconsin data shows scale did not lower cost: iLife, the largest at about 14.8k participants, cost more per head than GT at about 8.5k.

The payroll-certainty SLA is table stakes, and the evidence is that states do not reward it. The Kentucky listing already requires vendor performance report cards and penalty structures. Wisconsin's contract treats a missed payroll as grounds for fiscal corrective action. After New York's day-one payroll failures, a $162M wage settlement and a DOJ suit, PPL was still Wisconsin's top-scoring bidder in Jan 2026. I found no evidence of any DOH contract penalty or audit of PPL's payroll. So the market shows no price premium for reliability. The funded backstop is the real cost. PPL told New York plans it lacked cash to pay workers without advance funding, and the plans pre-funded it. A challenger who truly fronts payroll needs the same $100M-class line, or about $60M a week for 85k participants, against a roughly 2% fee. That is a balance-sheet business dressed up as a services pitch.

Incumbents answer on price, and their visible price understates their economics. New York's $68.50 PMPM and Wisconsin's $82.77 are now the reference points. The idea's $75-115 band sits at or above them. The DOJ complaint alleges PPL bid $68.50 as its sole compensation, then tried to bill managed care plans at higher per-hour rates. If true, an incumbent can underbid in a marginal state while earning elsewhere. A challenger cannot copy that. PPL (18 states, PE-backed), Tempus (nonprofit, $2.13B pass-through revenue in 2024, 0.4% net in 2023) and Acumen can each cut price on a rebid. The dossier's best Wisconsin operator earned only +2% to +6.5%. A 10-15% margin is not supported by any public data.

The prize is locked and the addressable pool is small and shrinking. The only $100M-class contract (New York, about $172-205M a year in fees) is held by PPL with no rebid scheduled. A slot opens only through a receivership or a legislative reversal. The DOJ motion to dismiss was fully briefed on Sep 11 with no ruling found, and the multi-FI bill's status is unknown. New York volume already fell from about 280k authorized to 209k registered. The dossier's fee pool is $0.7-0.9B, and states are cutting self-direction (Maryland proposed a $14.5M cut and Missouri $17M; neither is confirmed enacted). Live wedges are tiny or unknowable: Kentucky lists no participant count, no term, no past-performance weights, and conflicting due dates (Nov 6, 2026 versus Mar 9, 2027). West Virginia-size wins are about $6M a year. Pre-mortem for 2028: lost Kentucky to an incumbent with statewide past performance, could not buy a target below sponsor multiples, held a 4% reserve and a $100M line against 0-6% margins, and the Wisconsin and New York outcomes made states wary of new single vendors.

result.what_would_change_my_mind:
Any of these would move me toward manageable:
(1) Wisconsin's protest outcome showing a non-incumbent or small operator winning on a reliability or price basis, or a state scoring rubric that gives payroll accuracy more weight than past performance.
(2) A state that pays for a payroll guarantee, such as a priced SLA tier or bonus, rather than imposing penalties.
(3) Kentucky's RFP showing more than 30k participants, a term of 5 years or more, and a waived or low-weighted past-performance requirement, or a teaming path with a displaced New York FI.
(4) Two FI operators disclosing cost per participant-month at or below $65 at 10k participants with their current software. That would show the scale and process edge exists and that HHAX/Annkissam does not already give it to everyone.
(5) A real acquisition target with a clean record, a statewide contract and at least 5 years of term left, available at 5x EBITDA or less.
(6) A New York receivership or a multi-FI mandate that opens carved-out slots, or a financing source for a $100M-class payroll float at a cost the fee can bear.
(7) Evidence that HHAX will not extend its self-direction workflow to FIs on an equal footing.
Without at least two of these, I would treat the idea as a thin-margin $15-35M services acquisition at best, not a $100M company.

objections: TIMING / BUYER HEALTH: the buyer pool and budget line are shrinking right now, which the dossier treats as a tailwind ('plan margins squeezed'). Squeezed plans cut or in-source vendors, and a savings-only contract is the first thing to go. Elevance guides a 2026 Medicaid operating margin of about -1.75%, with Medicaid membership down from 8.9M (end 2024) to 8.3M (Jun 2026). It has left DC (Aug 1 2026), Healthy Blue Louisiana ends at the end of 2026, and it says more state exits come within 12-18 months. Industry Medicaid MLR rose from 88% (2023) to 91% (2024), and Elevance says cost trend is outpacing funding for 2027 bids. Centene guides 2026 revenue down about 3%, is offering buyouts to most of its roughly 61,000 staff, reportedly plans to exit Arkansas's expansion program in 2027, had its Arizona ALTCS award cancelled and rebid (new contract date October 2027), and is in Georgia and Texas protests and Hawaii non-renewal. Molina lost Virginia. Aetna's Ohio MyCare plan ended Jan 1 2026. On the D-SNP side the sharpened pick depends on, Becker's reports HCSC, Aetna, Centene, Humana and CareSource each pulling dual plans from more than 100 net counties for 2027. The one big aligned D-SNP/Medicaid parent growing SNPs is UnitedHealthcare, which owns Optum and Amedisys and is the least likely to buy from a neutral vendor. The 6-10 reachable parents are volatile: a vendor's volume swings with each state rebid or protest.

REGULATION / EXECUTION: the $100M-profit path requires taking capitated downstream risk, and that is a state-by-state licensing and approval gauntlet. Savings-only is dead (the dossier's own math needs 9-18% of all managed-LTSS users). Maine's insurance code prohibits non-carrier downstream risk arrangements unless licensed or expressly waived (24-A sec. 4331-4332). Maryland regulates downstream risk contracts, including for Medicaid MCOs. Texas requires reserves for delegated services outside the delegate's license. Alabama requires Medicaid RCO reserves. Rhode Island has pending provider-risk certification bills. Under 42 CFR 438.230 the plan keeps ultimate responsibility, so plans will demand revocability, audit rights and indemnity. New subcontracts also need state sign-off: Arizona requires administrative-services subcontracts to be submitted 60 days before the effective date, and 42 CFR 438.66 readiness reviews run at least three months ahead of a program start. My inference is a 9-18 month cycle per state-and-plan pair, and I found no regulator saying an HCBS management vendor on sub-capitation is exempt. Liability is also unresolved. An algorithmic hours or assessment case, Bessey v. Nebraska DHHS, was filed May 2026, Arkansas ARChoices set the precedent, and 2026 state AI laws (Colorado HB 26-1139, Iowa HF 2635, Georgia SB 444 effective Jan 1 2027, Arizona effective Jul 1 2026) are mostly aimed at utilization-review denials. So far liability has run against the state agency, not the vendor, but any product that steers hours or networks will be indemnified by the vendor to the plan.

CAPITAL / NEUTRALITY CONTRADICTION: the funding model undermines the product and the capital market is not shaped for it. The dossier estimates $100-200M to reach 30-50k members. The pick funds that with 2-3 plan co-investors and a plan governance seat. That is the CareBridge template, where Anthem invested in 2022 and bought the company in 2024, so co-investors get first look at an exit and the neutrality claim fails. Rock Health says H1 2026 digital-health funding was $7.4B across 244 deals, with 45% going to 19 companies in 20 rounds of $100M or more (median deal $14M), and the money is flowing to AI. A 3.4-5% margin Medicaid risk manager is not that pattern. The closest precedent for a vendor paid fixed fees by MCOs and states is ModivCare, which filed Chapter 11 in Aug 2025 and cut about $1.1B of debt. It blamed declining state Medicaid reimbursement and said many or all of its largest customers were considering budget cuts. States and plans now diligence vendor solvency, so a thinly capitalized neutral vendor is hard to place. Risk contracts priced off 'historic spending' also land the vendor in a market where trend is outrunning funding. CareBridge's parent absorbs that squeeze and a standalone neutral cannot.

SAVINGS THESIS IS LEAKY AND THE D-SNP ALIGNMENT WHY-NOW IS SOFTER THAN CLAIMED: the independent evidence on care management for high-LTSS members is thin or negative, and the only strong numbers are Elevance's (12% fewer admissions, 10-15% MLR improvement, no methods). NBER Working Paper 35055 (Apr 2026) finds managed LTSS raised dual-eligible hospitalizations 4.2% in Florida and had no significant effect in New York. Older reviews find hospitalization cuts without net savings. Medicare-side savings only pay if the buyer holds both products, so alignment is the crux. But the CY2027 MA final rule (Apr 2, 2026) added new exceptions to integration, and TD Securities calls the 2027 duals integration cliff a 'minimal overall impact on D-SNP enrollment' and gradual to 2030. The non-aligned disenrollment requirement does not bite until 2030, and states control much of it through SMACs. The plan's share of any savings is also capped. Capitation is set prospectively for 12 months and rebased, and Texas contracts share profit above about 3% of revenue with the state (figure from a 2022 HHSC slide seen only via search summary; the PDF 404'd on fetch). Network steering, one of the pitched levers, is limited because 1915(c) HCBS keeps free choice among willing qualified providers and many states set rate floors. The binding constraint is aide supply (71% fill rate in the survey the gate cited), which the vendor does not control because it employs no aides.

ADDRESSABLE POOL AND DATA DEPENDENCE: the headline pool overstates what an aligned-plan HCBS operating system can reach, and its key input belongs to the closest competitor. The dossier's 58% concentration in five states hides two problems. California's 312,162 managed-LTSS users are mostly institutional or limited services, because IHSS (the largest Medi-Cal LTSS program) stays outside plan risk; a 2026 CHCF paper treats bringing it in as a future option. New York's 346,892 are mostly MLTC-only partial-capitation members, not aligned D-SNP members. Together that is about 35.5% of the 1,856,121 count (my arithmetic). Separately, the EVV data the product runs on sits in state aggregators that HHAeXchange operates or feeds. Illinois requires providers using third-party EVV to transmit visit data to HHAX, Minnesota third-party systems must connect to HHAX, and payers push authorization files into HHAX. HHAX also sells payer analytics and program-integrity tools to the same plans, and the state free tier is free for agencies. A neutral vendor's core data pipe is therefore controlled by a horizontal competitor, and I found no public source on data-use or resale terms. That is a gap, not proof of a block.

(3) A written no-license-needed or licensed-pathway answer from two target-state insurance departments (for example Texas, Florida, Pennsylvania) for an HCBS management vendor on sub-capitation, plus a plan willing to carry the 42 CFR 438.230 delegation oversight without demanding equity or a board seat. (4) An independent evaluation, or a plan-shared claims analysis with methods, showing Medicaid-side savings of at least 5% for a high-LTSS cohort after rate rebasing, since Elevance's mid-teens claim has no methods and the NBER paper points the other way. (5) Capital: at least $50M from non-plan investors, or plan money without governance rights, so the first 30,000 members are funded without a CareBridge-style strategic exit. (6) HHAeXchange or state EVV contract language confirming a plan can pass full-fidelity visit and authorization data to an unaffiliated vendor under a BAA, without paying a competitor for it. If (1) and (3) both come back positive, I would downgrade this from serious to manageable as a regional, contract-anchored risk manager built for acquisition. I would still not upgrade the standalone $100M-profit case, since the dossier's own arithmetic says that needs about 67,000 at-risk members at a 5% margin the analogs only reach at the top of their range.

objections: The 'payroll-certainty SLA' is not the vendor's to deliver, and no buyer pays a premium for it. Connecticut is the live test: GT Independence (the 'best operator' in this dossier) still had hundreds of aides with missing, delayed or partial pay in Nov 2025 to Feb 2026. GT says it 'can only execute payments when the state green-lights the funds'. The state (DSS) blames its own incomplete or miscalculated authorization files, plus employers exceeding monthly hours (10% of self-directing employers). The union won a partial settlement of just under $1M in backpay, and the state, not the vendor, was left holding the political problem. If the FI guarantees payroll anyway, it becomes an unsecured lender against hours the state later refuses to reimburse. Arithmetic (A): if just 1% of payroll fronted is unreimbursable, that is about $30 per participant-month at New York's ~$36k per participant-year, or 37% of an $80 fee. In Wisconsin (~$51.7k per participant-year) it is about $43, or 56% of the $76.50 fee. The buyer side also already treats payroll timeliness as a penalty clause, not a priced feature (Wisconsin's contract allows withholding fees for missed payroll; Connecticut has 'enhanced contract monitoring' and a 2026 late-pay penalty bill). In Kentucky, the one live RFP, the state's own FAQ says financial management agencies may bill claims before paying PDS employees, so there is no payroll float for a backstop to cover. Pitch failure mode: the SLA is either un-backable (state-caused misses) or un-monetizable (table stakes).

The price the buyer pays is a commodity floor, and at that floor the sector loses money. I extracted Wisconsin's state-reviewed 2025 FEA financials myself: revenue $76.50, operating cost $84.87, net -$9.53 per participant-month (-12.5%) across four FEAs. Only GT is positive (+$1.46, about 2%); iLife -$9.67, Premier -$25.51, Outreach -$38.41. Total FEA revenue for the whole state is only ~$25.5M, with a net loss of $3.2M. The fee is about 1.8% of spend (A: $918 per participant-year vs ~$51.7k, using the dossier's $1.5B / 29,000). The winner in Wisconsin (PPL) and New York ($68.50 bid) won by being the lowest-price, highest-scoring incumbent. A challenger that must hit $65-70 cost to earn 10-15% margin at $77-83 is promising unit costs below every Wisconsin operator's. The gate's own 'drop the 30% under headline' concession doesn't fix this, because the SLA gets no price uplift in competitive awards ($68.50-82.77). Rate-card states (CO $103, TX $114, KY planned $121) pay more, but those are not competitively bid, so a newcomer can't sell its way into them. Realistic result: $20M revenue at roughly zero profit, which is not a fundable business.

The reachable-volume and sales-cycle math is far worse than 'live RFPs in Kentucky and Ohio'. (a) Cycle time: Wisconsin RFP S-1640 DMS-25 reached notice of intent on Jan 29 2026, protests were filed within the 10-day window, review began Feb 8, I found no resolution as of Oct 18 2026, and transfers start 'no earlier than 2027'. That is 18-24+ months from RFP to first revenue, with a funded bid team and a $100M-line-of-credit-class balance sheet (New York's RFP demanded one, per the dossier's Holland & Knight cite). (b) Kentucky, the wedge, is small: FMS there is run by local Area Development Districts, total 1915(c) enrollment was ~27,000 in an older Appendix K figure, and PDS is a subset. If PDS is 10-20% of that (A, my assumption), at the planned $121 rate it is about $3.9-7.8M per year. The prior version of the same RFP number was 2018, so it re-bids rarely. (c) Ohio DODD closed Jan 14 2026 and I found no award notice. (d) CAC per win is a full multi-month proposal plus teaming and acquisition spend for roughly one competitive statewide award per year nationally, based on what I found: NY, WV, WI, NJ, CO, CT, MA. $100M is about four Wisconsins at current prices.

Every competitive award I could trace went to an existing multi-state incumbent, so 'buy a small FI for past performance' targets assets that are either not for sale or wasting. Switches found: PPL to Palco in West Virginia (2024), PPL to Acumen in New Jersey DDD (2025), Acumen out of Colorado to Palco/PPL (April 2021), Allied to GT in Connecticut (2024), three vendors to Tempus in Massachusetts, and PPL as the Wisconsin intent-to-award and New York sole FI. The qualifying holders are funded or non-profit: GT (H.I.G., Nov 2025), Acumen (Alpine-backed), PPL (DW Healthcare/Linden), Tempus (non-profit), Kentucky's ADDs (public bodies). The only 'cheap' statewide contract holders are the Wisconsin losers, whose contracts end April 2027 if the PPL award survives protest, and who lose $9-38 per participant-month. I ran two searches for FMS M&A deals or prices and found none, so the entry ticket cannot even be priced. The dossier's own hidden-incumbent point stands and is stronger than it says: a funded consolidator (H.I.G.) already exists, and the bid requires prior statewide experience that a startup lacks by construction.

The only $100M-class customer is closed or hostile, and the demand base is under political attack. New York is locked to ~2030, and DOJ's June 2026 suit (E.D.N.Y. 1:26-cv-3601) is fully briefed (PPL reply Sep 11 2026). I found no ruling on the motion to dismiss or the receiver request. A 'sham procurement' finding would make the state more closed to untested vendors, not less, and NY bills would restore multiple FIs, which splits the volume rather than handing one buyer a big contract. NY volume itself fell ~25% in one rebid (280k authorized to 209k registered, per the dossier). The MCO-delegated channel is price-resistant: NY plans told PPL that a $0.55-per-hour rate demand violated antitrust law (Dec 2025), and PPL threatened to terminate plan contracts. Self-direction's core users are family-paid caregivers, which is exactly what budget-stressed states are cutting: Maryland wage tables (~$47 to ~$29.98/hr for some, ~3,900 self-directors), Idaho ended a paid-family service in July 2025, and Indiana, Missouri and Colorado proposed 2026 cuts, ahead of the Jan 1 2027 federal Medicaid cut. Section 3504 agent status and joint-employer exposure (Calderon settled at $162M, about 79-94% of a year of NY fee revenue per the dossier) is tail risk a thin-margin, small-balance-sheet buyer-of-assets cannot carry.

# C06 dossier: Overnight Yard Crews (pool P102, idea 2)

Researched 2026-10-18. Tags: (S) read this session; (S-snip) from a search result I did not open; (A) my arithmetic or assumption; (U) unverified.

## 1. Bottom line

The gate's "weak" verdict holds, and on market size I would grade it lower.

- The pain is real. ATRI found 65.5% of shops understaffed and 19.3% of positions unfilled (S: https://truckingresearch.org/2025/08/new-atri-research-addresses-shortage-of-qualified-diesel-techs-in-trucking/). Fullbay's 2026 report shows median technician pay at $36.50 an hour, up 14.1% per FreightWaves' summary (S: https://www.freightwaves.com/news/fullbay-2026-heavy-duty-repair-report-technician-shortage).
- At least eight scaled players already sell mobile, on-site or standard-work PM to fleets. Several have 2 to 15 times the technician base (about 640 people) the idea needs for $100M.
- The outsourced checklist-labor pool inside the idea's own customer segment is about $0.25-2.2B a year (A). $100M is then 5-41% share.
- The unit economics only work with cheap Level-1 labor at high utilization. Posted pay for entry-level mobile technicians is $34-36 an hour at one national player.
- The remote-master-tech, OEM second-payer and Workforce Pell legs are each weaker than pitched.

Best realistic outcome (judgement): a $10-25M regional services business. Under round 2's no-shrinking rule this is a kill unless the section 9 pilot tests pass.

## 2. Competitors: gate list confirmed, plus new names

| Player | Scale and evidence |

Pit Stop deal (July 2024) added about $24M of revenue; Torque then had about 200 technicians in 140 markets (S: https://www.freightwaves.com/news/ryder-acquires-mobile-fleet-maintenance-provider-pit-stop). The idea's "six states" is stale. |

The real competitors are strategics and PE. The free substitute is fleets hiring their own lube and PM technicians (section 4).

## 3. Bottom-up market

I queried the FMCSA census (https://data.transportation.gov/resource/az4n-8mr2.json) on Oct 18, 2026 for active carriers whose MCS-150 was updated since Oct 2024 (S). Results:

- 15,040 carriers hold 50 to 1,999 power units, with 2.41M units in total (about 44% of the roughly 5.5M units once 352 records reporting 2,000+ units, which look inflated, are excluded).
  - 9,171 are for-hire (1.42M units).
  - 5,692 are private (0.96M units).
- Self-reported driver mix puts 36% of for-hire drivers and 68% of private drivers in the "within 100 miles" bucket. That implies about 1.19M yard-returning units (A).
- This is the realistic reach of an overnight-yard model. Over-the-road trucks sleep on the road.
- Caveats: the data is self-reported and ages; it omits school, transit and municipal fleets that lack USDOT numbers.
- Context: ATA's 2020 data says 97.4% of fleets run fewer than 20 trucks (S: https://www.freightwaves.com/news/ata-stats-2020-volume-lower-but-trucking-still-rules-freight-movement). The idea's customer is about the top 1.7% of fleets by count (15,040 of 904,630 carriers in my pull, A).

Spend per payer is my assumption: 20 labor-hours a year of PM, inspection, tire, brake and lighting work per truck at $115, about $2,300.

| Basis | Gross labor if 100% outsourced | At 9% outsourced | At 25% | At 40% | $100M as share (9% / 25% / 40%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Yard-returning units (1.19M) | $2.7B | $0.25B | $0.68B | $1.09B | 41% / 15% / 9% |
| All 50-1,999 fleets (2.41M) | $5.5B | $0.50B | $1.39B | $2.22B | 20% / 7% / 5% |

Outsourcing shares come from MacKay: fleets did 91% of PM labor in-house, and about 75% of all service work, in 2013 (S: https://www.truckinginfo.com/articles/service-survey-fleets-say-they-want-to-outsource-more). By 2015 only 68% of fleets did all service in-house, down from 75% in 2011 (S: https://www.ttnews.com/articles/technician-shortage-spurs-fleets-outsource-more-work). I found no current PM-specific outsourcing rate.

The idea's $35B "checklist labor" pool is unsourced (the gate also could not source it). It includes in-house labor and fleets of under 50 trucks that the idea does not target.

Cross-check from the supply side: a crew billing 3,000 hours covers about 150 trucks at 20 hours each. The 290-crew plan therefore serves about 43,500 trucks (A), or 3.7% of yard-returning units in the target fleets. The truck share is small, but only if fleets hand over all of their PM labor, which has historically been the least-outsourced category. Ryder's SelectCare and related revenue was $680M in 2025 on 44,100 contract vehicles, about $15.4k a vehicle including parts (S, Ryder 10-K above). The full-service incumbents already hold the biggest slice.

## 4. Demand and willingness to pay

For demand:
- The shortage is documented. Fullbay reports 54% of shops understaffed and 40% saying hiring got harder (S, FreightWaves link above).
- Rush's 10-K says demand for technicians is very high and reports 35.0% technician turnover in 2025 (S, Rush 10-K).
- Incumbents are paying to expand: Ryder's two acquisitions, Cox's two, Rush's mobile investment, the True North platform.
- The freight market has flipped. DAT data cited in September 2026 coverage shows spot rates about 35% above a year earlier and tender rejections near 13-14%. Fleets have cash and miles (S-snip: https://ielfreight.com/truckload-market-update-september-2026/ and https://www.ryantrans.com/september-2026-industry-update-truckload-rates).

Against demand:
- Only 33% of fleet respondents in Fleet Maintenance's December 2025 benchmarking said they were understaffed; 54% said staffing was about right (S: https://www.fleetmaintenance.com/shop-operations/employees-and-training/article/55338548/2025-fleet-maintenance-benchmarking-report-the-technician-shortage). The 65.5% ATRI number is shops, not fleets.
- Fleets that run yards already staff or contract the work: Ryder has 155 on-site shops inside customer yards. A 2018 HDT piece quotes C&S Wholesale Grocers as doing 70% in-house, with no one right model (S: https://www.truckinginfo.com/279627/how-fleets-are-looking-to-outsource-maintenance-and-repairs).
- The cheapest substitute is the buyer hiring its own PM or lube technician. A truck-capable lube-tech posting pays $16-22 an hour (S-snip: https://recruiting.paylocity.com/Recruiting/Jobs/Details/4134626). Even at $30 loaded, that is about a quarter of $115.
- I found no RFP, contract or complaint set showing private fleets paying a premium for hourly L1 crews. The hard demand evidence I found is public-sector, which belongs to idea 6.

Price benchmarks. Fullbay's median shop labor rate is $149 and mobile runs about $160 (S, FreightWaves link). So $115 is a 23-28% discount (A). Public bids for full-skill heavy-duty labor are $105-165 an hour in Erie County NY in 2025 (S-snip: https://www3.erie.gov/purchasing/sites/www3.erie.gov.purchasing/files/2025-04/memo-trucks-heavy-equipment.pdf) and $175-215 in San Antonio (S-snip: https://webapp1.sanantonio.gov/RFPFiles/IFB_5481_202408020219120.pdf). A $115 price is credible but not a bargain against incumbents who can match it.

## 5. Unit economics

Anchors:
- Ryder's whole fleet-management segment earned 8.6% pretax on $5.845B in 2025 (S, Ryder 10-K).
- Posted pay for L1-type roles:
  - $16-22 an hour for a truck-capable lube technician (Paylocity link above).
  - $25-35 for a Rush Level-1 union diesel job (S-snip, aggregator: https://grabjobs.co/us/job/full-time/others/level-1-union-diesel-mechanic-147718944).
  - $34-36 for Kooner's entry-level mobile diesel technician, with a conflicting $25-30 salary field (S-snip: https://www.careerbuilder.com/job-details/entry-level-mobile-diesel-mechanic-technician-1909-hayward-ca--60b0334c-a99a-40a7-bb3d-e77d162a8a78).
- Conflict on median pay: FreightWaves gives $36.50 (+14.1%); the gate's forum source reports $32 (https://forum.freightwaves.com/t/fullbay-s-2026-report-heavy-duty-shops-face-structural-technician-shortage/9024). I could not reach Fullbay's primary report.

My model (A): the crew bills 2 techs x 2,080 hours x utilization x $115. Costs are:
- L1 wage x 1.3 burden.
- One $108k loaded mentor per 4.8 crews (the idea's 60 mentors per 290 crews).
- $25k a year for van, tools and fuel.
- 28% of revenue for insurance (6%), consumables (4%), regional management, recruiting and training (10%), and sales and G&A (8%).

| L1 wage | EBITDA margin at 72% utilization (the idea's 1,500 hrs) | at 65% | at 55% | Break-even utilization |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $20 | 27% | 22% | 13% | 46% |
| $24 | 21% | 15% | 5% | 52% |
| $30 | 11% | 5% | -8% | 61% |
| $34 | 5% | -2% | -16% | 68% |

If the wage is $30-34 (consistent with the Kooner posting and 14% wage inflation), the model needs 60-70% utilization just to break even. I found no published utilization benchmark for mobile or yard heavy-duty crews; the only mention is a low-quality bookkeeping blog describing a 50% example. Utilization is an open gap.

Capital (A): 290 crews x about $100k for van, tools and parts kits is about $29M. Add roughly $8-12M of receivables on net-30 to net-45 terms, plus 12-18 months of ramp losses. That is roughly $40-60M of capital to reach $100M, all of it assumption. The credible alternative is a PE roll-up, which is the True North route.

## 6. Regulatory and liability landscape

- Annual-inspection qualification, 49 CFR 396.19: an inspector needs a federal- or state-sponsored program, or a combination of training and experience totaling at least one year (S: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/49/396.19). The gate was right that a 4-6 week hire cannot be the inspector.
- Brake-inspector qualification, 49 CFR 396.25, bars carriers from letting unqualified employees be responsible for brake inspection and repair. It requires a recognized apprenticeship, a state or federal program, or one year of related training or experience (S: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/49/396.25). My reading: each crew needs at least one qualified person of record, so this is a staffing constraint, not a legal bar.
- A remote video mentor cannot be the inspector of record. Diesel Laptops and OEM remote diagnostics exist, but nothing I read lets a remote party sign the inspection.
- Carrier duty does not transfer. 49 CFR 396.3 lets a carrier have maintenance performed by others, but the carrier stays responsible and keeps the records (S: https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/49/396.3).
  - California's *Maloney v. Rath* treats the brake duty as nondelegable (S-snip: https://www.pastpaperhero.com/resources/maloney-v-rath-69-cal-2d-442-cal-1968).
- Repair-liability exposure is real. A plaintiff firm reports an $18.79M Alabama verdict over a dealer shop's detached lateral control rod (S-snip: https://www.beasleyallen.com/article/mobile-county-jury-returns-18-79-million-verdict-to-man-paralyzed-by-negligent-repair/). Brake work needs garage liability with completed-operations cover plus garagekeepers (S-snip: https://www.insurancejournal.com/magazines/mag-features/2014/02/10/319390.htm). I found no premium figures (gap).
- Workforce Pell does not help in the first years:
  - Programs must run at least 8 weeks and 150 clock hours, hit 70% completion and 70% placement, and come from Title IV institutions with governor approval (S: https://www.newamerica.org/insights/workforce-pell-what-you-need-to-know/).
  - By Aug 4, 2026, Pennsylvania had approved 2 of 40 submitted programs (both CDL) and I found no diesel-technician approval (S: https://tradecolleges.org/blog/trades-news/trades-news-roundup-week-of-july-27-2026).
- I found no state licensing regime for heavy-duty technicians (absence of evidence, not confirmation).

## 7. Why-now: partly real, partly absorbed

- Real: shortage metrics, wage inflation, and a freight recovery that gives fleets cash.
- Absorbed by incumbents: Torque (2023), Cox's FleetNet and Corcoran's deals (2023), True North (Nov 2025), Rush's mobile push, and software vendors now handling the PM scheduling the idea treated as an edge.
- Working against the idea: 14% wage inflation erodes the labor arbitrage, and a tight freight market means all bidders chase the same technicians.
- ATD's 2024 dealer study put entry-level and trainee technician turnover at 44% (S-snip: https://www.trucknews.com/transportation/what-can-trucking-fleets-do-to-hire-retain-technicians/1003212233).

## 8. Audit of the upside-case assumptions

| Assumption | Finding |
|---|---|
| 290 crews, about 580 L1 plus 60 mentors | Torque had about 200 technicians in July 2024, a year after launch with Pit Stop folded in, and added 20+ in Jan 2026. Hiring 580 L1 from scratch would be about 3x Torque's headcount (A). Revenue per technician in the plan ($172k of labor alone) is above the roughly $125-130k per technician implied by Amerit's aggregator revenue estimate (U). |
| $115 an hour at 1,500 billable hours per tech | Unproven, no benchmark. The 23-28% discount to market is what the incumbents can match. Unit economics hinge on L1 pay under about $25. |
| 4-6 week L1 training | Penske's TechStart already runs six weeks. ATRI says untrained entrants need 357 hours and $8,211 of trainee wages, and over 30% of program graduates were unqualified in 20 core skills (S, ATRI link). It is feasible but not a moat. |
| Fleets outsource their checklist work | PM was 91% in-house in 2013. The 1998 and 2003 MacKay studies predicted more outsourcing and it did not materialize (S, truckinginfo link above). No current PM rate found. |
| OEM campaign budget as second payer | Love's holds Freightliner ExpressPoint (400+ locations; light warranty, roadside warranty, campaigns) (S: https://www.loves.com/news/2024/january/loves-and-freightliner-complete-rollout-of-freightliner-expresspoint-exclusive-repair-service). Its International page covers warranty work of three hours or less, excluding Texas and Louisiana (S: https://loves.com/international). The on-highway claims pool is about $0.8B in the gate's WarrantyWeek read, not $3.94B (gate-cited: https://warrantyweek.com/archive/ww20260521.html). I found only dealer-run warranty programs at Volvo and Mack, and nothing on PACCAR. |
| Workforce Pell ladder | Not usable (section 6). |
| Remote master tech as differentiator | Commoditized and legally non-substitutable (section 6). |

Scale comparison (A): Ryder's Torque at about 200-220 technicians and $150-170k per technician implies roughly $30-40M of revenue, built in three years with a large balance sheet and two acquisitions. That is a third to two-fifths of this idea's $100M. The path to $100M runs through M&A or an incumbent's balance sheet.

## 9. Verdict and what would change it

Scorecard (judgement, 0-10): market size 2, competition 2, unit economics 3, legal and liability 5, why-now 4. Median revenue in 5-7 years about $10-15M; upside about $40-60M with acquisitions; $100M is not a credible organic outcome. This matches the gate (median $18M, upside $90M) on the median and is more skeptical on the upside.

Three cheap tests that would reopen it:
1. Three fleets with yards each pay at least $115 an hour for L1 crews for 90 days at 65% or higher utilization, with all-in L1 wage under $25.
2. A written insurer quote for brake and tire work at 6% of revenue or lower, plus a documented inspector-of-record structure.
3. Evidence from a fleet maintenance director that PM outsourcing is rising materially above the 2013 level, with named buyers and budget lines. I found none.

## 10. Gaps and unverified items

- No Torque, Cox or Amerit pricing; no mobile utilization benchmark; no current PM-outsourcing rate.
- The ATRI claim of 48% (5-25 truck fleets) and 62% (1,000+ truck fleets) in-house maintenance is not in the ATRI release or the FreightWaves ATRI summary I read; still unconfirmed.
- The Fullbay/Stripe survey figures and Fullbay's PM share of repair lines come from the idea file; the gate could not source the survey and I did not rely on either.
- Cox's $100M FleetNet price is single-sourced (https://www.globalfleet.com/en/fleet-strategy/north-america/news/cox-automotive-boosts-connected-services-fleetnet-america), and Amerit, Penske and Love's scale figures are company claims.
- The FMCSA census is self-reported and includes stale records; the 20-hours-per-truck labor assumption is mine.
- Several fetches returned 403, so some facts rest on search-result summaries marked S-snip.

objections: TIMING: the why-now is mostly spent and the one open door is not enterable. As of 2026-10-18: New York is locked to PPL (sole FI since 2025-04-01, award upheld on appeal Oct 2025, no rebid found). West Virginia was awarded in 2024. Wisconsin gave PPL a notice of intent on 2026-01-29 with a protest review still unresolved on a DHS page last revised 2026-10-08, and transfers not before 2027. Ohio DODD closed 2026-01-14 and Alabama FMS RFP 2026-03 closed in June 2025 with multi-award and no award found. That leaves Kentucky (due 2026-11-06, 19 days from now): the listing is a re-procurement of a 2018 RFP, carries stale 2018 text, names no incumbent, participant count or value, and Kentucky is mid-transition of PDS oversight to waiver operating agencies by 2027-01-01. A not-yet-formed company cannot assemble past performance, an EVV integration, a bid lead and a funded payroll line in 19 days. The realistic cycle is RFP to first revenue of about 2 years (Wisconsin: RFP S-1640, NOI Jan 2026, protest open 8+ months, go-live 2027), all pre-revenue burn. Entry requires past performance, which means buying an FI, which means bidding against H.I.G. (GT Independence, Nov 2025), DW Healthcare/Linden (PPL, $425M refinanced in 2025) and General Atlantic (bought TEAM Services, a home-care and payroll platform that includes FMS, for about $3B including debt at about 10x EBITDA, April 2026).

THE PAYROLL-CERTAINTY SLA SOLVES A PROBLEM THE DOSSIER'S OWN BEST ANALOG DOES NOT HAVE. The pitch is a credit-line backstop 'if the state's payment is late'. In Wisconsin's CY2026 FEA contract (the hard analog) the Department itself releases Medicaid funds into the disbursement account for worker and vendor payments, and the FEA may not draw ahead of settlement. Missed payroll there is a fiscal corrective-action trigger and fee-withholding ground, i.e. table stakes, not a differentiator. The documented payroll failures in NY, PA and NJ were FI-side operations (enrollment, onboarding, call-center, deductions), not late state money. So the backstop mostly insures the FI's own execution failure, uncompensated, while requiring a very large credit facility (the dossier's own math is about $120M for a two-week float at 85k participants; NY plaintiffs allege a $100M line of credit was an entry barrier). Where the state pays after the fact (MCO-paid states like NY, PA, NJ, TX), the float is real but is a balance-sheet cost, and I found no price any state pays for it. The 'earned secret' (30-40% of timesheets need a human) remains unsourced.

WHAT YOU WOULD ACQUIRE IS A REVOCABLE LICENSE, NOT A MOAT, AT PE-LEVEL PRICES AND NEAR-ZERO MARGIN. Wisconsin's FEA contract runs one calendar year (ends 2026-12-31), either party can non-renew or terminate for convenience on 90 days' notice, DHS can withhold monthly rate payments, bar expansion while under corrective action, and terminate and move participants. 'Switching costs from a multi-year state contract' is not in the contract text. States do switch (WV PPL to Palco, parts of NJ to Acumen/Palco). Margins: Wisconsin's four FEAs lost 12.5% at $76.50 per participant-month; the best (GT, about 8,500 people) made +$1.46 on $77.47; the largest (iLife, about 14,800) costs more per head than GT, so scale did not lower cost. Competitive awards price at $68.50 (NY) to $82.77 (WI). A consolidator that buys at institutional multiples a stream earning 0-6% on at-will, annually renewable, price-compressing contracts has no path to a return, and I found no FMS-only deal price to show a cheap small-FI entry exists.

REGULATORY, LIABILITY AND POLITICAL TAILS RUN AGAINST THE 'CONSOLIDATOR' FRAMING. (a) The consolidation pattern is now politically toxic: DOJ sued PPL, NY DOH and the Medicaid director on 2026-06-16 calling the award a 'sham procurement' and seeking a receiver (motion to dismiss fully briefed 2026-09-11, no ruling found); Wisconsin's audit co-chairs have questioned the PPL award; NY bills would restore multiple FIs; Alabama explicitly multi-awards with participant choice. A bid whose thesis is consolidation arrives as the backlash does. (b) Liability: a Section 3504 agent is jointly and severally liable for each participant-employer's payroll taxes; the Calderon class settlement was $162M for about 200,000 personal assistants over 14 months of NY service, on the order of a year of NY fee revenue, and an acquirer inherits legacy wage-hour exposure. (c) Demand-side policy risk the dossier does not price: the depth of the paid-family-caregiver base in self-direction is a stated federal target (Paragon urges to 'investigate, curb, and consider prohibiting' family-paid care; per search summaries only, the HHS Secretary called such programs 'rife with fraud' in April 2026 and CMS is reviewing claim-level identifiers for self-directing users). No binding rule exists yet, but the 540k-participant pool outside CA and NY is exposed.

THE WEDGE AND THE PRICE ANCHOR ARE WEAKER THAN THEY LOOK. 'EVV equals timesheet' is a shipping vendor feature (HHAX CarePay launched 2026-08-19; DCI and CYMA serve FI payroll), and EVV for self-direction depends on each state's chosen system: Michigan said its state EVV needed work before it could handle FI-run self-directed arrangements, and Virginia's EVV rollout (about 50,000 caregivers) is being contested as rushed. Federal EVV scope covers personal care and home health services, so much developmental-disability waiver FMS work (respite, supports, goods) is outside it (background knowledge, not verified this session). The $68.50 NY anchor is unreliable: the DOJ complaint says PPL later earned revenue through hourly billing 'outside the contract's stated financial structure', and advocates allege wage-and-benefit spreads, so a clean entrant may not be able to replicate whatever made NY pencil. Also two dossier items are plaintiffs' allegations, not RFP text: the $100M line of credit and prior-statewide-experience barriers come from NY petitions (Holland & Knight, Nov 2024).

objections: BUYERS DO NOT SCORE WHAT THIS COMPANY SELLS, AND A START-UP CANNOT EVEN QUALIFY. I pulled the actual Austin Energy evaluation matrix (RFP 1100 MMH3038, 7FA+e, the only 2026 public F-class independent-LTSA award found). The five scored criteria are Price 25, Technical Plan 25, Experience and Personnel 25, Business Organization 5, and two 10-point local/small-business preferences. None rewards condition-based pricing. Scores: Hanwha 61 (price 11, tech 21, experience 25, org 4); Allied 29 (price 25, tech 0, experience 4); GE 20 (price 7); MD&A 30 (price 16, tech 8). The buyer passed over the cheapest bid (Allied, full 25 price points) and paid up for the bidder with references. A no-reference entrant scores about 4 on experience. Even if it won all 25 price points it tops out near 39 (25 + about 8 tech + 4 + 2) against 61, because 50 of 100 points are technical plan and track record. The RFP also demands 100% payment and performance bonds (minimum $10M each) and five references per scope. The 10-20% condition-pricing discount is the one thing the evaluators barely weight, and the one thing a start-up cannot substitute for proof.

THE SALES CYCLE AND RAMP ARE FAR LONGER THAN A START-UP'S RUNWAY, AND THE 'FREE AUDIT' DOOR IS A COMMODITY. Austin took 163 days from RFP issue (2026-02-16) to award recommendation (2026-07-29), before council approval and contract negotiation. NRECA's 2026 co-op guidance says co-ops 'may need to allow for two years of fine-combing contract language' on third-party LTSAs and that exit is 'difficult and costly'. My plan is 12-24 months from first call to first fee, per customer, with 1-3 contracts a year at best (the dossier found about four press-announced independent F-class term deals in 19 years). Only about 26% of GE's installed base is on an LTSA, with about 10 years average remaining life (GE 10-K), so the 'expiring LTSA' trigger that makes the audit urgent applies to few units. Troutman (200+ LTSAs) and consultants (IEM, Mercer Thompson) already sell LTSA reviews, so the free audit is not differentiated. CAC is five unpaid forensic audits per prospect, a 6-24 month cycle, and bond/reference gating, against a 12-18% gross margin. Payback is not plausible before the capital is gone.

THE SAVING IS SMALL RELATIVE TO WHAT THE BUYER RISKS, AND THE TARGET CUSTOMER CLASS IS BEING ABSORBED. The pitch saves $0.3-1M per unit-year on a $3-5M fee. A 230 MW unit at the idea's own PJM cap price of $325/MW-day earns about $27M a year of capacity revenue (my arithmetic), so the saving is roughly 1-4% of the revenue the unit protects. Winter Storm Elliott penalties ran at about 83% of capacity payments for penalized resources, and the buyer is asked to hand the maintenance of that asset to an unproven counterparty. Austin's choice of the highest-reference bidder at a price score of 11/25 shows the buyer behaviour. The idea's named first customers, 'PE-backed IPPs', are the segment being rolled into in-house platforms. NRG closed 13 GW from LS Power, Vistra closed Lotus (2.6 GW) and has Cogentrix (5.5 GW) closing late 2026, Talen has about 2.6 GW of Energy Capital Partners plants pending, and Constellation closed Calpine on 2026-01-07 (55 GW combined). That is roughly 24 GW of mostly private-equity-held gas fleet moving to scale owners in about 12 months, perhaps 60-80 large-frame turbines (my arithmetic, assuming 300-400 MW of plant output per turbine). What remains is co-ops and municipals: RFP-bound, bond-requiring, board-approved, two-year cycles, and rate-case sensitive. Sulzer's H1-2026 report also notes customers deferring service cycles on high energy prices.

THE CORE 'PROBLEM' IS OVERSTATED, AND THE DATA NEEDED TO SOLVE IT IS HELD BY THE INCUMBENT. The pitch says OEM equivalent-hours formulas are fleet averages, so a clean baseload unit subsidizes a start-heavy neighbor. GE's factored-hours method (GER-3620, per Combined Cycle Journal) already scales by base vs peak hours, starts, trips, fuel, and turning-gear hours, and PJM's Market Monitor shows OEMs use different unit-specific weightings (for example starts x15 + base hours + peak hours x5). I only reached these through search summaries; the PJM file served an HTML block page. The real leftover is formula conservatism against measured condition. That is already sold, unbundled, to non-LTSA owners as rotor and hot-section life-extension work (MD&A, consultants), and Austin's RFP bundles rotor end-of-life assessment into the fixed fee. I searched specifically for an OEM or owner offering or asking for condition-priced LTSAs and found none. The dossier reads that as white space; with no owner request found either, I read it as absent demand. The condition model also needs controller and operating data, which OEMs control through LTSA and technology-sharing terms (US patent 8,332,910; Yokogawa describes OEM LTSAs 'restricting control functionality and data availability'). The units you want to take out of OEM contracts are the ones where the OEM can throttle your data.

UNIT ECONOMICS AND THE INSURER WRAP DO NOT CLOSE. Independent turbine services are a thin-margin business. EthosEnergy, the largest independent with about 3,600 staff, contributed $34M adjusted EBITDA to Wood in 2023, and Wood got $138M for its 51% stake. The dossier already shows the 12% gross margin comes from non-OEM parts (about 30% below list), which every independent has, not from condition pricing. $100M of fees is therefore about $12-18M gross profit before the reinsurance premium, bond premiums (1-3% of contract value per broker guidance), and the fixed-price tail risk on a 10-year obligation. Wear and tear is generally excluded from property cover, and insurers say an OEM LTSA is 'viewed favorably', which makes the independent the less insurable counterparty. A parts-cost cap on wear is a near-certain attritional cost rather than a classic insurable risk, so a reinsurer is really underwriting the start-up's credit. WTW's September 2026 review calls the power property market soft (rate cuts of about 40% achievable for clean risks). That cuts both ways: reinsurers have capacity, but owners' own cover is also getting cheaper, and I found no reinsurer product of this kind. Casting scarcity (GE Aerospace paying $11.75B for CPP) hits the independent's parts supply at least as hard as the OEM's, so the 10-20% discount can disappear in the cycle.

result.what_would_change_my_mind: Specific, testable evidence in this order. (1) Demand: written LOIs or RFP language from at least 3 owners (co-ops, municipals, or non-platform IPPs) that make condition-based pricing a scored criterion or a budgeted line, plus 5 completed audits where measured savings versus the equivalent-hours price are at or above the gate's 8% threshold after non-OEM parts are stripped out. If most of the saving is just cheaper parts, it is not a condition-pricing business. (2) A credit-bearing counterparty: a surety willing to bond $10M+ annual contracts, or a bonded ISP (Hanwha, Allied, MD&A, Wood) that agrees to be the contracting party and white-label the pricing and underwriting layer. That turns this into a capital-light software and underwriting business with no references problem. (3) A written reinsurer quote for a parts-cost excess-of-loss priced below the customer saving, with fronting-carrier counsel confirming it is not unlicensed insurance. (4) A reference path: one paid first contract that is not a 9-10-year bonded LTSA, for example a 3-year hot-gas-path or rotor condition-assessment agreement on one co-op unit, proving the model before the scored RFP. (5) Proof that the OEM will not match: a case where GE, Siemens or MHI refused to reprice a top-quartile unit when an independent bid arrived. (6) A corrected addressable-unit list built from EIA-860 and OEM install data showing at least 300 F-class units that are not in a scale fleet, not under a long LTSA, and over about 10 years old. Without (1) and (2), I would not move off a kill."

objections: The strongest responder is not the OEM, it is the independent that already owns the wedge, and condition pricing is a contract term it can copy. Hanwha Power (PSM merged with Hanwha Power Systems in March 2026, Hanwha Group behind it) is the company the DOJ named in 2015 as the other leading 7FA aftermarket provider alongside GE. It already sells modular LTA/LTMA/Frame agreements with no parts exclusivity, a remote-monitoring 'Intelligent Data' platform, and a new 9-year US LTSA (Trumbull, June 2026). Adding a measured-wear true-up and a reinsurance quote is a pricing clause, not hardware. Counter-positioning (the idea's moat) only works against a party that would cannibalize an existing book. Hanwha, Allied, MD&A and Ethos have no averaged-hours book to protect, so nothing stops them from copying. The entrant also owns no hardware: its pooled spares and serial-level condition data come from ideas 1 and 2, which the gate found are already ISP products (PSM ready-to-install exchange, MD&A seed rotors, Ethos rotor program, ProEnergy's $350M pool). So the startup is a channel-conflicted middleman sitting on its own competitors' parts, repair and outage data. The dossier's ~12% gross margin is already after parts substitution that every independent has. Capital is also consolidating around the incumbents in 2026: Capstreet bought TOPS (Feb), Allied bought Ethos's generator assets (Apr), Allied bought TRS (Aug), and Warren Equity acquired Allied.

The only hard market test shows buyers do not buy on price, and a startup scores near zero on the criteria that decide the award. In Austin's RFP 1100 MMH3038 (7FA+e, July 29, 2026) the weights were price 25, technical plan 25, experience 25, small and local business 20, organization 5. Allied had the lowest price (25/25) and finished at 29. It scored 0/25 on technical plan and 4/25 on experience. Hanwha had a worse price score (11/25) but 21/25 on technical plan and 25/25 on experience, and won with 61. GE scored 7/25 on price and 20 total. MD&A scored 30. A new entrant bidding 10-20% under the OEM would score roughly 25 + 0-8 + 4, or about 29-37, against 61, because evaluators score references and a proven technical plan. The RFP requires a payment bond and a performance bond, each 100% of the annual contract, a 5% bid bond, and five references each for similar maintenance, parts supplied and monitoring. 'Condition' is already table stakes: the same RFP asks for rotor end-of-life assessment or exchange and optional remote monitoring inside a fixed quarterly fee. The pitch's differentiators are not what the buyer scored, and the thing the buyer scored (track record) cannot be bought in year one.

The contestable demand is small and the biggest competitor is non-consumption. GE's filings say it holds annual service contracts on 'over 25%' of its gas installed base and serves the rest through transactional outage and parts sales (~1,800 of ~7,000 units under LTSA at end-2025). So roughly three quarters of owners have already chosen not to sign a multi-year contract, and the pitch asks them to sign a 10-year fixed obligation with an unproven counterparty. The Form 10 also puts GE's LTSA renewal rate at about 70%, and it says more than 70% of existing agreements have over 10 years left, so near-term roll-off is thin. My rough flow math (derived, with assumptions): if 1,800 units roll off evenly over 10 years that is ~180 a year globally. At 30% non-renewal, ~54 units a year leave GE contracts. If US F-class units are 15-25% of those (my assumption, not sourced), that is ~8-14 units a year, and Hanwha, Allied, MD&A, Wood Group and Ethos all bid for them. The $100M path needs 25-35 units, which is 2-4 years of every US F-class unit leaving an OEM LTSA. Taking units from existing independent contracts means beating the incumbent independent on references. The 'free forensic LTSA audit' door is also a commodity: Troutman says it has structured LTSAs for 200+ turbines, and IEM and Mercer Thompson present on LTSA rethinks at the 7F Users Group.

The OEM does not need to respond, and where it does respond it reprices selectively, so the adverse-selection logic is untested and the 'overcharge' is partly negotiable. GE lost Austin with a price score of 7/25 and did not move, which fits a supplier with a 116 GW backlog that prioritizes capacity for new equipment. Losing small-municipal 7FA bids costs it little, and it leaves the price umbrella for Hanwha and Allied rather than for a new entrant. When a large buyer pushes, OEMs reprice. NV Energy reportedly renegotiated LTSAs across a ~6,500 MW fleet (CCJ, via search summary) and signed a 12-year GE 7FA/D11 agreement. A GE presentation (via search summary) says inspection intervals are baselines adjustable to unit duty and fuel. Contract guidance tells owners to benchmark parts against the open market, strip out the OEM's embedded collateral-damage cover and buy it separately, and negotiate a right to reprice or terminate if non-competitive. The biggest fleets (FPL 52 units, Southern 39, Calpine 34) are in-house or on fleet-wide OEM deals. So the prize is a slice of mid-size owners, and each of those can reopen its OEM deal with a free consultant's help and an independent bid in hand. GE's Gas Power also states guarantees (outage duration, availability, reliability) as a standard LTSA feature, which weakens the 'delay and availability guarantee' as a differentiator.

The insurer wrap is the least proven piece, and it can be bought around the entrant or by its competitors. No parts-cost excess-of-loss for gas-turbine hot gas path was found in any search. Standard property cover excludes wear and tear (Aon authors in POWER), and the same piece says OEM-performed LTSA maintenance is 'viewed favorably' by insurers, which is a point against an independent. Parametric forced-outage cover already exists and is 'implemented at various assets in the U.S.', so the availability-risk piece can be bought directly by an owner with no LTSA middleman. The closest cost-cap precedents are wind (GCube Enhanced Defects Coverage; Holmes Murphy extended warranty), and GCube's own 2021 report said low-priced, broad-terms entrants took large losses and pushed insurers to exit. The 2026 energy insurance market is soft, with overcapacity and 10-50% rate cuts per Willis and Gallagher. That helps the entrant get a quote, but the same cheap capacity is available to Hanwha and Allied, and soft-market capacity tends to leave mid-term, while the entrant's 10-year fixed-price obligation (about $300M or more of contingent liability across 30 units, per the dossier) stays. A weaker point: a condition model built from borescope, NDE and operating data needs data the entrant sees only after it signs. Controls and historians sit with the OEM, and outage inspection data sits with whoever performs the outage (GE, Hanwha, Allied). Evidence on OEM data restrictions is thin (a Yokogawa paper and a patent), so treat that as unverified.

result.what_would_change_my_mind: Five things, any two of which would move me from fatal to serious. (1) A signed term sheet from a reinsurer or MGA for parts-cost excess-of-loss on F-class hot gas path at a premium below about 40% of the claimed saving, with a named fronting carrier. This is the dossier's kill test 1, and a quote that exists only for the entrant, not for any ISP, would be the real moat. (2) A surety that will write 100% payment and performance bonds for a new entrant on multi-million-dollar annual contracts, plus a parent or guarantor with enough balance sheet. (3) A written, exclusive or priority hardware, repair and data agreement with one established ISP (Hanwha, Allied, MD&A, Ethos or Sulzer) at cost-plus. That would fix the channel-conflict and no-hardware problem, but it also means the ISP could do this itself, so the question becomes why it would not. (4) Three or more RFPs or private bids where no independent offered any condition-based or true-up element and the buyer said it would have paid for one. Austin shows the opposite, since condition is already bundled. (5) A built roll-off list from EIA-860 and OEM install data showing at least 15 US F-class units a year leaving OEM LTSAs in 2027-2029, with at least five owners saying they would sign a 7+ year fixed-price deal with a startup if a reinsurer stood behind it. Separately, a pivot that sells the condition and underwriting layer to the ISPs (Hanwha, Allied) instead of competing with them would sidestep objections 1 and 2. It is a different, unproven business, and I found no evidence for or against it."

verdicts.substitutes: (1) ERCOT and PUCT run the Batch Zero verification and audit in-house via RFIs to transmission and distribution providers, with a Dec 10, 2026 report; no outside verifier role described. (2) The posted deposit is itself the reality test: ERCOT already excluded 373 projects / 302 GW from Batch Zero and conditionally included 362 projects / about 194 GW. (3) Utilities screen with collateral and tariffs: AEP Ohio pipeline fell from more than 30 GW to 13 GW, Exelon from 43 GW to 25 GW with about $1B collateral posted. (4) Banks write letters of credit; surety bonds are a cheaper substitute (brokers quote 1-3% of bond amount; NYISO accepts them; Batch Zero acceptance unconfirmed). (5) Law firms and engineering consultancies advise on documentation and load studies. (6) ERCOT is a single queue, so intra-Texas duplicates are visible to ERCOT already.
verdicts.revenue_math_check: Their $100M at 100% penetration does not survive reachable counts. Utilities with 1 GW+ pipelines: six clearly qualify, my estimate is 30-50 (not 100), so 45 x $400K = $18M ceiling, not $40M. ISOs: 7 x $2M assumes ISOs buy a third-party registry; they buy workflow software or build in-house, realistic is 2-3 buyers. 2,000 applications x $15-20K assumes the scored applicant pays; only happens if an ISO makes the attestation mandatory, with no sign of that. Credit layer: the $80-145M per cycle pool relied on 80% forfeiture, which is not in the adopted rule; financing refundable security costs about 1-3% a year (surety range) and is a balance-sheet business for banks, sureties and funds, and the July 2026 Batch Zero posting window has closed. Realistic ceiling about $27M data layer plus $10-18M arranger fees.
verdicts.upside_assumptions: FERC or at least two ISOs adopt a standard cross-queue verified-ready attestation; statutory and confidentiality limits on furnishing duplicate-request data are cleared; 3 ISOs at $2M, 20 utilities at $400K, 500 paid applications at about $16K, 45 lender/insurer seats at $100K (about $27M); plus $10-18M arranger fees on third-party deposit funding at a 15% share of a $20-90M annual fee pool across 2-3 states copying the Texas design. Even then it stays well under $100M.
verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: FAILED on a key number. The PUCT adopted 16 TAC 25.194 (Project 58481) on Sept 18, 2026, effective Oct 8. The 80% forfeiture at a six-month grace period was in the March draft; the adopted rule gives 24 months measured against the energization schedule as a whole, then draws only for amounts owed, keeps 20% tied to unused capacity and returns the rest; zero allocation returns the security. Security is posted within 60 days after ERCOT's study allocates capacity. Sources are Utility Dive and colocationscout (White & Case describes a staged 20% release); I did not read the order itself. Also unverified and likely adverse: per the House committee analysis of SB 6, the PUC must bar utilities from selling, sharing or disclosing duplicate-request disclosures, which collides with a furnisher-funded registry; the enrolled text was not read. Lending licensing for the credit layer is open.
verdicts.deciding_reason: The $50,000-per-MW deposit is itself the reality test, ERCOT already ran the filter and runs the audit in-house as a one-time process ending Dec 10, 2026 (before any product could ship), and the adopted rule removed the 80% forfeiture that made the credit layer big. What remains is a diligence-data shop competing with Enverus, Wood Mackenzie, Cleanview and LandGate, with no budget-bearing buyer for a cross-queue registry and a statute that discourages data sharing. Kill rather than shrink into a boutique.

verdicts.legal_or_premise_check: Cost-share tiers and rate-year rules confirmed (CRS IN12723: 5%/10%/15% at 6/8/10%; FY2028 uses lower of FY2025 or FY2026; FY2029 on uses the rate from 3 years earlier; 13.33% delay). Policy risk: Senate Agriculture draft (Aug 6, not advanced) would delay to FY2029 and raise the top tier to 20% in FY2031. Gainshare is legally poisoned: the Wisconsin/Osnes contingent-fee pattern drew DOJ action (a $751,571 False Claims Act settlement), USDA OIG flagged the conflict of interest, FNS found 42 of 53 agencies using biased practices, and FNS QC Policy Memo 16-02 requires 30-day notice to FNS and treats non-compliant consultant activity as unallowable. I did not retrieve 2 CFR 200.324 or find an express gainshare ban. Medicaid sec. 71106 (3% threshold, FY2030) is a real mandate but incumbents are subsidizing implementation.
verdicts.deciding_reason: There is a real mandated budget and independence from the integrator is a genuine angle, but the only lever that scales to $100M, a share of the avoided cost-share, rides on a practice FNS, OIG and DOJ already punished. Without it this is a $10-30M niche where SAS, Maximus, PCG and KPMG already sell the adjacent product, states do much of the fixing in-house, and the first year new tooling can move cost-share is FY2030. Weak, not worth a pick.

result.pool_note: Zero picks. Neither idea reaches a $20M median or a defensible $100M upside (medians about $5M and $8M, upsides about $45M and $60M). The headline pools are real (the $9.7B deposit ceiling and the $9.4B a year SNAP cost shift), but the person who signs for a tool is not the person who bears the penalty, and the money that moves goes to balance sheets, large incumbents or in-house staff. In both cases the mandate that created the why-now also created the free or incumbent substitute: ERCOT's own one-time audit and the deposit itself in Idea 1, and SAS/Maximus/PCG, state QC units and nonprofits in Idea 2. Idea 1 also failed on a premise number (the adopted PUCT rule dropped the 80% forfeiture at six months). Full report: /Users/asherperemel/projects/business-idea-search-work/biz/round2/gate/R1.md

objections: THE INSURER WRAP, THE ONE THING THAT IS SUPPOSED TO BE DIFFERENT, IS PROBABLY UNINSURABLE OR DUPLICATIVE. New York's insurance regulator (opinion 04-05-01, 2004) held that an insurer may not indemnify a maintenance-agreement maker for the cost of performing scheduled maintenance, because there is 'no fortuitous occurrence under the agreement to insure against.' A 'parts-cost cap' on planned hot-gas-path and major-inspection work is exactly that. What remains insurable is unplanned resulting damage, which owners already buy under property and equipment-breakdown cover, and the 2026 power market is soft (WTW: rate cuts of about 40% for clean risks), so the wrap adds little. Wear and tear is excluded and insurers view an OEM LTSA favorably (Aon, via POWER, per the dossier). That leaves two outcomes. Either the tail stays on the start-up's own balance sheet, or it is dressed up as insurance, the exact pattern that killed the round-1 home-value-guarantee finalist. The NY opinion is old and one state, so it is a strong signal, not a ruling. But nobody has produced even one reinsurer quote, and the gate itself made that the kill test.

THE ENTRY TICKET IS CLOSED, AND THE 'FREE AUDIT' DOOR IS BLOCKED BY PROCUREMENT LAW. The target buyers (munis, co-ops) must run competitive RFPs. Austin's RFP required payment and performance bonds of 100% of annual value ($10M minimum) and five references per category, and experience was worth 25 of 100 points (a new entrant scores about 4). Sureties also require a general indemnity agreement backed by the owners' personal assets, which a first-time founder cannot give. Public-procurement rules commonly bar a vendor that helped draft the scope or specification from bidding (Iowa AG manual, MARTA guidance, GAO protest practice). A free LTSA forensic audit that shapes the owner's re-bid is the textbook conflict, so the takeout either goes to RFP without you or you are disqualified. The dossier's best evidence, Austin's 2026 award to Hanwha, is probably an incumbent renewal, not a displacement of an OEM. Austin's council approved an 84-month Sand Hill Unit 5 maintenance contract with Power Systems MFG (now part of Hanwha Power, merged March 2026) in 2011 for a cap of $22.9M, about $3.3M a year. That is my inference (no document names Hanwha as incumbent). It means the one 'independent wins' data point shows buyers rewarding incumbency, not novelty.

THE CUSTOMER POOL IS SMALLER AND SHRINKING, AND THE ROLL-OFF 'WHY NOW' IS OLD. GE Vernova has about 1,700 to 1,800 of about 7,000 gas turbines on LTSAs with a roughly 10-year average remaining life, and says renewal is about 70% (spin-off filings). So the expiring-LTSA flow is small and mostly renews. The pitched buyers are also being absorbed. Vistra agreed to buy Cogentrix (5.5 GW, $4B, from PE owner Quantum) in January 2026 after buying Lotus (2.6 GW) in October 2025, Talen is buying two PJM CCGTs for $3.5B, and Q1 2026 US power M&A hit a six-year high. Those acquirers run in-house or OEM-master programs, so the PE-backed IPP segment is turning into the segment least likely to sign with a start-up. What is left is munis and co-ops, which run into objection 2. The overlap of 'wants a non-OEM LTSA', 'is not a big fleet' and 'can legally sole-source or pick a start-up' is likely a few dozen units, below the dossier's 150-300 estimate. Nobody has built the EIA-860 list of expiring units, and I found no US F-class unit count by model either.

CONDITION PRICING IS PARTLY ALREADY THERE, PARTLY UNMEASURABLE, AND INVITES ADVERSE SELECTION AND MORAL HAZARD. GE's own maintenance method (GER-3620) already counts factored hours and starts separately, with factors for fuel, peak load, injection and trips (CCJ, PJM). So 'OEM prices on a fleet-average formula' is overstated for GE. Siemens-style EOH conversions are the more averaged case. The true remaining life of hot-gas-path parts is only observable when the machine is opened, so the 'annual true-up to measured condition' is a retrospective price change at the outage. Borescope data is a surface snapshot, not remaining life. The provider is not the operator (Power Engineering): starts, trips, tuning, dispatch and fuel quality are the owner's choices, and the owners who volunteer for condition pricing are the ones who know their unit is better than the formula. The Austin Monitor (2013) reported three Austin Energy gas-turbine maintenance agreements (GE, TransCanada Turbines and Wood Group P&W) needing amendments of up to $8.3M on a $16M deal (about 52%) for unanticipated maintenance as units cycled harder, and the utility bore it. The model also needs OEM controls and operating data, which OEM LTSAs reportedly restrict (Yokogawa, a vendor with an interest). That adds contract fights and NERC CIP access burdens before the first price is quoted.

THE ECONOMICS AND CAPITAL DO NOT CLOSE. The dossier's own build gives about 12% gross margin from non-OEM parts substitution, which every independent already has, before reinsurance premium, bond cost (about 1-3% of bond value per year, per surety guidance), condition-model cost and overhead. A 10-year fixed-price promise on 30 units is $300M+ of contingent liability. The cost side is exposed to the same scarcity the pitch cites as its why-now: single-crystal castings are the 'most stubborn constraint' (WoodMac; GE Aerospace's $11.75B CPP deal closes 2H 2027), so a fixed-price seller at 10-20% under the OEM carries parts-inflation risk, and OEM quotes already moved from about 4 to 12-16 weeks. The PJM price collar ends after 2029/30, inside the term. The incumbents are PE-backed with thin profits: Wood said EthosEnergy added $34M of adjusted EBITDA in 2023 with about 3,600 staff, and sold its 51% stake for $138M. Even GE, with all the data and the hardware, lists its ability to estimate long-term service obligations as a risk factor, and paid a $200M SEC penalty (December 2020) over power-segment LTSA revenue accounting, which is a disclosure issue, not a loss, but shows how hard these contracts are to value. The one tailwind, a soft insurance market, is cyclical and not under the venture's control. A plain independent LTSA with none of the three differentiators survives, but it is the Hanwha/Wood/Allied/MD&A product already on offer, with a 2-year build and no moat.

result.what_would_change_my_mind: Five things, any one of which would move this from fatal to serious. (1) A written, priced quote from a rated carrier or reinsurer for a parts-cost excess-of-loss that covers scheduled hot-gas-path and major-inspection costs, not only unplanned damage, at a premium below about half the claimed saving. It would need a counsel opinion that the structure is a service contract or surety in the intended states (the NY fortuity problem), or a licensed fronting carrier that accepts it. (2) A surety indication for a $10M+ per year performance and payment bond for the start-up, with a rated parent or sponsor guarantee standing in for personal indemnity. (3) Written confirmation from at least three of five target munis or co-ops that they can sole-source or negotiate, or that a free audit vendor may still bid, plus an EIA-860 and OEM-install list showing 40+ US F-class units outside large fleets with LTSA expiry or transactional exposure in 2027-2030. (4) Evidence from five real audits that the median saving versus the owner's actual OEM price is at least 8% after the independent-parts discount is stripped out, meaning condition pricing itself adds value. (5) A signed data-rights arrangement showing condition data can be obtained without OEM gatekeeping. If the reinsurer quote and the surety indication both fail, as the gate's own kill test already anticipates, the venture is only a plain independent LTSA, which is a crowded product and not a venture-scale new business.

objections: CAPITAL. The money that would fund this business already goes to qualified incumbents, so a new entrant is not the cheapest way to buy capacity. Doncasters' prospectus describes customer-funded capex of up to 80% at an incumbent. Howmet's CFO says its investments are backed by customer contracts. Siemens Energy, the obvious 'non-GE' IGT buyer, announced about $1B of US investment on 2026-02-03. That includes a Tampa blade-and-vane expansion and sits next to its existing $139M dedicated Chromalloy JV. Chromalloy separately put $16.5M into Tampa casting in May 2026, with new vacuum furnaces installed in July and a ramp planned for early 2027. Incumbent brownfield adds cost $50-70M (Howmet Wichita Falls about $70M, Doncasters Auburn $50M, Bochum $52M). Greenfield is $150-300M per $100M of revenue. At independents' 16-22% EBITDA margins, one plant earns $18-22M a year on that capex. Even Doncasters is not self-funding: its FY2025 net loss was $173M on $222M of interest, which the prospectus blames mostly on non-cash PIK interest. A founder with no qualified positions cannot get a lower cost of capital than the incumbents. Nobody has prepaid an unqualified entrant; the researcher and I both found zero cases.

TIMING. The why-now window closes before the plant could produce a qualified part. Howmet says commitments made in August 2026 yield capacity around August 2028. Doncasters' partnerships reach run rate in 2028 and its greenfield plant in 2029. Safran Rennes opens in 2027, and Chromalloy Tampa ramps in early 2027. The one secondary source on OEM qualification, a blog about a blade supplier, gives 18-48 months, and Doncasters says approvals often take years. A plant funded in 2027 and built in 2028-29 therefore ships qualified single-crystal parts around 2030-31. The best case is that GE Vernova's backlog is still climbing (116 GW in Q2, 125 GW expected by year-end, 2031 slots being sold). That makes OEMs lock in incumbent capacity now, not a 2031 newcomer. A 10-year take-or-pay signed in 2027 would also run through the 2026 orders peak that Wood Mackenzie expects. No buyer's CFO would accept that risk on an unqualified plant.

REGULATORY AND STRUCTURE. The 'buyer consortium plus open-book cost-plus plus 10-year take-or-pay' design is a joint purchasing and information-exchange arrangement among competing turbine OEMs. The FTC and DOJ withdrew the 2000 Competitor Collaboration Guidelines, which contained the purchasing safety zones, in December 2024. They opened a replacement inquiry in February 2026 (comments closed 2026-04-24), and I found no replacement. Co-funders would be structuring in 2027 with no safe harbor and a lawyer's bill. Foreign OEM co-funders (Siemens Energy, Mitsubishi) in a plant that also takes defense or Navy work raise FOCI, ITAR and CFIUS questions. That last point is my inference, not sourced. The only regulatory event that could hand a founder a qualified nucleus is a forced CPP divestiture. I found no reporting of any FTC or DOJ review or remedy. GE says CPP will run as a separate unit, like Avio Aero, Unison and Dowty, and CPP is only about 20% power, so the pressure for divestiture is weak.

EXECUTION: inputs, yields and people. Doncasters vertically integrated into superalloy melt and ceramic cores because external supply chains are 'capacity constrained'. A new foundry would buy master alloy and cores from suppliers whose output incumbents already hold. Critical-mineral inputs are tight: US-bound yttrium shipments are reportedly down about 75% in 2026 from China's export controls, and North American coating lines have paused. Yttria is used in thermal barrier coatings; I could not confirm a shell or facecoat link. Rhenium, a by-product minor metal, has about 80% of its demand in aerospace. Single-crystal yield is the classic new-entrant killer: DOE says yields are low, and an industry analyst quoted by Reuters says 'half or more' may be scrapped on new designs. Furnaces carry 'long lead times for installation, commissioning and approval'. The 20 or so key people (melt, core, DS/SX furnace, NDT Level III) are being recruited by SpaceX and GE at the same time, and quality roles take 6-12 months to train. SpaceX's own Bastrop foundry still has state permits pending, so even the best-funded entrant has not cleared the permit stage.

MOAT AND EXIT. Neutrality is not a durable power. Doncasters' prospectus already sells 'dedicated capacity' to OEMs, so counter-positioning is taken. If the neutral foundry succeeds, it becomes the next acquisition target. Pursuit Aerospace (CD&R) is on its sixth casting deal since 2023. CPP itself was a neutral independent until GE bought it, which is the idea's own origin story. Lenders and consortium members will demand change-of-control and no-captive covenants, which cap the exit. The premium multiples cited (CPP 5.9x revenue, Doncasters about 8x sales) attach to qualified installed positions, not to a de novo plant. The 'lost neutral supplier' premise is mostly false. GE Vernova is a separate company from GE Aerospace. Howmet holds over 50% of IGT blades. Doncasters, PCC and Chromalloy remain. The gate and dossier both found the same, so there is no customer pain acute enough to prepay a newcomer.
