result.pricing: Fixed PMPM per enrolled high-need HCBS member, priced at no more than 95% of the plan's fully loaded in-house cost for the same work, with 10-15% of fees at risk on operational KPIs. R1 desk $20-35 PMPM (about $300 per member-year). R2 operations stack $40-60 PMPM (about $600). R3 coordination capacity, inclusive of R2, $110-150 PMPM (about $1,300-1,800). Three-year terms with per-plan minimums and wind-down fees. No savings share before R4. After R4 opens, shared savings (about 20%) apply only to parents holding both Medicare and Medicaid risk, on benchmarks pre-registered from stepped-wedge data. The fee replaces existing admin, so it does not take a new slice of medical dollars.
result.why_now: Plan Medicaid margins are at a trough and SG&A is being cut (Centene about $480M of 2026 savings; Medicaid HBR 93.9% in Q2 2026), while caseload ratios and KPIs are mandated and do not shrink. Big Five Medicaid enrollment fell 6.5% in the year to June 2026, which turns fixed in-house teams into the problem and makes variable-cost capacity the benefit. Exits and rebids (Elevance in DC and Louisiana, Centene leaving Arkansas expansion, the Arizona ALTCS rebid) force plans to stand up or wind down LTSS operations on a deadline. EVV is universal, so exception data exists in every state. CMS and state enforcement attention to personal care makes claims leakage a board topic. CareBridge's growth and D-SNP extension show plans buy the category, which makes a second source valuable.
result.moat: Scale economies is the primary power. A 24/7 desk and flex coordinator bench have a staffing floor (illustratively about $280 per member-year at 3,000 members versus about $100 at 30,000). A sub-scale plan cannot staff nights, weekends and vacancies efficiently. A pool across competing plans can, and only a non-plan can organize it. It is reached when 3 or more plans in a state, or about 30k members, share the desk. Switching costs are secondary: delegation embedded in plan workflows, state-notified subcontracts, audit trail and 3-year terms. A cornered-resource position is conditional and later: multi-plan stepped-wedge outcome data, which nobody has. Neutrality itself is not a power, since Elevance can copy a clause in a quarter. It is kept as free customer-held contract rights (no plan equity, change-of-control exit, audited firewall).
result.bottom_up_market: Managed-LTSS users, July 2024: 1,856,121 (CMS, via the dossier). Remove California (312,162, mostly institutional or limited services; IHSS sits outside plans) and New York (346,892, MLTC-only plans, unstable procurement), leaving 1,197,067. At about 55% HCBS-using (unverified), that is about 660k members. Plan spend on HCBS coordination plus operations is about $1,800-2,800 per member-year (assumption: coordination of $1,300-2,100 from caseload ratios of 1:48-75 times about $100k loaded cost, plus $500-700 of operations), so the pool is about $1.2-1.8B a year. $100M is 6-8% of that. Reachable payers: about 6-10 non-Elevance parents with over 50k LTSS lives, plus perhaps 15-25 regional, Blue and provider-sponsored entities (unverified). NY MLTC (347k) is a second wave, not counted. Upside needs 85k lives, about 13% of the base or about 8% with NY. Sources: CMS data via the dossier; Truven/AdvancingStates caseload table (pre-2018); VCU on CCC Plus 1:75; SCDHHS SFY 2027 rate certification.
result.upside_assumptions: Net revenue is fees retained (no pass-through), year 8. The case is built to find the minimum assumptions that clear $100M: R1 20k lives at $300 ($6M), R2 25k at $600 ($15M), R3 40k at $1,500 ($60M), R4 KPI pool plus shared savings on 20k aligned lives ($10M), R5 modules ($10M), for about $101M on 85k lives. Named assumptions: (1) 85k lives is about 13% of the 660k base, or about 8% with NY MLTC added, roughly CareBridge's reach without its captive volume. (2) 8-10 plan contracts in 8-10 states across about 6 parents, none over 30% of revenue and no state over 35%. (3) R3 sells at 95% of in-house cost at a 10-15% margin. Blended gross margin is about 34% and EBITDA about 14%, so $100M of revenue is roughly $14M of EBITDA. (4) First paid pilot by month 9-18, R3 live by month 24-30. (5) Without R3 the revenue is only about $55-60M. Odds of this case are 5-8% (judgment). Sensitivity: +10k R3 lives is about +$9M, and +$100 on the R3 price is about +$4M.
result.competitors_and_edge: CareBridge/Carelon (Elevance): scale, at-risk model, nearly 200k patients, D-SNP extension in 2025. We lose where a plan wants risk transfer or Carelon discounts hard. We win on fixed price, simpler procurement with no downstream risk, and being the second source that disciplines Carelon's price. HHAeXchange: 180+ MCOs, payer analytics, launched managed RCM for agencies in Apr 2026; a software seat, not operations labor, and also our data dependency and a possible channel or acquirer. CareCentrix (independent LTSS, guaranteed savings), Cityblock/Homeward (delivery plus capitation, 10k-life first contracts), Papa, ShiftMed and Optum are adjacent. The biggest competitor is plan in-house teams (Centene 338K LTSS lives); the bet is on sub-scale plans. Evolent shows the failure mode: FY2025 revenue down 26.6%, top four customers 68.5% of revenue, explicit insourcing risk. The honest edge is moderate: price, pooled 24/7 scale for sub-scale plans, no downstream-risk procurement, and credible non-plan ownership. It is not a technology lead.
result.riskiest_assumption: A non-Elevance, non-UnitedHealth Medicaid LTSS plan will pay a fixed, non-contingent fee (about $40+ PMPM for operations, about $110+ PMPM for ratio-assured coordination) from its administrative or care-coordination budget to an unaffiliated vendor, rather than insource, buy from CareBridge, or insist on savings-only. Behind it sits a second assumption: our cost to serve R3 leaves a 10-15% margin at 95% of the plan's in-house cost, even though caseload ratios stop automation from cutting headcount below the ratio.
result.two_week_test: A priced-offer call sprint costing $0-3k. Days 1-3: write a one-page offer (R1 $300, R2 $600, R3 $1,500 per member-year; 90-day paid pilot at cost plus 10%) and list 40 contacts at 10 or more non-Elevance, non-UHC plan entities, using ex-plan operators for introductions and optionally 3-4 expert-network calls. Days 2-12: hold 12 or more calls, at least 8 with director-level or higher budget-relevant people. Ask five things: (1) fully loaded cost per HCBS member-year for coordination and for HCBS operations; (2) exception volume and time to resolve; (3) what they pay CareBridge or others; (4) who signs and which budget line pays; (5) fixed fee versus savings-only. Request a de-identified data sample for a free retrospective. In parallel, desk-check caseload and delegation language in six state contracts and the state subcontractor lists (Iowa, Tennessee, Texas, Ohio, Arizona) to see whether non-Elevance plans still use CareBridge. Pass: at least 5 of 8 give a loaded cost within $900-2,500 and call a fixed fee at or below 95% of it worth a pilot conversation; at least 2 distinct parents name a budget owner above the VP of LTSS and agree to a retrospective on 2,000+ members; no more than 3 of 8 say savings-only or nothing; measured exceptions of at least 0.5 per member-month or resolution times over 4 hours. Kill: at least 6 of 8 insist on savings-only, in-house or CareBridge, or no one will name a budget owner or share a number. Then the idea reverts to the regional boutique the critics describe, and alive becomes false.
result.how_critiques_were_addressed: Concessions, then structural changes. (1) Neutral vacuum and demand: conceded that rivals already buy from CareBridge and nobody has shown they pay for neutrality. Neutrality is dropped as the pitch and price premium and kept only as free customer-held contract rights (no plan equity, change-of-control exit, audited firewall) plus a pooled-scale argument. The reason to buy is fixed price, capacity and performance. (2) MLR and unit economics: verified in 42 CFR 438.8(e)(2)(v)(A) that vendor admin, network development and utilization management are non-claims, so the fee is priced as substitution for the plan's existing admin at 95% or less of in-house cost, not as a share of spend. Care coordination is named as a quality-improvement activity in 45 CFR 158.150, so R3 may count in the numerator (to be confirmed per plan). The $30k and 5% base is dropped. $100M is re-derived as about 85k lives at $300 / $600 / $1,500, and the file states that without the labor-bearing R3 the ceiling is about $55-60M. (3) Unproven savings: no acute-savings promise in R1-R3. Fees rest on ops KPIs, capacity and hard-dollar claims leakage, and a stepped-wedge rollout generates the evidence before R4. (4) Regulation and liability: R1-R3 carry no downstream risk, so no insurance licensing; R4 comes only after per-state counsel; no hours-setting algorithm; the plan keeps authorization decisions; launch states are chosen by delegation rule. (5) Capital and neutrality contradiction: no plan equity, ROFR or board seat, capital-light with $50-80M through year 5 (versus $100-200M), non-plan growth equity, and risk capital from reinsurers or surety later. (6) Buyer health: shrinkage and SG&A cuts become the trigger for variable-cost capacity; concentration caps (no parent above 30%, no state above 35%), multi-year terms and wind-down fees. (7) Pool and data: pool recomputed without CA and NY (1.197M, about 660k HCBS-using); EVV-agnostic ingestion through the plan's own data rights is a gate in the test. Not conceded: that the whole business must shrink to a regional boutique; a layered path to about $100M exists, at 5-8% odds.

remaining_holes: The premium-price evidence is cherry-picked and partly mis-specified. In Minnesota's CFSS budget model the FMS fee is negotiated with each participant and paid out of the participant's own service budget, not by the state or a plan (MN DHS provider pages, search summary). It is tiered by budget size, not flat. Listed fees run $50-150 at MRCI, $110-150 at Lifeworks, $135-155 at PICS, $50 then $165 at GT, $165 at Accra and $200-400 at Aspen. The '$165-250' figure is the top of the range, and the small nonprofit operators the plan wants to buy charge less. A $150 blended fee on 28k participants has no support, and the 'payer and signer' section is wrong for the single biggest line in the upside.

Colorado is mislabeled as an enrollment market. HCPF ran a 2023-24 RFP and awarded FMS contracts for five years starting 2024-07-01 (HCPF IM 24-003, search summary; PDF returned 403, so awardee names are unconfirmed). Participants choose only among the awarded vendors, which in 2025 were Palco and PPL at $103.21 each. A new entrant can reach Colorado only by buying a contract holder, which is the closed-auction problem the rewrite claims to avoid. This is the same objection critique 2 raised about rate-card states, and it is not answered.

In Texas, where open enrollment is real (HHSC takes FMSA applications year-round and contracts noncompetitively), entry is free. The qualification therefore needs no purchase. What a buyer pays 1x revenue for is a book of participants who can switch FMSA at will, plus the seller's referral relationships. The rewrite's own selling point, participant choice, is what makes the acquired asset non-sticky and key-person dependent. A fixed rate with free entry also means every funded entrant competes for the same margin, and Texas FMSA counts and profitability are not sized.

Rate cards are revocable and tied to budgets. Colorado applied a 1.6% across-the-board cut in Oct 2025 (the FMS PMPM was untouched that time). Texas sets its rate by biennial review. Critique 2 listed state cuts to self-direction in MD, MO, ID, IN and CO. The rewrite files policy risk as 'not fixable' and then concentrates the thesis in budget-authority, family-caregiver-heavy programs, which are the segment most exposed to the federal and state fraud and cut push.

The acquisition math contradicts itself. The plan buys at about 1.0x revenue and calls that 6x EBITDA, which implies sellers earn about 17% EBITDA. The median case then earns 5-8% EBITDA on about $25M revenue, or $1.3-2M. On roughly $24-26M invested (about $20M of acquired revenue at 1.0x, plus about $4M of reserves, plus bid costs), that is 12-20x EBITDA actually paid. An exit at 8-10x would return $10-20M on $25M, a capital loss. The 'median' case is effectively a bear case, and the real success probability is the 8-10% upside only. This is my arithmetic from the rewrite's own figures.

Even the upside is a mediocre financial outcome. $103M of revenue at a blended 10-12% EBITDA is about $10-12M. At the roughly 10x multiples the rewrite cites for TEAM and GT, that is $100-125M of enterprise value against $60-75M of equity and debt invested over about 7 years. That is roughly 1.4-2.1x, or about 5-11% IRR before fees and dilution (my arithmetic). Revenue of $100M is not the right success test for a roll-up.

The deal count and capital do not fit the pitch. The pitch says 'buy two or three' operators with 2-6k participants each. At $110-150 PMPM that is about $8-32M of revenue in total. The upside needs 43k participants in the choice and plan segments ($69M of revenue) and budgets $35-45M of acquired revenue. That implies 6-17 deals, or 25k+ participants of organic growth in referral-driven markets with unknown customer acquisition cost. The de novo CAC read is a side note and has no result. The count of non-sponsor operators of 2-6k participants with clean records is unknown and is probably small. The only small non-sponsor operators with public financials, three of the four in Wisconsin (iLife, Premier, Outreach), lose money, and the rewrite excludes them.

The two-week test cannot reliably resolve the riskiest assumption. Seller self-reports of margin are biased upward. Asking prices anchor high. 'Fewer than 5 of 25 will share numbers' is a likely outcome for cold calls from an unknown with no capital, and it would kill the idea on access rather than on truth. The plan also says a seasoned FMS co-founder is a precondition for owner-operator trust, but sequences that recruitment after the test. A pass (3 operators with cost at or under $90, 2 open to a sale at or under 1.0x) still would not show that a buy at scale works.

Several upside links remain unsupported. The roughly 6-10 statewide rebids in the window versus about one competitive award a year nationally is an unreconciled assumption. A first-time winner taking 2 of them against PPL, Tempus, Palco and GT is optimistic. Dropping statewide RFPs from the plan would remove $23.6M, but the plan keeps them because the qualification thesis needs them. Statewide pricing at $77-83 has only loss-making and +2% cost data behind it. The New York slice depends on a receivership or statute that is unconfirmed.

HHAX sits under the plan-delegated segment as prime vendor and can squeeze the fiscal agent to a subcontract fee (the rewrite admits this). The Acumen-TEAM link remains unconfirmed, so the sponsor-comp logic is shaky in both directions. The Wisconsin protest outcome is still unknown. No FMS deal price exists anywhere, so the entire entry thesis is a stipulated multiple. A seasoned co-founder and $60-75M of capital are preconditions that the founder does not have, so this is a search-fund or PE roll-up and not a startup.
result.which_critiques_were_dodged_not_answered:
Real concessions: the payroll SLA as a price lever, technology as a moat, the Kentucky and Ohio wedge, the revolving credit line (now prefunding), the New York base case, and the 10-15% margin claim. These were dropped, not defended. That honesty is the rewrite's main credit, but it also means the original idea is gone and a different one was substituted.

Dodged or answered only by assertion:
1. Critiques 1 and 2 both said the cheap targets are the sick ones and the healthy ones sell to sponsors at about 10x. The rewrite answers with a stipulated population of healthy, non-sponsor, 15-20% margin owner-operators who sell at about 6x EBITDA. No such operator is evidenced, no deal price exists, and the only observable small non-sponsor operators (Wisconsin's) lose money. 'Relationships with owners who won't sell to a sponsor' relies on a co-founder who does not exist yet.
2. Critique 2 said rate-card states pay more but are not competitively bid, so a newcomer cannot sell into them. The rewrite's answer is 'enter by enrollment.' That holds for Texas. It fails for Colorado (a five-year RFP-awarded vendor list, per a search summary of HCPF IM 24-003). For Minnesota it conflates a participant-paid, tiered, price-transparent fee with a payer-set rate. The core objection is half answered.
3. Critique 3 said the asset is a revocable license. The rewrite redefines the asset as a 'qualification stack,' but in open-enrollment markets that stack is free to obtain, and in choice markets the acquired book is switchable at will. It never addresses that rate cards are unilaterally revocable by the state.
4. Critique 2's demand-side attack (family-caregiver cuts, federal scrutiny) is labeled 'not fixable.' The rewrite then shifts the thesis into the budget-authority, family-caregiver-heavy segment where that risk is highest.
5. Critique 1 asked for evidence that scale or process lowers cost. The rewrite concedes 'scale unproven' and offers a measurement program, but it builds a margin plan on a cost structure it has no data for.

The new risks it created (deal-count inconsistency, purchase multiple versus median margin, sequencing of the co-founder after the test) were not acknowledged.
result.upside_believable:
No. The $103M case needs at least five things to hold together and several are weakly evidenced or contradicted.
(1) $150 blended PMPM on 28k choice participants. The rate-card evidence is $103 (CO), $114-121 (TX; proposed $120.55 in 2024), and $106 (LA). The only prices near $150 are Minnesota's, where the fee is participant-paid out of the care budget and tiers down to $50-155 at the smaller nonprofit providers. A realistic $110-120 on that segment gives about $37-40M, not $50M, and the total falls to about $90M with NY and about $80M without it.
(2) 79k participants in 7 years. That is 1.6x the footprint GT built over about 21 years with H.I.G. capital, delivered here by a handful of acquisitions of 2-6k-participant operators plus unspecified organic growth in markets where PPL, Palco, GT and Acumen already operate.
(3) Winning two mid-size statewide RFPs as a first-time winner while the plan itself says about one competitive award occurs per year nationally.
(4) A New York slot opening through unconfirmed litigation or legislation.
(5) $60-75M of capital available for a business whose median case yields about 5-8% on invested capital.
The probabilities of 8-10% for the upside, about 45% for the median and 40-45% for the bear are reasonably candid, but the upside is a joint event of several low-probability conditions, so 8-10% is probably generous. And even if the upside is hit, the return is roughly 1.4-2.1x over about 7 years. The upside is not believable and, if achieved, not attractive on a capital basis. The idea is worth only the two-week test and a harder look at Minnesota, Texas and Colorado specifics before anything else.

result.rationale:
This is a services roll-up, not a seed-stage company, and it scores as a decent-sounding but capital-heavy, thin-margin small-business thesis.

Demand and pain (4): The spend is real, mandated and state-signed, with about $0.7-0.9B a year in fees. But the demand is not for anything this company sells. States and plans don't have an urgent, unmet pain that a new fiscal agent solves. The customer is a seller-owner of an existing operator, and the dossier found no FMS-only deal price. The premium-fee segment ($140+) rests on mis-specified evidence. Minnesota's fee is participant-paid and tiered, with small nonprofits charging $50-155. Colorado is a closed five-year RFP list, not an enrollment market. Texas has free entry, so there is nothing to buy except a switchable book. The only public cost data (Wisconsin) shows small operators losing money. The first-10-customers test is just a single acquisition, which needs capital the founder doesn't have.

Unit economics and capital efficiency (very poor): The plan assumes a 5-8% EBITDA margin in the median case. It buys at about 1.0x revenue, so the effective multiple paid is roughly 12-20x EBITDA on the median case. That is a capital loss at the 8-10x exit multiples it cites. Even the $103M upside is about $10-12M EBITDA, or roughly 1.4-2.1x on $60-75M invested over about 7 years. For a founder who builds profitable companies, this has the wrong shape: heavy capital, low margin, long hold, and licenses that states can revoke.

Feasibility (2): The plan needs a seasoned fiscal-agent co-founder (who doesn't exist yet) and $60-75M of sponsor-style capital. It competes for the same small targets against H.I.G. (GT Independence) and General Atlantic (TEAM). The deal count doesn't fit the pitch: "buy two or three" operators versus the 6-17 deals the upside needs. The two-week cold-call test is biased toward a kill on access (fewer than 5 of 25 sharing numbers), not on truth.

Defensibility (3): The plan itself concedes that technology is not a moat and that scale economies are unproven. The "qualification stack" is held by contracts that can be lost. Rate cards are unilaterally revocable. The consolidation backlash is a counter-positioning leg that depends on policy trends and an unconfirmed New York statute.

Timing (4): Policy is swinging toward multi-vendor choice, which is a genuine tailwind. But sponsor capital is already crowding the best targets, the open procurements are not enterable, and demand-side risk is rising. Family-caregiver programs face federal fraud scrutiny and state cuts, and the thesis shifts toward exactly that segment.

Originality (3): A roll-up of fiscal agents with a rented-software stack is what PE is already doing.

Upside (3): It is honest about 8-10% odds of the $103M case, and that case is probably generous. The outcome is a modest, long-dated financial return.

Credit: The rewrite is unusually candid, conceding five critiques and writing a kill threshold into the two-week test. But candor doesn't change the shape. This is a search-fund or PE-style roll-up, and a decent small business at best, not a venture-scale opportunity.

This is a decent-sounding small-cap services roll-up, not a seed-stage venture opportunity. A seed fund would pass on it, and a search fund or PE sponsor would be the right audience.

Size of prize: The whole US fee pool is roughly $0.7-0.9B. The pitch's own upside is $103M of revenue at a blended 10-12% EBITDA. That is about $10-12M of EBITDA and perhaps $100-125M of enterprise value at the ~10x multiples cited. It would take $60-75M of equity and debt over about 7 years. The second-round critic's arithmetic gives roughly 1.4-2.1x, which is far below venture return. The "median" case is $25M of revenue at 5-8% margin. At ~1x revenue purchase prices, that implies something like 12-20x EBITDA paid. In practice it is a bear case, so the real success case is an 8-10% joint event. Seed benchmarks like Stripe, Toast and Samsara had multi-billion outcomes with credible 100x paths. This has none.

Why now: The policy swing toward multi-vendor choice (the DOJ suit against New York's PPL award, Wisconsin audit scrutiny, Alabama and Minnesota multi-award) is real, as is commoditized FMS software (HHAX, Annkissam, DCI, CYMA). But sponsors (H.I.G. in GT Independence, General Atlantic in TEAM at ~10x) are already buying the same assets, which makes entry more expensive. Federal and state pressure on family-caregiver self-direction is the main demand-side risk. The open procurement windows (New York, West Virginia, Alabama, Ohio, Wisconsin) are mostly closed or locked. So timing is mixed: the political backlash helps the counter-positioning story, but the roll-up window is closing.

Non-consensus and right: The rewrite is honest and it conceded most of the early critiques. Its idea is to buy the qualification stack rather than build technology, and to enter through enrollment and rate-card markets. That is a thoughtful, non-obvious roll-up thesis, but the premise is shaky in specifics. Colorado is an RFP-awarded vendor list, not open enrollment. Minnesota's $165-250 fee is participant-paid and tiered down to $50-155 for small nonprofits. In Texas, where entry really is free, qualification needs no purchase, and an acquired book is switchable at will. Rate cards can be revoked by the state. So the "scarce asset" is partly free where it is open and closed where it is scarce.

Feasibility and defensibility: The riskiest assumption is unevidenced. No FMS-only deal price exists, and the only observable small non-sponsor operators (Wisconsin's) lose money. The deal count also does not fit, since 2-3 buys of 2-6k participants cannot reach 79k. The seasoned co-founder is a precondition that is sequenced after the test, the founder lacks the $60-75M, and the two-week test is biased by seller self-reporting and cold-call access. Defensibility is moderate at best: technology is explicitly not a moat, scale economies are unproven, and the contracts are revocable and annually renewable.

Evidence of demand: The spend is mandated and signed by a state, so the market exists. But there is no evidence of a willing seller at a workable price, no evidence that a premium-fee segment is large, and no evidence that anyone pays for reliability.

Net: a capable operator might build a $20-30M-revenue services business, which is a decent small business, but not venture-scale.

The insight is real but small. The refined idea sees that multi-state qualification, not software, is the scarce asset. It also sees that entry should go through rate-card and enrollment markets, where an incumbent cannot underbid, and not through statewide auctions. That is a better reading than the original SLA pitch, and the 2025-26 policy swing toward multi-vendor and choice (the DOJ suit against PPL, Wisconsin's protest, Alabama's multi-award) is a real anchor. Most of the rest is a thesis about what to buy. It is not a product or a distribution edge, and I would not call it contrarian in a way that creates durable advantage.

Seed-stage calibration is where it fails. Even the stated upside is about $103M of revenue at 10-12% EBITDA. That is roughly $100-125M of enterprise value on $60-75M invested over about 7 years, or 1.4-2.1x. The critic's arithmetic on the median case is worse: buying at 1x revenue and earning 5-8% EBITDA means paying 12-20x EBITDA, so the median is a capital loss. Success is effectively the roughly 8-10% upside, which is itself a joint event of several weakly supported conditions: $140+ blended fees, two first-time statewide wins at about one competitive award a year, a New York opening, and 79k participants. This is a search-fund or PE roll-up, not a venture-scale company, and it is far from Stripe, Toast or Samsara.

Feasibility and defensibility are low. The founder needs a seasoned fiscal-agent co-founder and $60-75M of capital that do not exist yet. No fiscal-agent deal price has been found anywhere. The only small non-sponsor operators with public financials (three of Wisconsin's four) lose money, and the healthy ones plausibly sell to H.I.G. or General Atlantic at about 10x. Entry is free in Texas. Colorado is closed by a five-year RFP list, so it is not the enrollment market the pitch calls it. The Minnesota fee is participant-paid and tiered, so the $165-250 figure is the top of a range. Rate cards are revocable by the state. Acquired books can switch fiscal agent at will, depend on the seller's referral relationships, and sit in the family-caregiver segment most exposed to fraud and cut politics.

Demand for the underlying service is real, mandated and state-signed. Demand for this particular strategy is unproven: sellers' willingness to sell, their margins and their prices are all unverified. The two-week test is well designed and can kill the idea honestly, but cold outreach is likely to fail on access, not on truth. The idea is honest and well stress-tested, but it is a decent small-to-mid services roll-up with a thin edge, not a venture-scale opportunity.

remaining_holes: Demand is still unevidenced. The rewrite drops 'neutral' as the reason to buy and swaps in price, capacity and performance, but offers no sign that any non-Elevance plan will pay a fixed, non-contingent fee. It also bans plan equity and board seats. That removes the investor-as-customer anchor that made CareBridge's first deals work (critic 1 flagged this) and supplies no replacement for a cold entrant.

The R3 margin is asserted, not derived. R3 is priced at 95% of the plan's loaded in-house cost, yet it targets a 10-15% margin. That implies a 15-20% structural cost advantage in a licensed, in-person, caseload-ratio-bound labor business. The rewrite itself says automation cannot cut headcount below the ratio. Pooling helps a 24/7 desk, not per-coordinator wages, and offshoring is unlikely for licensed in-person coordination. The plan's gain is about 5%, roughly $75 per member-year, in exchange for taking on delegation oversight, state sign-off and layoffs. Maximus's US Services segment runs about 11-12% margins (search summary), so the figure is not absurd, but that is a scaled incumbent, not a discount-priced entrant. A Truven/AdvancingStates deck (search summary) calls full delegation of LTSS coordination rare.

The 'why now' for R3 contradicts itself. The pitch says caseload mandates 'don't shrink' as membership falls, but a caseload ratio is a ratio, so required headcount falls with membership. The only real fixed cost is a staffing floor plus hiring lag. The pitch also sells variable-cost flex while charging 3-year terms with per-plan minimums and wind-down fees, and the vendor carries the stranded labor.

R1 pricing undercuts the scale thesis. If a desk costs about $280 per member at 3k members and about $100 at 30k, the $300 price exceeds 95% of the in-house cost for a 3k-member plan (about $266). For a 30k-member plan it is roughly 3x what building in-house would cost. The wedge definition includes plans with up to 60k HCBS members, who can build the desk themselves. The pooled-scale argument only holds for plans below about 5-10k members.

The upside arithmetic has a gap. The stated components (R1 $6M, R2 $15M, R3 $60M, R4 $10M, R5 $10M) sum to $101M. Removing R3 leaves about $41M, not the $55-60M stated. $65M only follows if the 40k R3 lives are downgraded to R2, which the file does not say. R4 and R5 ($20M) are unsupported. R4 is about $500 per life of savings share, while the rewrite itself disclaims acute savings and critic 3 cited an NBER finding that managed LTSS raised hospitalizations. The 34% blended gross margin implies roughly 65% gross margin on the non-R3 labor-bearing rungs if R3 earns 10-15% (inferred, not shown).

The yardstick moved. The dossier defined $100M as profit ('Profit is what matters', 67k members at 5% of $30k). The rewrite's $101M is fee revenue that comes to about $14M of EBITDA, roughly 7x smaller. It discloses this but still calls the result 'a layered path to about $100M'. Raising $50-80M for a $14M-EBITDA outcome at 5-8% odds is not a funded-venture shape. The capital plan (non-plan growth equity, later reinsurer or surety risk capital) is asserted with no evidence, and the Rock Health point from critic 3 is not engaged.

The two-week test is too soft to kill or confirm. Pass bars include 'call a fixed fee worth a pilot conversation' and 'agree to a retrospective', which are cheap talk. There is no LOI, base PMPM or named budget. The middle zone (4-5 of 8 calls) is undefined. Intros through ex-plan operators and expert networks select for people willing to talk to vendors. 40 contacts yielding 12 calls with director-level budget holders in 12 days is optimistic. The file says EVV-agnostic data rights 'is a gate in the test', but no pass criterion tests it.

Operational liability is unaddressed. The 'no risk' claim ignores E&O and indemnity exposure when a 24/7 desk fails to escalate a missed visit for a high-need member. Only algorithmic liability is discussed.

The wedge filter contradicts its own example. It requires states that allow subcontracting 'by notice rather than prior approval' but cites the Arizona ALTCS rebid as a trigger. Critic 3's evidence says Arizona requires administrative-services subcontracts to be submitted 60 days ahead. No count of states or plans meeting all the filters is given.

The 'trough' framing is partly stale. I checked Centene's Q2 2026 release via search summary: Medicaid HBR was 93.9% and SG&A savings were about $480M (the $480M comes only from MarketBeat). The same quarter raised EPS guidance and the consolidated HBR improved to 89.6% from 93.0%. Centene is recovering at the corporate level, so the 'margins at a trough' claim is overstated for it, though it does hold for Elevance.
result.which_critiques_were_dodged_not_answered: Genuinely answered: (a) the neutrality premium, conceded outright with neutrality kept only as free contract rights; (b) the MLR and fee-base problem, re-priced as substitution for admin, with the wrong $30k/5% base dropped; (c) unproven savings, since R1-R3 no longer promise acute savings; (d) downstream-risk licensing, avoided by taking no risk until R4; (e) the CA/NY pool, recomputed; (f) concentration, with caps added. I confirmed the 45 CFR 158.150(b)(2)(i)(A) care-coordination citation. It is accurate, though (c)(1) excludes cost-containment activities and (c)(5) excludes claims-adjudication work, so R1's pre-pay edits and a 'cheaper than in-house' R3 pitch sit near those exclusions.\n\nDodged or only gestured at: (1) The core critique, that no one has shown a plan will pay a non-Elevance vendor anything. It is converted into a test, but the rewrite's own plan needs the very anchor customers it forbids itself to take on as investors. (2) ModivCare, the closest fixed-fee Medicaid vendor, which went Chapter 11, is never mentioned. (3) The Rock Health and capital-market critique is answered with a restatement of intent, not evidence. (4) Aide supply (the 71% fill rate) is the binding constraint on 'activate backup care', and the rewrite does not say where the backup aides come from when the vendor employs none. (5) Competition from payer BPOs (Maximus, Sagility, offshore operators) is absent from the competitor list even though the rewrite repositions the idea as an ops utility. (6) HHAeXchange and CareBridge data dependency is called a test gate, but the test has no such criterion. (7) The Evolent concentration and insourcing failure mode is named but the rewrite offers only caps, not evidence that a new vendor avoids it. (8) The rewrite relabels the business into a lower-margin BPO category and calls that an answer. It is a retreat to the 'regional boutique' the critics described, yet the rewrite explicitly says it does not concede that.
result.upside_believable: Not believable at the stated 5-8%. The upside needs 85k lives across 8-10 plan contracts in 8-10 states, including 40k labor-bearing, state-approved, delegated coordination lives. It needs a first paid pilot by month 9-18 and R3 live by month 24-30. It also needs a roughly 20% cost advantage in a labor business, 6 or more parents each giving a new vendor a fifth or more of their LTSS lives (my read), and none of the five big rival buyers to insource. CareBridge needed about four years, $180M, and four plan investors who were also customers to reach about 115k. The rewrite reaches for 85k with those anchors removed, and plans are cutting costs and shrinking, with Elevance, Centene and Aetna exiting markets. I put the $100M-revenue case nearer 1-2%. Even if it lands, it is about $14M of EBITDA, not $100M of profit. The $18M median is only plausible conditional on surviving the first test. As an unconditional median it is optimistic, because no demand evidence exists. The idea is alive as a cheap, falsifiable regional ops-services hypothesis. It is not alive as a $100M business.

result.rationale:
The real insight is that Medicaid plans are shrinking (Big Five enrollment down 6.5%), their margins are squeezed, and their mandated LTSS work does not shrink in step. So a variable-cost, fixed-price ops utility could beat in-house teams. That is a genuine 2025-26 shift, and the 2026 timing score reflects it. But the refinement gave up the contrarian bet that made the original interesting. It dropped neutrality as the reason to buy and became a payer back-office outsourcer. That is a crowded, low-margin BPO category (Maximus, Sagility, offshore operators, and plans' own teams) in which tech does not lead.

Defensibility is weak. The only moat is pooled-scale economics, and that works only for plans under roughly 5-10k HCBS members. At the $300 price, a 30k-member plan could build the desk for about a third of that. The R3 licensed-coordination rung is where the revenue is, and it needs a 15-20% structural cost advantage in an in-person, caseload-ratio-bound labor business that the file itself says automation cannot shrink.

The upside math does not clear a venture bar. The $101M case needs 85k lives across 8-10 states with 40k labor-bearing, state-approved delegated lives. The critic puts its odds at 1-2%, against the file's 5-8%. Even if it lands, it is about $14M of EBITDA. Components are loosely supported: removing R3 leaves about $41M, not the stated $55-60M, and R4/R5 ($20M) are unsupported. At seed, this looks like a $10-25M-revenue regional services company, not a decade-defining deal.

Demand evidence is close to zero. No non-Elevance plan has been shown to want to pay a fixed fee to an unaffiliated vendor. Rivals already buy CareBridge (Iowa), and the plan-investor anchors that made CareBridge work are now barred. The dossier found no RFP or defection, and ModivCare's bankruptcy is the closest fixed-fee Medicaid-vendor precedent. Operational liability from a missed escalation is unaddressed, and aide supply is the binding constraint on backup care.

Feasibility is middling. The two-week test is cheap, falsifiable and sensible, which is its strength. But its pass bars are soft ("worth a pilot conversation"), and state subcontract approvals plus 90-day pilots mean 18-30 months to real revenue. This is a decent, cheap-to-test small business hypothesis, not a venture-scale opportunity.

I scored this as a decent regional ops-services business, not a venture-scale company.

Where it is strong:
- The rewrite fixed the worst problems. It prices as substitution for existing admin or care-coordination budget, takes no downstream risk until R4, drops the neutrality premium, and ships a falsifiable two-week test. A discounted, fixed-fee, no-risk service replacing cost the plan already carries is the kind of offer that can reach profit without heroic capital.
- The timing is real. Medicaid plans are shrinking, margins are squeezed, SG&A is being cut, and rebids force deadline-driven LTSS operations changes. CareBridge proves plans buy this category.

Why the score stays at 4:
- Demand is unevidenced. Rivals bought from CareBridge, and no rival has shown willingness to pay a non-affiliated vendor a fixed fee. The pitch gives up the plan-investor anchors that made CareBridge's early deals work, and nothing replaces them. Medicaid delegation needs plan CFO, compliance and state sign-off, so a 9-18 month cycle is more likely than 6-12. The 90-day pilot looks like one or two logos in year one, not ten.
- The R3 economics look wrong. Pricing at 95% of in-house cost while targeting a 10-15% margin implies a 15-20% structural cost advantage in a licensed, ratio-bound labor business where automation cannot cut headcount. Pooling helps a 24/7 desk, not per-coordinator wages. The R1 pricing contradicts the scale thesis: $300 is above 95% of in-house cost for a 3k-member plan, and about 3x what a 30k-member plan could build for.
- Defensibility is weak. The moat is a staffing-floor scale economy that only matters for sub-scale plans, plus switching costs that come later. The company has no technology lead. CareBridge/Carelon, HHAeXchange, CareCentrix, payer BPOs and plan in-house teams all compete for the same budget.
- The upside is thin. The $101M case is revenue, not profit: about $14M of EBITDA, at 1-8% odds depending on whose estimate you believe. Without R3, the stated components leave about $41M, not the $55-60M claimed. Concentration risk is Evolent-like, and the buyers are shrinking and exiting states. This is a good business at the $10-20M revenue level and a poor venture shape.
- Operational risk is unaddressed. Missed-shift escalation failures for high-need members create E&O and indemnity exposure that the "no risk" framing ignores.

What keeps it above 3: the first-product wedge is cheap to test, uses existing budget lines, and does not depend on unproven clinical savings. A founder who has run profitable services companies could build a $5-20M/yr margin business here if two or three plans say yes.

Size of prize: the refined pitch is a labor-bearing BPO and coordination-staffing business. The author's own numbers put the $100M-revenue case at 5-8% odds, and the critic puts it nearer 1-2%. That revenue is only about $14M of EBITDA, so a hit would be a modest exit on $50-80M raised. The median case is about $18M of revenue. Tech-only rungs cap near $55-60M, and the stated components don't reconcile: removing R3 leaves about $41M, not $55-60M. A seed fund can't underwrite that distribution. It is a decent regional services business, not a Stripe, Toast or Samsara-style category outcome.

Why now: the squeeze on Medicaid plans is real. Enrollment is down about 6.5%, margins are at a trough, SG&A is being cut, there are exits and rebids, and EVV data is universal. But it cuts both ways. Shrinking plans cut vendor spend and insource, and Centene is already recovering at the corporate level. The R3 argument that mandated caseloads don't shrink contradicts itself, since a ratio shrinks with membership. The 3-year minimums also put stranded labor on the vendor.

Non-consensus and right: weak. The original non-consensus bet was a neutral vacuum after Elevance bought CareBridge. The refinement concedes nobody has shown they will pay for neutrality, and the dossier found rivals still buying from CareBridge in Iowa and elsewhere, with no defections. What's left is price, capacity and an ops desk, which is a conventional BPO pitch. It is also the regional boutique the critics described. The one real insight is pooled 24/7 scale for sub-scale plans, but the numbers undercut it. At $300 PMPY, R1 exceeds 95% of in-house cost below roughly 3-5k members and is about 3x in-house cost at 30k, so the argument only holds for very small plans.

Feasibility: hard. The R3 margin of 10-15% at 95% of in-house cost implies a 15-20% structural cost edge in licensed, in-person, ratio-bound labor, and that edge isn't derived. State approval or notice for each subcontract, delegation oversight, E&O exposure, and aide supply (a 71% fill rate that the vendor doesn't control) all slow or limit it. First revenue is likely 18-30 months out. Capital is plausible given the capital-light framing, but the growth equity is unevidenced and the ModivCare and Evolent failure modes are close analogs.

Defensibility: low. Neutrality is a copyable contract clause. Scale economies only bite at 3+ plans or about 30k lives per state, which is hard to reach. Switching costs are modest. Competitors are CareBridge/Carelon, HHAeXchange, CareCentrix, Cityblock, Maximus-type BPOs, and plans' in-house teams.

Evidence of demand: the dossier found no plan RFP, LOI, or fee benchmark for a non-Elevance fixed-fee vendor. Category demand is proven only by CareBridge, whose first deals were anchored by plan investors this design forbids. The two-week test is cheap and sensible but soft, because its pass bars are talk rather than signed commitments.

Overall: a falsifiable, cheap-to-test regional ops-services hypothesis. As a seed-fund deal it lands in the decent-small-business bucket, not venture-scale.

result.title: Anchor-Funded Independent Foundry Platform
result.one_liner: Buy a qualified, sub-scale independent superalloy caster that several OEMs already depend on, then expand it with those OEMs' own reservation payments, with contract terms that protect their capacity from conflicted owners.
result.pitch:
The original Non-GE Foundry is dead. A greenfield plant, a consortium of rival OEMs, a 10-year take-or-pay and neutrality as a premium all failed the critics, and I conceded every one of them. What is left is a different and harder business, and it is not a solo-founder startup.

Buyers do pay for dedicated capacity. Doncasters' June 2026 prospectus says customers fund up to 80% of capital investment and that three of its strategic partnerships carry volume commitments for the life of the agreement. Howmet's new IGT capacity is largely committed for 2027-2029 and it holds over 50% of IGT blades. Rystad says 2025 orders ran 30% above what OEMs could deliver and the gap has not closed. So the two suppliers doing this are full, and demand spills over.

The refined business buys the qualification instead of building it. The target is a qualified investment caster with $30-70M of revenue and at least two non-captive buyers in its top five customers. GF's Precicast sale (about 600 staff, CHF 220M) suggests mid-size assets trade near 1.4-2.4x revenue on my arithmetic. Anchors then fund brownfield lines at that approved site through 5-7 year agreements with a reservation payment, a volume floor and a make-whole on early termination. Expansion capex runs near $1 per $1 of added revenue, so capacity lands in 2028-29 beside the incumbents, not after them. Each deal is bilateral, which avoids the antitrust problem. Neutrality survives only as a contract term: a right of first offer if the plant is sold to a competitor of the customer.

Buyers widen beyond non-GE IGT makers to about 20-25 payers, including GE and missile and drone engine makers. Kratos plans 3,000 engines in 2027.

What stays unsolved: no one has shown customer money going to a non-incumbent owner, the mid-size target pool is being consolidated by CPP, Arcline and Pursuit, and OEMs also buy supply themselves (Siemens Energy bought core maker CIC). It needs roughly $130-175M of other people's equity and a proven casting operator. My odds of reaching $100M are about 5%, rising to about 12% with both in hand on day one. A two-week buyer test kills it cheaply if anchors will not name dollars.
result.wedge_customer: Non-captive buyers of hot-section castings that depend on one or two qualified independent casters and fear a conflicted or distracted owner. These are Ansaldo, Baker Hughes and Solar in IGT; Siemens Energy and GE Vernova for dual-sourcing overflow; and missile and drone engine makers such as Kratos. The entry point is the top-five customers of one specific acquisition target.
result.payer_and_signer: The VP Supply Chain or Chief Procurement Officer signs the 5-7 year agreement, with the blades-and-vanes or supplier-capacity lead running it. The CFO signs the reservation payment, funded from the supplier capacity and tooling investment line that already funds Doncasters. A second payer is the equity provider: an infrastructure or PE fund, or an independent-sponsor partner.
result.first_product: The approved part numbers the acquired plant already ships, so revenue is real at closing. The first funded expansion is non-rotating hot-section hardware (vanes, nozzle segments, shrouds, small-engine turbine nozzles and wheels) in equiaxed and DS alloys. DS and SX capability is added later with customer-funded qualification. Single-crystal rotating blades are explicitly not the first product.
result.pricing: Market pricing with metal, energy and labor pass-through on published indices, as in Doncasters' agreements. No open-book cost-plus and no neutrality discount. Target EBITDA is 18-22%. Each anchor pays a capacity-reservation fee covering 60-80% of its line's capex, credited against invoices over 5-7 years. A volume floor of 70-80% of reserved capacity applies, with a make-whole payment of the unamortized balance on early termination.
result.why_now: Orders ran about 30% above what OEMs could deliver in 2025 and Rystad says the gap has not closed. Hot-section castings are among the tightest constraints, with order books running toward 2030. Howmet and Doncasters are full, so demand spills over. GE's CPP deal (2026-09-08, closing 2H 2027) has made every OEM focus on who owns its caster, and anchors are most willing to commit before that settles. Mid-size carve-outs are trading, as with GF's Precicast sale. Missile and drone engine makers are a new buyer class with no incumbent agreements. The DoW plan names castings a single point of failure.
result.moat: Switching costs are the main power: OEM approvals take years, and they arrive on day one by acquisition. This is the incumbents' moat, bought rather than invented. Cornered resource follows in years 2-3 through approved part numbers, furnace slots, the operator bench and customer-funded dedicated lines. Counter-positioning is narrow, from change-of-control rights that protect customers against owners who compete with them. It is real against OEM-owned captives but weak against PE-owned peers. Scale economies in melt, cores and NDT arrive from year 4 at three or more plants.
result.bottom_up_market: About 20-25 reachable payers: non-big-3 IGT makers, big-OEM overflow, non-captive aeroengine makers including GE, and drone and missile engine makers. The pools are about $2.6B for IGT airfoils (Howmet gas turbine sales of about $1.28B annualized at over 50% share) and about $8-10B or more for aeroengine hot-section castings (from the dossier). BNEF projects output up more than 50% by 2030, implying about $1.3B a year of added IGT airfoil demand by my arithmetic. Lanes by my estimate: non-big-3 IGT at 10% of a 10-15% slice is $25-40M; big-OEM overflow at 3-4% of added demand is $40-50M; aeroengine at 1-1.5% of the pool is $80-150M; unmanned propulsion is $15-60M. Six to eight anchors at $12-25M each give $100-160M, about 1% of the combined pool. The obstacle is access and capital, not share.
result.upside_assumptions: The $200M is a year-7 figure. (1) Three acquisitions at 2x revenue or less: Plant A $45M, a $40M bolt-on in year 3, and a $55M carve-out or divestiture in year 5. (2) At least five anchor deals averaging $15-20M each, with 65% customer-funded capex at about $1.0 of capex per $1 of added revenue. (3) A $15M unmanned or small-engine line. (4) The turbine order cycle holds through about 2030. (5) About $340M of total uses, of which $52M is customer-funded, about $115M is debt at 4x EBITDA, and $130-175M is equity. (6) Blended EBITDA of 18%, about $36M. The median of $55M is conditional on closing a first deal: Plant A at $45M plus about $10M from one anchor-funded line. The unconditional median is $0, because most attempts never close a first deal.
result.competitors_and_edge: Howmet (customer-backed capex, full through 2029); Doncasters (the only incumbent claiming dedicated capacity, four partnerships adding over $200M at run rate); Chromalloy (Siemens-exclusive Tampa JV); PCC; CPP under GE, which is also buying Precicast; Arcline (American Casting Company); Pursuit (Aeromet and the Tunis site; its Creasey deal is magnesium and aluminum sand casting, not hot-section); Fabri and Rangeview; and captives at Pratt, Safran, Rolls-Royce and SpaceX. Siemens Energy has also bought core maker CIC. The edge is thin against the well-funded buyers: deal flow sourced through customers who dislike a conflicted owner, expansions funded by customers so less equity per dollar of revenue, and willingness to serve every buyer including GE. None of it is technology.
result.riskiest_assumption: At least one non-captive buyer will sign a dollar-denominated, multi-year capacity reservation with make-whole to fund a line at a qualified caster owned by a non-incumbent. In other words, customer money follows the qualified asset and a protective contract rather than the incumbent's name. No OEM prepay to a non-incumbent owner has been found by me or any of the three critics.
result.two_week_test: Days 1-3: list 12 qualified independent superalloy casters, excluding Howmet, PCC, CPP, Doncasters, Pursuit and Arcline, and note each one's likely top customers. Days 3-12: reach 20 supplier-capacity, blades-and-vanes sourcing and procurement leads at non-captive buyers (Ansaldo, Baker Hughes, Solar, Siemens Energy and GE Vernova dual-sourcing teams, Honeywell, Kratos, Anduril, Williams) through ex-employee referrals or paid expert calls. Also reach 3-5 sell-side advisors who ran recent aerospace casting sales. In each call, show a one-page term sheet and ask: is any part family's only qualified source at risk on capacity or ownership; what reservation payment and minimum term would you sign if an independent owner with committed capital bought it; who signs and how long does it take. Pass: at least 3 of about 10 responding buyers name $10M or more over 5 or more years, at least 1 agrees to mark up a draft LOI, and at least 2 advisors confirm 3 or more targets could trade at 2.5x revenue or less within 24 months. Kill: one buyer or fewer gives a number, or the answer is "only through our existing partners" or "we would buy it ourselves".
result.how_critiques_were_addressed: Product already exists: conceded, and used as proof that buyers pay; the business is a third and fourth place for that money. Incumbent response and the cycle: switched to brownfield at an acquired plant, so capacity lands in 2028-29, and funded capex plus a make-whole moves cycle risk to the customer. Insourcing: acknowledged as live (Siemens Energy bought CIC, GE Vernova bought Woodward's site); the multi-customer character of the target is the argument against single-OEM ownership, and it remains unproven. No prepay precedent and a thin signer set: dropped the unqualified plant, the consortium, the 10-year take-or-pay, open-book pricing and the neutrality premium; every deal is now bilateral, which also removes the antitrust exposure. Capability and inputs: acquire the approvals, furnaces and staff rather than build them, with retention packages and a core and shell capability added later. Moat and exit: admitted that the moat is the incumbents' own, bought. Not answered: the cost-of-capital gap versus Howmet, the consolidation of mid-size targets by CPP, Arcline and Pursuit, and the fact that this is a capital-allocation business needing a proven operator and $130-175M of other people's equity. One factual correction: Pursuit's Creasey deal is not hot-section capacity.

result.title: Capped Outage: scope- and date-guaranteed gas-turbine overhauls for owners with no LTSA
result.one_liner: A neutral prime that sells owners with no OEM long-term service agreement a fixed-price, growth-banded, date-guaranteed, surety-bonded turbine outage, priced on measured condition and performed by third-party shops, then converts the best accounts to 3-5 year programs.
result.pitch:
About three-quarters of GE's installed gas turbines are not under a long-term service agreement (about 1,800 of 7,000 at end-2025). Their owners buy each outage as an event: a base-scope price that grows by change order once the unit is opened, from OEMs whose transactional prices are rising or independents whose rotor queues run into 2028-29. The contractor earns more when more is found; the owner carries the variance and the days. Austin Energy's three turbine maintenance agreements were amended by up to $8.3M on a $16M original. At PJM's $325-333/MW-day capacity price, a 230 MW unit's overrun day is roughly $75k of revenue exposure.

We are a neutral prime selling those owners what they actually buy, one outage at a time: a fixed price near the incumbent's base-scope quote with as-found growth up to a set band already included, a hard return-to-service date with liquidated damages, and a surety-bonded performance guarantee. Price comes from measured condition (borescope and NDE we commission before quoting, plus hours, starts and trips), and a unit that opens better than forecast earns a rebate. Qualified shops do the work under frame agreements with reserved slots; we hold no hardware at first. A sponsor's balance sheet backs the bonds, a retained-risk fund absorbs growth variance across a book, and insurance covers resulting damage and delay. We do not claim to insure scheduled maintenance; a New York regulator has held that is not an insurable event.

This is not the original ten-year LTSA takeout. It sells what owners buy rather than a contract three-quarters of them decline, needs about $40-60M of capital at $100M revenue instead of $300M of contingent liability, and does not depend on a reinsurer inventing a parts-cost cap.

What stays hard: independents already sell fixed-scope turnkey outages, Hanwha has the balance sheet to copy a growth cap, and revenue is mostly pass-through at 10-14% gross margin, so $100M of revenue is $10-14M of gross profit. The moat arrives late, as a forecast-versus-as-found dataset after about 50 outages. The gate is demand: do non-LTSA owners bear 10%+ growth today, and will they award to a teamed newcomer to cap it? Two weeks of calls will tell us.
result.wedge_customer: Owners of 1-6 older-design F-class (7FA.03, 7FA+e, 501F) or 7EA units, with a hot-section or major outage in fall 2027-2028, who are outside any OEM LTSA and buy OEM-transactionally today. These are co-ops and other buyers with negotiating room, non-platform IPPs and fund-owned plants, and industrial cogens. Excluded in phase 1: the scale fleets (NRG, Vistra, Constellation, Talen, FPL, Southern) and statutory scored-RFP buyers. Sized at roughly 200-300 US units, central 250.
result.payer_and_signer: VP Generation or plant manager signs the event. The CFO or treasurer co-signs because a fixed-price counterparty needs a credit review. Co-op boards approve above their thresholds. Budget line: major-outage O&M or the maintenance reserve. The lender's independent engineer is an influencer only; the earlier claim that it is the real buyer had no source and is dropped.
result.first_product: A fixed-price outage package (hot-gas-path, combustion or major inspection) for one 7FA.03, 7FA+e, 501F or 7EA unit at a non-LTSA owner, for a fall-2027 or spring-2028 outage. The deliverables are: a pre-outage borescope and condition forecast; a fixed price with an as-found growth band; a return-to-service date with liquidated damages; a performance bond; a named qualified shop under a frame agreement; and a post-outage report of forecast versus as-found with a condition rebate. The door is a free written fixed-price bid in 5 business days from the owner's last outage report and OEM quote. It is a bid, not a free audit, which avoids the procurement conflict of shaping the owner's spec.
result.pricing: Fixed price at about 1.00-1.02 times the owner's OEM-transactional (or incumbent ISP) base-scope quote. As-found growth up to 20% of base scope is included, growth from 20% to 40% is shared 50/50, and the owner holds the option above that at pre-agreed unit rates. Owner deductible of about 5% of base scope. Liquidated damages after a grace period, capped at about 10% of price. A condition rebate of 30-50% of the unused growth reserve if the unit opens better than forecast. The owner's saving is the growth and delay we absorb (expected 10-15% of base, to be measured) rather than a headline discount. Target gross margin 10-14%, from non-OEM parts substitution and multi-sourcing. Programs later: $/EOH with an annual true-up. There is no price room against owners whose alternative is an ISP at 85-90% of the OEM price, so they come second.
result.why_now: Moderate, and narrower than the original pitch. (1) Casting scarcity (GE Aerospace paying $11.75B for CPP) and independent rotor queues into 2028-29 make a guaranteed date worth more than before. (2) The OEM's 116 GW new-unit backlog deprioritizes transactional service on old frames, and its transactional prices are rising. (3) PJM capacity at the $325-333/MW-day cap raises the cost of every overrun day, though the collar is approved only through 2029/30. (4) The 2026 soft insurance market makes tail capacity cheap, though it may leave mid-cycle. The LTSA roll-off wave is dropped as a why-now: it is old and thin.
result.moat: No durable moat for roughly the first four years. Two of the 7 Powers are reachable. Scale economies: risk loading per dollar and frame-agreement pricing both improve between 5 and 25 packages a year, reached at about 15-20 a year. Cornered resource: a proprietary forecast-versus-as-found dataset spanning shops and OEMs that no single ISP sees, valuable after about 50 packages, so year 5-6. Early and fragile: counter-positioning against time-and-materials incumbents who earn margin on change orders. This is logic, not evidence, and calls 1-25 should test it. Single events carry low switching costs; 3-5 year programs raise them modestly. Hanwha could match a growth cap within 18-24 months, so the window is speed, early references and neutrality.
result.bottom_up_market: US F-class units 900-1,100 [assumption, dossier]. Less scale or in-house fleets (40-50%): 450-660. Less units under long OEM LTSAs (26%, GE's rate applied to all OEMs): 330-490. Less units under 10 years old or mid-term on a 7+ year ISP deal (about 25%, assumed): 250-370. Less statutory scored-RFP buyers (about 20%, assumed): 200-300 units, central 250. Outage wallet $3-4M per unit-year (NYPA 2007 independent deal implies about $2.75M nominal; EIA cross-check about $3.8M); I use $3M. US wedge wallet is about $600-900M a year, central $750M. Adding Canada, Mexico, UK and Gulf (+30%) and teamed public bodies in phase 2 (+20%) gives about $1.1B. $100M is about 13% of the US-only wedge and about 9% of the full $1.1B, which is about 20 packages a year at $5M against a wedge flow of roughly 200 packages a year. That is roughly an average competitor's share among about eight, so aggressive but under the 20% heroic line. Sources: GE Vernova FY2025 10-K for the LTSA share; dossier for unit counts and fee per unit-year. Haircuts marked assumed are untested.
result.upside_assumptions: Year 8-9, about $110M revenue and $11-15M gross profit. (1) First package in year 2, then 2, 5, 9, 13, 16, 19, 22 packages a year over years 2-8 at about $5M each. (2) Mix: US events about $63M, US 3-5 year programs about $26M, teamed public-body awards about $7M, Canada, Mexico and other about $12M. (3) A sponsor commits $15-25M by month 18 and $40-60M by year 5, plus a surety line of about $60M in force. (4) Frame agreements keep rotor and casting slots through the squeeze, and a $20-30M owned spare-set pool is added in phase 2. (5) Realized growth inside the band averages 9% of price or less, with gross margin holding at 12%. (6) Hanwha and Allied take at least 3 years to match the cap, or match it at lower scale. (7) Win rate about 1 in 4 on 80+ bids a year by year 6. (8) 40% of accounts convert to programs by year 5. Probability of reaching this is about 3% (about 40% to pass the demand gate, then 40% to clear capital, surety and supply, then 20% to scale). Median case: if every gate passes, about $30M in year 7 (about 6 packages a year), roughly break-even, most likely sold to an ISP for $20-40M. The most likely outcome overall is death at a gate. EBITDA at the upside is only about $4-7M.
result.competitors_and_edge: Hanwha Power (PSM merged with Hanwha Power Systems, Mar 2026): LTA/LTMA/Frame tiers, monitoring, Hanwha Group balance sheet. The most dangerous copier. The 2011 Austin agenda shows Power Systems Mfg held the Sand Hill Unit 5 contract, so the 2026 award to Hanwha is probably a renewal, not a displacement. Allied (Warren Equity), MD&A, Ethos (One Equity Partners), Wood, Sulzer and Chromalloy: fixed-scope turnkey outages with schedule claims already exist (MD&A 19-day 7FA hot gas path, sponsored content). Their gap is scope-growth risk on thin PE balance sheets, and they cannot be neutral across rival shops. GE, Siemens and Mitsubishi: no cap or date guarantee outside an LTSA, and transactional prices are rising. Advisers (Troutman, IEM, Mercer Thompson): advise but take no risk, so they are a referral channel. Parametric forced-outage cover (Aon) covers owner availability, not outage cost. O&M primes such as NAES (ITOCHU, about 200 plants, cost-plus-fee) hold owner relationships, references and bonding but take no maintenance price risk, which makes them a channel hypothesis. Edge: neutral multi-shop sourcing, a sponsor balance sheet that ISPs lack, a cap on growth that change-order economics discourage, and measured-condition pricing. The edge is thin and copyable.
result.riskiest_assumption: Owners at non-LTSA F-class units bear material, volatile as-found cost growth and schedule slip today, which a fixed-price contractor is not already absorbing. They would pay roughly half of the expected overrun to cap it, and would award to a newcomer teamed with a named, bonded shop. If incumbents already absorb scope growth in turnkey deals, or growth is small, there is no product and the business is a crowded plain independent contractor.
result.two_week_test: Run 25 calls in 14 days, at least 15 with non-LTSA, non-scale-fleet F-class owners, sourced from 7F Users Group attendee lists, APPA and NRECA generation contacts, plant managers on LinkedIn, and referrals from two LTSA consultants. For each owner's last 2-3 outages, ask: awarded price versus final cost, days late, contract form, who bore the growth, and who earned margin on it. Then show a one-page term sheet (price near the OEM base quote, 20% growth band, liquidated damages, bond, named shop) and ask whether they would take a bid, what premium they would pay for a hard cap, whether they would send their last two outage reports and an OEM quote for a written bid in 5 days, and whether they can export hours, starts and trips. In parallel, pull at least 15 public council or board change-order and amendment records for F-class maintenance and outage work to measure award-to-final variance. Pass: median growth at least 10% on at least 60% of sampled outages, at least 8 of 25 would take a bid from a teamed newcomer, and at least 5 would share records. Kill: median growth below 6%, or 70% or more say their ISP already absorbs growth, or fewer than 3 would consider a newcomer. Cost is near zero. This is stated preference, so only a signed event is strong evidence. Separately, a gate in months 3-9 asks 5 brokers and underwriters for appetite on the insured slice and a stop-loss.
result.how_critiques_were_addressed: Critique 1 (Hanwha can copy; no hardware; consolidation). The product is no longer condition pricing, which I accept is a clause. It is risk transfer (growth cap, date, bond) plus neutrality across several shops. No hardware at first; shops are suppliers under frame agreements, and consolidation is handled by signing non-prime repair houses early. Counter-positioning moves from the OEM averaged-hours book to change-order economics, which is unverified. Hanwha can still match in 18-24 months. Critique 1 on the Austin RFP and critique 2 on references and bonds. Phase 1 sells to private and negotiating buyers where a $4-10M event bond is a 1-3% cost item, back-to-back with the shop's bond and a sponsor indemnity, and builds references there. Scored RFPs wait for phase 2, teamed with a referenced shop or an O&M prime. A sponsor and a surety line are now explicit gates. Critique 3 on the small contestable flow and non-consumption. The base is the stock of annual outage wallet at non-LTSA units (about $750M US), not expiring LTSAs. We sell the per-event product the 75% already buy. Critic 1 on OEM non-response and standard guarantees. Those guarantees are LTSA features, and transactional units get none, so we target OEM-transactional buyers. Insurer wrap (all three). Dropped the parts-cost cap. Insure only fortuitous resulting damage and delay. Bond performance, which the NY opinion expressly allows (I fetched it). Retain and diversify growth variance. Treat stop-loss or service-contract reimbursement cover as upside needing counsel. Capital need falls from $300M+ of contingent liability to $40-60M at $100M revenue. Free-audit commodity and procurement conflict. Replaced with a free written fixed-price bid. Condition pricing partly exists (GER-3620), moral hazard and OEM data. Condition is an underwriting input, with an owner deductible and an operating-profile corridor, using owner-held data. Economics: 12% margin is parts substitution. Agreed and stated; the cap is funded by it. Not fully answered: Hanwha copying, ISP allocation of scarce slots to their own customers, adverse selection on early packages, and thin profit (about $4-7M EBITDA at $100M revenue).

result.title: Level-1 Bench (refined from Overnight Yard Crews)
result.one_liner: A hire-train-deploy technician workforce company: six-week academy-trained W-2 Level-1 technicians placed by the hour into heavy-duty shops, dealers and yard fleets that cannot fill entry slots, converting to the customer's payroll for a fee.
result.pitch:
US heavy-duty repair is short about 76,000 technicians (ATRI: 19.3% of positions unfilled, 65.5% of shops understaffed; Fullbay: 54%), and the shops feeling it most are the ones that cannot build a training program: the median shop has five technicians. Their certified techs, now at a $36.50 median and up 14% in a year, spend much of the day on checklist work: PM, lube, tires, lights, brake and DOT inspection assist. Trade schools supply roughly 10,000 candidates a year, 9 to 18 months late. Penske, Love's and Ryder's Torque solved this privately with single-employer pipelines. Everyone else is stuck.

Level-1 Bench is the missing middle: a hire-train-deploy workforce company. We recruit people already in adjacent $16-22 jobs, run a six-week academy (two weeks classroom, four weeks billed in-bay), employ them W-2 hourly, and place them in the customer's shop or yard under the customer's own certified lead. The customer pays about $52 an hour, a premium of roughly $14 over a direct hire's all-in cost and far below the $149 an hour the shop bills for the work. If the placement works, the customer converts the technician for about $7,000, less than the $8,211 ATRI says it costs to train an entrant itself.

The critics broke the original: no $115 hourly price, no sub-$25 wage, no remote master tech, no vans, no OEM second payer, no Workforce Pell, and no fight with Ryder, Cox and Amerit for fleets' PM budgets. What survives is the insight that the shortage is partly a task-allocation and training-capacity problem, sold to buyers who lack scale.

The unit of sale is a bench of 1-24 people. $100M is about 950-1,050 FTE and 215 accounts (25 enterprise), or 4-9% of Level-1-fillable open slots, instead of 1,100-3,000 fleet accounts. Capital is academies and payroll float, about $15-30M, not $60-90M of trucks.

It is honestly a 5-12% EBITDA business. It dies if shops will not pay about 1.9x the wage; breakeven is a $47.50 bill rate. Nothing I found shows shops buy temporary technicians at scale. A two-week pre-sale to 40 targets, counting signed order forms, tests it.
result.wedge_customer: Independent heavy-duty repair shops and franchised-dealer service departments with 4-30 technicians and at least one Level-1-type requisition open more than 60 days, plus private-fleet in-house shops with the same problem, in one dense metro (Dallas-Fort Worth, Atlanta, Houston or the founder's home metro, wherever a diesel instructor can be hired). Understaffing is a shop problem more than a fleet problem: Fullbay 54% of shops, ATRI 65.5% of shops, but only 33% of fleet respondents (Fleet Maintenance, per critic). Median Fullbay shop has 5 technicians. Small for-hire carriers are excluded in years 1-3 to avoid credit risk.
result.payer_and_signer: Shop owner or service director (labor, overtime and recruiting budget; the open requisition is the budget line). At private fleets, the maintenance director. For dealer groups, lessor networks and roll-ups (True North, Amerit sites), the VP of service operations plus procurement on a master services agreement. Not a fleet-by-fleet PM contract. Secondary: state workforce boards reimburse employers up to 50% of trainee wages in on-the-job training, up to 75% under some local policies (reduces training cost, not counted as revenue).
result.first_product: Level-1 Bench: pre-trained W-2 hourly Level-1 technicians (PM, lube, tire service with OSHA 1910.177 training, lighting, brake and DOT-inspection assist) placed into the customer's shop or yard under the customer's certified lead, who stays the inspector of record under 49 CFR 396.19/396.25. Two-week minimum, 30-day free replacement, temp-to-hire conversion option. Six-week academy: two weeks classroom and shop, four weeks billed in-bay with a buddy. Year 2: Night Yard Pods (three-person pods working parked trucks overnight, per-service pricing) only where a fleet supplies the certified lead.
result.pricing: Base bill rate $52 per Level-1 hour (range $48-58); +$3 night differential; tire- and brake-qualified pods $55-58. Conversion fee about $7,000, falling to zero after roughly 1,000 hours (below the $8,211 ATRI trainee-wage cost the customer avoids; staffing norm is 11-21% of first-year salary). Weekly invoicing, ACH autopay for new accounts, exposure capped at two weeks of billing. Model: wage $27, burden 1.30, 2,000 paid hours at 92% billed gives $97.8k revenue and 7.3% EBITDA per FTE-year; breakeven bill rate about $47.50; wage ceiling about $29.50 at a $52 bill rate.
result.why_now: Moderate, not strong, and I say so. The shortage is chronic (ATRI 65.5% of shops understaffed, 19.3% of slots unfilled; Fullbay 54%; median technician pay $36.50, up 14.1%), so the 2019 version would also have worked in principle. What changed: wage inflation makes each untrained entrant who quits more expensive to replace; PE roll-ups (Amerit, True North, Ryder) create multi-site buyers that need a shared Level-1 pipeline; the freight market has tightened, making shops busier; trade schools supply only about 10,000 candidates a year against roughly 76,500 open slots; and WIOA on-the-job-training reimbursement offsets part of training cost.
result.moat: Weak at the start, moderate at best. Reachable powers, in order: scale economies (a fixed recruiting, instructor and curriculum engine spread over more cohorts; test is cost per graduate falling from about $11k to under $7k by year 3); switching costs via enterprise master agreements with customer-specific work cards, records and conversion ledger; cornered resource (exclusive high-school, community-college and military-transition pipelines plus an instructor bench); process power only if 12-month retention beats the 35-44% turnover quoted for the trade. No counter-positioning. Likeliest end state is acquisition by a consolidator.
result.bottom_up_market: Open slots: 319,900 diesel service technicians (BLS 2024) with 19.3% unfilled (ATRI) gives about 76,500 open slots (my arithmetic). Level-1-fillable share unknown; I use 15-35%, or 11,500-26,800 slots, which is $1.1-2.6B a year at $97.8k per FTE. $100M is about 1,000 FTE: 4% of fillable slots at the 35% case, 9% at the 15% case, under the 20% heroic line. Cross-check: Fullbay's 5,000 shop locations x 54% understaffed x ~1.5 L1 slots = about 4,000 FTE or $390M, before dealers, lessor and fleet shops, and school or transit garages. Account math: 25 enterprise accounts x 24 FTE + 90 mid x 4 + 100 small x 1 = about 215 accounts and 1,060 FTE (enterprise ACV about $2.3M). Sources: ATRI, BLS, Fullbay 2026 report via FreightWaves; the fillable share and account mix are assumptions.
result.upside_assumptions: All must hold: (1) blended bill rate at or above $55 (L1 $52, tire/brake-qualified $58, night yard pods) with the L1 wage at or below $27; (2) cost per graduate at or below $6,500 via the two-weeks-classroom plus four-weeks-billed design, WIOA on-the-job-training reimbursement and about 78% completion; (3) 25 enterprise master agreements (dealer groups, lessor networks, roll-ups, tire-dealer groups, large private fleets) averaging 24 FTE, plus 90 mid accounts at 4 and 100 small at 1; (4) 12 metro hubs each graduating about 70 a year, roughly 830 graduates and 1,060 enrollees a year at maturity, recruited from adjacent $16-22 jobs; (5) 25% attrition and 35% annual conversion at $7,500; (6) year-end FTE of 25, 90, 220, 420, 650, 850, 1,000 across years 1-7 (about 98M recognized in year 7, 106M exit run-rate); (7) $15-30M total capital, no vans. Median case is conditional on clearing the 90-day gates (about 205-215 FTE by year 7). My odds of $100M: roughly 3-5% unconditional, about 10% if the gates pass. Unconditionally the median outcome is a failed pilot. Unmodeled upside: off-highway, bus and ag-equipment dealers, tuck-in acquisitions, inspector-qualified Level-2s at higher bill rates.
result.competitors_and_edge: LAUNCH TransTechs: W-2 technician staffing for bus, delivery and truck fleets, bought from TrueBlue (reason unknown); experienced techs at roughly $18-26 an hour, no entrant training. Perm recruiters (Boggs, others). General staffing firms without ASE or OEM depth. Single-employer academies: Penske (about 9,000 techs, 1,000+ Lincoln Tech hires over 10 years), Love's apprenticeship, Amerit Trailer Tech Academy (employees only), Torque by Ryder (entry mobile $23-26 an hour plus $2,000 retention bonus). Schools: UTI $835.6M FY2025 revenue across programs, about 29,800 starts, graduates 9-18 months later at student cost. Mobile and yard PM providers (Ryder, Cox, Rush, Amerit, Coltrain, Kooner) are now labor competitors and possible acquirers, not the product's rivals. Analog: Tradesmen International crossed $100M of US skilled-trades staffing revenue (SIA). Edge: a multi-employer, employer-paid, six-week program with a conversion option and a ladder to the 12-month inspector qualification, sold to buyers too small to run their own academy.
result.riskiest_assumption: Independent shops, dealers and private-fleet shops with open Level-1 work will pay a staffing-style bill rate of at least $50 an hour (about 1.85x the Level-1 wage; a 93% markup against a 35-45% skilled-trades staffing norm) for pre-trained Level-1s with a conversion option, instead of hiring direct at $24-28. Breakeven is about $47.50 an hour. I searched and found no evidence that shops or fleets buy temporary technicians at scale.
result.two_week_test: Cost under $500, one person, one metro. (1) Write a one-page offer: pre-trained Level-1 at $52 an hour, two-week minimum, 30-day replacement, $7,000 conversion after 520 hours, start in 4-6 weeks, with a non-binding order form that says plainly cohorts are not yet running. (2) Contact 40 targets: 15 independent heavy-duty shops, 10 dealer service managers, 10 private-fleet maintenance managers, 5 tire dealers with commercial service. Ask for open Level-1 requisitions and age, work turned away last month, current all-in cost of a direct hire, and a signed order form.
